emulation.c: Emulation Em`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. aemulatio: cf. F. émulation.] 1. The endeavor to equal or to excel another in qualities or actions; an assiduous striving to equal or excel another; rivalry.

emulative.c: Emulative Em"u*la*tive (?), a. Inclined to emulation; aspiring to competition; rivaling; as, an emulative person or effort. “Emulative zeal.” Hoole.

emulatively.c: Emulatively Em"u*la*tive*ly, adv. In an emulative manner; with emulation.

emulator.c: Emulator Em"u*la`tor (?), n. [L. aemulator.] One who emulates, or strives to equal or surpass.

emulatory.c: Emulatory Em"u*la*to*ry (?), a. Pertaining to emulation; connected with rivalry. [R.] “Emulatory officiousness.” Bp. Hall.

emule.c: Emule Em"ule (?), v. t. [F. émuler. See Emulate.] To emulate. [Obs.] “Emuled of many.” Spenser.

emulge.c: Emulge E*mulge" (?), v. t. [L. emulgere, emulsum; e out + mulgere to milk; akin to E. milk. See Milk.] To milk out; to drain. [Obs.] Bailey.

emulgent.c: Emulgent E*mul"gent (?), a. [L. emulgens, p. pr. of emulgere to milk out: cf. F. émulgent. So called because regarded by the ancients as straining out the serum, as if by milking, and so producing the urine.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the kidneys; renal; as, emulgent arteries and veins. -- n. An emulgent vessel, as a renal artery or vein.
Emulgent E*mul"gent, n. (Med.) A medicine that excites the flow of bile. [Obs.] Hoblyn.

emulous.c: Emulous Em"u*lous (?), a. [L. aemulus. See Emulate.] 1. Ambitiously desirous to equal or even to excel another; eager to emulate or vie with another; desirous of like excellence with another; -- with of; as, emulous of another's example or virtues.

emulously.c: Emulously Em"u*lous*ly, adv. In an emulous manner.

emulousness.c: Emulousness Em"u*lous*ness, n. The quality of being emulous.

emulsic.c: Emulsic E*mul"sic (?), a. Pertaining to, or produced from, emulsin; as, emulsic acid. Hoblyn.

emulsify.c: Emulsify E*mul"si*fy (?), v. t. [Emulsion + -fy.] To convert into an emulsion; to form an emulsion; to reduce from an oily substance to a milky fluid in which the fat globules are in a very finely divided state, giving it the semblance of solution; as, the pancreatic juice emulsifies the oily part of food.

emulsin.c: Emulsin E*mul"sin (?), n. [See Emulsion, Emulge.] (Chem.) (a) The white milky pulp or extract of bitter almonds. [R.] (b) An unorganized ferment (contained in this extract and in other vegetable juices), which effects the decomposition of certain glucosides.

emulsion.c: Emulsion E*mul"sion (?), n. [From L. emulgere, emulsum: cf. F. émulsion. See Emulge.] Any liquid preparation of a color and consistency resembling milk; as: (a) In pharmacy, an extract of seeds, or a mixture of oil and water united by a mucilaginous substance. (b) In photography, a liquid preparation of collodion holding salt of silver, used in the photographic process.

emulsive.c: Emulsive E*mul"sive (?), a. [Cf. F. émulsif.] 1. Softening; milklike.

emunctory.c: Emunctory E*munc"to*ry (?), n.; pl. Emunctories (#). [L. emunctorium a pair of snuffers, fr. emungere, emunctum, to blow the nose, hence, to wipe, cleanse; e out + mungere to blow the nose: cf. F. émonctoire, formerly spelled also émonctoire.] (Physiol.) Any organ or part of the body (as the kidneys, skin, etc.,) which serves to carry off excrementitious or waste matter.

emuscation.c: Emuscation Em`us*ca"tion (?), n. [L. emuscare to clear from moss; e out + muscus moss.] A freeing from moss. [Obs.]

emyd.c: Emyd E"myd (?), n.; pl. E. Emyds (#), E. Emyd?? (#). [See Emydea.] (Zoöl.) A fresh-water tortoise of the family Emydidæ.

emydea.c: Emydea ‖E*myd"e*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Emys a genus of tortoises, L. emys a kind of fresh-water tortoise, Gr.?.] (Zoöl.) A group of chelonians which comprises many species of fresh-water tortoises and terrapins.

en.c: En- En- (?). 1. [F. en-, L. in.] A prefix signifying in or into, used in many English words, chiefly those borrowed from the French. Some English words are written indifferently with en-or in-. For ease of pronunciation it is commonly changed to em-before p, b, and m, as in employ, embody, emmew. It is sometimes used to give a causal force, as in enable, enfeeble, to cause to be, or to make, able, or feeble; and sometimes merely gives an intensive force, as in enchasten. See In-.

-en -en. 1. A suffix from AS. -an, formerly used to form the plural of many nouns, as in ashen, eyen, oxen, all obs. except oxen. In some cases, such as children and brethren, it has been added to older plural forms.
En En (?), n. (Print.) Half an em, that is, half of the unit of space in measuring printed matter. See Em.
En bloc ‖En` bloc" (?). [F. Cf. Block, n. ] In a lump; as a whole; all together. “Movement of the ossicles en bloc.” Nature.

En passant ‖En` pas`sant" (?). [F.] In passing; in the course of any procedure; -- said specif. (Chess), of the taking of an adverse pawn which makes a first move of two squares by a pawn already so advanced as to threaten the first of these squares. The pawn which takes en passant is advanced to the threatened square.

En rapport ‖En` rap`port" (?). [F.] In accord, harmony, or sympathy; having a mutual, esp. a private, understanding; of a hypnotic subject, being in such a mental state as to be especially subject to the influence of a particular person or persons.
En route ‖En` route" (?). [F.] On the way or road.

enable.c: Enable En*a"ble (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enabled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enabling (?).] 1. To give strength or ability to; to make firm and strong. [Obs.] “Who hath enabled me.” 1 Tim. i. 12.

enablement.c: Enablement En*a"ble*ment (?), n. The act of enabling, or the state of being enabled; ability. Bacon.

enact.c: Enact En*act" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enacted; p. pr. & vb. n. Enacting.] 1. To decree; to establish by legal and authoritative act; to make into a law; especially, to perform the legislative act with reference to (a bill) which gives it the validity of law.

enactive.c: Enactive En*act"ive (?), a. Having power to enact or establish as a law. Abp. Bramhall.

enactment.c: Enactment En*act"ment (?), n. 1. The passing of a bill into a law; the giving of legislative sanction and executive approval to a bill whereby it is established as a law.

enactor.c: Enactor En*act"or (?), n. One who enacts a law; one who decrees or establishes as a law. Atterbury.

enaliosaur.c: Enaliosaur En*al"i*o*saur` (?), n. (Paleon.) One of the Enaliosauria.

enaliosauria.c: Enaliosauria ‖En*al`i*o*sau"ri*a (?), n. pl. [NL., from Gr.? marine (? in +? the sea) +? a lizard.] (Paleon.) An extinct group of marine reptiles, embracing both the Ichthyosauria and the Plesiosauria, now regarded as distinct orders.

enaliosaurian.c: Enaliosaurian En*al`i*o*sau"ri*an (?), a. (Paleon.) Pertaining to the Enaliosauria. -- n. One of the Enaliosauria.

enallage.c: Enallage ‖E*nal"la*ge (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.? an exchange, fr.? to exchange;? in +? to change.] (Gram.) A substitution, as of one part of speech for another, of one gender, number, case, person, tense, mode, or voice, of the same word, for another.

enamel.c: Enamel En*am"el (?), n. [Pref. en- + amel. See Amel, Smelt, v. t.] 1. A variety of glass, used in ornament, to cover a surface, as of metal or pottery, and admitting of after decoration in color, or used itself for inlaying or application in varied colors.
Enamel En*am"el, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enameled (?) or Enamelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Enameling or Enamelling.] 1. To lay enamel upon; to decorate with enamel whether inlaid or painted.
Enamel En*am"el (?), v. i. To practice the art of enameling.
Enamel En*am"el, a. Relating to the art of enameling; as, enamel painting. Tomlinson.

enamelar.c: Enamelar En*am"el*ar (?), a. Consisting of enamel; resembling enamel; smooth; glossy. [R.] Craig.

enameled.c: Enameled En*am"eled (?), a. Coated or adorned with enamel; having a glossy or variegated surface; glazed. [Written also enamelled.]

enamelist.c: Enamelist Enameler { En*am"el*er (?), En*am"el*ist, } n. One who enamels; a workman or artist who applies enamels in ornamental work. [Written also enameller, enamellist.]

enamor.c: Enamor En*am"or (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enamored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enamoring.] [OF. enamourer, enamorer; pref. en- (L. in) + OF. & F. amour love, L. amor. See Amour, and cf. Inamorato.] To inflame with love; to charm; to captivate; -- with of, or with, before the person or thing; as, to be enamored with a lady; to be enamored of books or science. [Written also enamour.]

enamorment.c: Enamorment En*am"or*ment (?), n. The state of being enamored. [R.]

enantiomorphous.c: Enantiomorphous E*nan`ti*o*mor"phous (?), a. [Gr. 'enanti`os opposite + morfh` form.] (Crystallog.) Similar, but not superposable, i. e., related to each other as a right-handed to a left-handed glove; -- said of certain hemihedral crystals.

enantiopathic.c: Enantiopathic E*nan`ti*o*path"ic (?), a. (Med.) Serving to palliate; palliative. Dunglison.

enantiopathy.c: Enantiopathy E*nan`ti*op"a*thy (?), n. [Gr.? of contrary properties or affections; 'enanti`os opposite +? suffering, affection, fr.?,?, to suffer.] 1. An opposite passion or affection. Sir W. Hamilton.

enantiosis.c: Enantiosis ‖E*nan`ti*o"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? contradiction, fr. 'enanti`os opposite.] (Rhet.) A figure of speech by which what is to be understood affirmatively is stated negatively, and the contrary; affirmation by contraries.

enarch.c: Enarch En*arch" (?), v. t. To arch. [Obs.] Lydgate.

enarched.c: Enarched En*arched" (?), a. (Her.) Bent into a curve; -- said of a bend or other ordinary.

enargite.c: Enargite En*ar"gite (?), n. (Min.) An iron-black mineral of metallic luster, occurring in small orthorhombic crystals, also massive. It contains sulphur, arsenic, copper, and often silver.

enarration.c: Enarration En`ar*ra"tion (?), n. [L. enarratio. See Narration.] A detailed exposition; relation. [Obs.] Hakewill.

enarthrodia.c: Enarthrodia ‖En`ar*thro"di*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? in +?. See Arthrodia.] (Anat.) See Enarthrosis. -- En`ar*thro"di*al, a.

enarthrosis.c: Enarthrosis ‖En`ar*thro"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, fr.? jointed;? in +? joint.] (Anat.) A ball and socket joint, or the kind of articulation represented by such a joint. See Articulation.

enascent.c: Enascent E*nas"cent (?), a. [L. enascens, p. pr. of enasci to spring up; e out + nasci to be born.] Coming into being; nascent. [Obs.] Bp. Warburton.

enatation.c: Enatation E`na*ta"tion (?), n. [L. enatare to swim out. See Natation.] A swimming out. [Obs.] Bailey.

enate.c: Enate E*nate" (?), a. [L. enatus, p. p. of enasci. See Enascent.] Growing out.

enation.c: Enation E*na"tion (?), n. (Bot.) Any unusual outgrowth from the surface of a thing, as of a petal; also, the capacity or act of producing such an outgrowth.

enaunter.c: Enaunter E*naun"ter (?), adv. [Pref. en- + aunter.] Lest that. [Obs.] Spenser.

enavigate.c: Enavigate E*nav"i*gate (?), v. t. [L. enavigatus, p. p. of enavigare.] To sail away or over. [Obs.] Cockeram.

enbibe.c: Enbibe En*bibe" (?), v. t. To imbibe. [Obs.] Skelton.

encage.c: Encage En*cage" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Encaged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engaging.] [Pref. en- + cage: cf. F. encager.] To confine in a cage; to coop up. Shak.

encalendar.c: Encalendar En*cal"en*dar (?), v. t. To register in a calendar; to calendar. Drayton.

encamp.c: Encamp En*camp" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Encamped (?; 215); p. pr. & vb. n. Encamping.] To form and occupy a camp; to prepare and settle in temporary habitations, as tents or huts; to halt on a march, pitch tents, or form huts, and remain for the night or for a longer time, as an army or a company traveling.
Encamp En*camp", v. t. To form into a camp; to place in a temporary habitation, or quarters.

encampment.c: Encampment En*camp"ment (?), n. 1. The act of pitching tents or forming huts, as by an army or traveling company, for temporary lodging or rest.

encapsulation.c: Encapsulation En*cap`su*la"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) The act of inclosing in a capsule; the growth of a membrane around (any part) so as to inclose it in a capsule.

encarnalize.c: Encarnalize En*car"nal*ize (?), v. t. To carnalize; to make gross. [R.] “Encarnalize their spirits.” Tennyson.

encarpus.c: Encarpus ‖En*car"pus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? containing fruit;? in +? fruit; cf. L. encarpa, pl., Gr.?.] (Arch.) An ornament on a frieze or capital, consisting of festoons of fruit, flowers, leaves, etc. [Written also encarpa.]

encase.c: Encase En*case" (?), v. t. [Cf. Enchase.] To inclose in or as if in a case. See Incase. Beau. & Fl.

encasement.c: Encasement En*case"ment (?), n. [Cf. Casement.] 1. The act of encasing; also, that which encases.

encash.c: Encash En*cash" (?), v. t. (Eng. Banking) To turn into cash; to cash. Sat. Rev.

encashment.c: Encashment En*cash"ment (?), n. (Eng. Banking) The payment in cash of a note, draft, etc.

encauma.c: Encauma En*cau"ma (?), n. [NL., from Gr.? mark caused by burning, fr.?. See Encaustic.] (Med.) An ulcer in the eye, upon the cornea, which causes the loss of the humors. Dunglison.

encaustic.c: Encaustic En*caus"tic (?), a. [L. encausticus, Gr.?, fr.? to burn in;? in +? to burn: cf. F. encaustique. See Caustic, and cf. Ink.] (Fine Arts) Prepared by means of heat; burned in.
Encaustic En*caus"tic, n. [L. encaustica, Gr.? (sc.?): cf. F. encaustique. See Encaustic, a.] The method of painting in heated wax, or in any way where heat is used to fix the colors.

encave.c: Encave En*cave" (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + cave: cf. F. encaver. Cf. Incavated.] To hide in, or as in, a cave or recess. “Do but encave yourself.” Shak.

ence.c: -ence -ence (?). [F. -ence, L. -entia.] A noun suffix signifying action, state, or quality; also, that which relates to the action or state; as in emergence, diffidence, diligence, influence, difference, excellence. See -ance.

enceinte.c: Enceinte ‖En`ceinte" (?), n. [F., fr. enceindre to gird about, surround, L. incingere; in (intens). + cingere to gird. See Cincture.] 1. (Fort.) The line of works which forms the main inclosure of a fortress or place; -- called also body of the place.
Enceinte ‖En`ceinte", a. [F., fr. L. in not + cinctus, p. p. of cingere to gird about.] Pregnant; with child.

encenia.c: Encenia ‖En*ce"ni*a (?), n. pl. [LL. encaenia, fr. Gr.? a feast of dedication;? in +? new.] A festival commemorative of the founding of a city or the consecration of a church; also, the ceremonies (as at Oxford and Cambridge, England) commemorative of founders or benefactors.

encense.c: Encense En*cense" (?), v. t. & i. [F. encenser, fr. encens. See Incense, n.] To offer incense to or upon; to burn incense. [Obs.] Chaucer.

encephalic.c: Encephalic En`ce*phal"ic (?), a. [See Encephalon.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the encephalon or brain.

encephalitis.c: Encephalitis En*ceph`a*li"tis (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'egke`falos the brain + -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the brain. -- En`ceph*a*lit"ic (#), a.

encephalocele.c: Encephalocele En*ceph"a*lo*cele (?), n. [Gr. 'egke`falos the brain + kh`lh tumor.] (Med.) Hernia of the brain.

encephaloid.c: Encephaloid En*ceph"a*loid (?), a. [Gr. 'egke`falos + -oid.] Resembling the material of the brain; cerebriform.

encephalology.c: Encephalology En*ceph`a*lol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. 'egke`falos the brain + -logy.] The science which treats of the brain, its structure and functions.

encephalon.c: encephalon en*ceph"a*lon (?), n.; pl. encephala (?). [NL. See Encephalos.] (Anat.) The contents of the cranium; the brain.

encephalopathy.c: Encephalopathy En*ceph`a*lop"a*thy (?), n. [Gr. 'egke`falos the brain + pa`schein, paqei^n, to suffer.] (Med.) Any disease or symptoms of disease referable to disorders of the brain; as, lead encephalopathy, the cerebral symptoms attending chronic lead poisoning.

encephalos.c: Encephalos En*ceph"a*los (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'egke`falos; 'en in + kefalh` head.] (Anat.) The encephalon.

encephalotomy.c: Encephalotomy En*ceph`a*lot"o*my (?), n. [Gr. 'egke`falos the brain +? a cutting.] (Surg.) The act or art of dissecting the brain.

encephalous.c: Encephalous En*ceph"a*lous (?), a. (Zoöl.) Having a head; -- said of most Mollusca; -- opposed to acephalous.

enchafe.c: Enchafe En*chafe" (?), v. t. To chafe; to enrage; to heat. [Obs.] Shak.

enchain.c: Enchain En*chain" (?), v. t. [F. enchaîner; pref. en- (L. in) chaîne chain. See Chain, and cf. Incatenation.] 1. To bind with a chain; to hold in chains.

enchainment.c: Enchainment En*chain"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. enchaînement.] The act of enchaining, or state of being enchained.

enchair.c: Enchair En*chair" (?), v. t. To seat in a chair. Tennyson.

enchannel.c: Enchannel En*chan"nel (?), v. t. To make run in a channel. “Its waters were enchanneled.” Sir D. Brewster.

enchant.c: Enchant En*chant" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enchanted; p. pr. & vb. n. Enchanting.] [F. enchanter, L. incantare to chant or utter a magic formula over or against one, to bewitch; in in, against + cantare to sing. See Chant, and cf. Incantation.] 1. To charm by sorcery; to act on by enchantment; to get control of by magical words and rites.

enchanted.c: Enchanted En*chant"ed (?), a. Under the power of enchantment; possessed or exercised by enchanters; as, an enchanted castle.

enchanter.c: Enchanter En*chant"er (?), n. [Cf. F. enchanteur.] One who enchants; a sorcerer or magician; also, one who delights as by an enchantment.

enchanting.c: Enchanting En*chant"ing, a. Having a power of enchantment; charming; fascinating. -- En*chant"ing*ly, adv.

enchantment.c: Enchantment En*chant"ment (?), n. [F. enchantement.] 1. The act of enchanting; the production of certain wonderful effects by the aid of demons, or the agency of supposed spirits; the use of magic arts, spells, or charms; incantation.

enchantress.c: Enchantress En*chant"ress (?), n. [Cf. F. enchanteresse.] A woman versed in magical arts; a sorceress; also, a woman who fascinates. Shak.

encharge.c: Encharge En*charge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Encharged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Encharging (?).] [OF. enchargier, F. encharger; pref. en- (L. in) + F. charger. See Charge.] To charge (with); to impose (a charge) upon.
Encharge En*charge", n. A charge. [Obs.] A. Copley.

enchase.c: Enchase En*chase" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enchased (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enchasing.] [F. enchâsser; pref. en- (L. in) + châsse box containing relics, frame, case, the same word as caisse case. See 1st Case, and cf. Chase, Encase, Incase.] 1. To incase or inclose in a border or rim; to surround with an ornamental casing, as a gem with gold; to encircle; to inclose; to adorn.

encheason.c: Encheason Encheson { En*che"son, En*chea"son (?) }, n. [OF. enchaison, fr. L. incidere to happen; in + cadere to fall.] Occasion, cause, or reason. [Obs.] Chaucer.

enchest.c: Enchest En*chest" (?), v. t. [Cf. Inchest.] To inclose in a chest. Vicars.

enchiridion.c: Enchiridion ‖En`chi*rid"i*on (?), n. [L., from Gr.?;? in +? hand.] Handbook; a manual of devotions. Evelyn.

enchisel.c: Enchisel En*chis"el (?), v. t. To cut with a chisel.

enchodus.c: Enchodus ‖En"cho*dus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a spear + 'odoy`s, 'odo`ntos, a tooth.] (Paleon.) A genus of extinct Cretaceous fishes; -- so named from their spear-shaped teeth. They were allied to the pike (Esox).

enchondroma.c: Enchondroma ‖En`chon*dro"ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? in +? cartilage + -oma.] (Med.) A cartilaginous tumor growing from the interior of a bone. Quain.

enchoric.c: Enchoric Enchorial { En*cho"ri*al (?), En*chor"ic (?), } a. [Gr.? domestic, native;? in +? place, country.] Belonging to, or used in, a country; native; domestic; popular; common; -- said especially of the written characters employed by the common people of ancient Egypt, in distinction from the hieroglyphics. See Demotic.

enchylemma.c: Enchylemma ‖En`chy*lem"ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? to pour in +? anything received.] (Biol.) The basal substance of the cell nucleus; a hyaline or granular substance, more or less fluid during life, in which the other parts of the nucleus are imbedded.

enchyma.c: Enchyma ‖En"chy*ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`gchyma an infusion; 'en in + chei^n to pour.] (Biol.) The primitive formative juice, from which the tissues, particularly the cellular tissue, are formed.

encircle.c: Encircle En*cir"cle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Encircled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Encircling (?).] [Pref. en- + circle: cf. OF. encercler.] To form a circle about; to inclose within a circle or ring; to surround; as, to encircle one in the arms; the army encircled the city.

encirclet.c: Encirclet En*cir"clet (?), n. [Encircle + -let.] A small circle; a ring. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

enclasp.c: Enclasp En*clasp" (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + clasp. Cf. Inclasp.] To clasp. See Inclasp.

enclave.c: Enclave En*clave" (?), n. [F., fr. L. in + clavus a nail.] A tract of land or a territory inclosed within another territory of which it is independent. See Exclave. [Recent]
Enclave En*clave", v. t. [Cf. F. enclaver.] To inclose within an alien territory. [Recent]

enclavement.c: Enclavement En*clave"ment (?), n. [F.] The state of being an enclave. [Recent]

enclitical.c: Enclitical Enclitic { En*clit"ic (ĕn*klĭt"ĭk), En*clit"ic*al (ĕn*klĭt"ĭ*kail), } a. [L. encliticus, Gr. 'egkli`tikos, fr. 'egkli`nein to incline; 'en in + kli`nein to bend. See In, and Lean, v. i.] (Gram.) Affixed; subjoined; -- said of a word or particle which leans back upon the preceding word so as to become a part of it, and to lose its own independent accent, generally varying also the accent of the preceding word.

enclitic.c: Enclitic En*clit"ic, n. (Gram.) A word which is joined to another so closely as to lose its proper accent, as the pronoun thee in prithee (pray thee).

enclitically.c: Enclitically En*clit"ic*al*ly, adv. In an enclitic manner; by throwing the accent back. Walker.

enclitics.c: Enclitics En*clit"ics (?), n. (Gram.) The art of declining and conjugating words.

encloister.c: Encloister En*clois"ter (?), v. t. [Cf. Incloister.] To shut up in a cloister; to cloister.

enclose.c: Enclose En*close" (?), v. t. [F. enclos, p. p. of enclore to enclose; pref. en- (L. in) + clore to close. See Close, and cf. Inclose, Include.] To inclose. See Inclose.

encloud.c: Encloud En*cloud" (?), v. t. [Cf. Incloud.] To envelop in clouds; to cloud. [R.] Spenser.

encoach.c: Encoach En*coach" (?), v. t. [Cf. Incoach.] To carry in a coach. [R.] Davies (Wit's Pilgr.)

encoffin.c: Encoffin En*cof"fin (?), v. t. To put in a coffin. [R.]

encolden.c: Encolden En*cold"en (?), v. t. To render cold. [Obs.]

encollar.c: Encollar En*col"lar (?), v. t. To furnish or surround with a collar. [R.]

encolure.c: Encolure ‖En`co`lure" (?), n. [F.] The neck of horse. R. Browning.

encomberment.c: Encomberment En*com"ber*ment (?), n. [See Encumberment.] Hindrance; molestation.[Obs.] Spenser.

encomiast.c: Encomiast En*co"mi*ast (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? to praise, fr.? encomium: cf. F. encomiaste. See Encomium.] One who praises; a panegyrist. Locke.

encomiastical.c: Encomiastical Encomiastic { En*co`mi*as"tic (?), En*co`mi*as"tic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?.] Bestowing praise; praising; eulogistic; laudatory; as, an encomiastic address or discourse. -- En*co`mi*as"tic*al*ly, adv.

encomiastic.c: Encomiastic En*co`mi*as"tic, n. A panegyric. B. Jonson.

encomion.c: Encomion En*co"mi*on (?), n. [NL.] Encomium; panegyric. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

encomium.c: Encomium En*co"mi*um (?), n.; pl. Encomiums (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? (a song) chanted in a Bacchic festival in praise of the god;? in +? a jovial festivity, revel. See Comedy.] Warm or high praise; panegyric; strong commendation.

encompass.c: Encompass En*com"pass (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Encompassed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Encompassing.] To circumscribe or go round so as to surround closely; to encircle; to inclose; to environ; as, a ring encompasses the finger; an army encompasses a city; a voyage encompassing the world. Shak.

encompassment.c: Encompassment En*com"pass*ment (?), n. The act of surrounding, or the state of being surrounded; circumvention.

encore.c: Encore En`core" (?), adv. or interj. [F. The last part of the word is fr. L. hora hour. See Hour.] Once more; again; -- used by the auditors and spectators of plays, concerts, and other entertainments, to call for a repetition of a particular part.
Encore En`core", n. A call or demand (as, by continued applause) for a repetition; as, the encores were numerous.
Encore En`core", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Encored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Encoring.] To call for a repetition or reappearance of; as, to encore a song or a singer.

encorporing.c: Encorporing En*cor"po*ring (?), n. [Pref. en- + L. corpus body.] Incorporation. [Obs.] Chaucer.

encoubert.c: Encoubert ‖En`cou`bert" (?), n. [F., Pg. encorberto, encuberto, lit., covered.] (Zoöl.) One of several species of armadillos of the genera Dasypus and Euphractus, having five toes both on the fore and hind feet.

encounter.c: Encounter En*coun"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Encountered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Encountering.] [OF. encontrer; pref. en- (L. in) + contre against, L. contra. See Counter, adv.] To come against face to face; to meet; to confront, either by chance, suddenly, or deliberately; especially, to meet in opposition or with hostile intent; to engage in conflict with; to oppose; to struggle with; as, to encounter a friend in traveling; two armies encounter each other; to encounter obstacles or difficulties, to encounter strong evidence of a truth.
Encounter En*coun"ter, v. i. To meet face to face; to have a meeting; to meet, esp. as enemies; to engage in combat; to fight; as, three armies encountered at Waterloo.
Encounter En*coun"ter, n. [OF. encontre, fr. encontrer. See Encounter, v. t.] 1. A meeting face to face; a running against; a sudden or incidental meeting; an interview.

encounterer.c: Encounterer En*coun"ter*er (?), n. One who encounters; an opponent; an antagonist. Atterbury.

encourage.c: Encourage En*cour"age (?; 48), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Encouraged (?; 48); p. pr. & vb. n. Encouraging (?).] [F. encourager; pref. en- (L. in) + courage courage. See Courage.] To give courage to; to inspire with courage, spirit, or hope; to raise, or to increase, the confidence of; to animate; enhearten; to incite; to help forward; -- the opposite of discourage.

encouragement.c: Encouragement En*cour"age*ment (?), n. [Cf. F. encouragement.] 1. The act of encouraging; incitement to action or to practice; as, the encouragement of youth in generosity.

encourager.c: Encourager En*cour"a*ger (?), n. One who encourages, incites, or helps forward; a favorer.

encouraging.c: Encouraging En*cour"a*ging (?), a. Furnishing ground to hope; inspiriting; favoring. -- En*cour"a*ging*ly, adv.

encowl.c: Encowl En*cowl" (?), v. t. To make a monk (or wearer of a cowl) of. [R.] Drayton.

encradle.c: Encradle En*cra"dle (?), v. t. To lay in a cradle.

encratite.c: Encratite En"cra*tite (?), n. [L. Encratitae, pl., fr. Gr.? self-disciplined;? in +? strength.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of a sect in the 2d century who abstained from marriage, wine, and animal food; -- called also Continent.

encrease.c: Encrease En*crease" (?), v. t. & i. See Increase. [Obs.]

encrimson.c: Encrimson En*crim"son (?), v. t. To give a crimson or red color to; to crimson. Shak.

encrinital.c: Encrinital Encrinal Encrinic { En*crin"ic (?), En*cri"nal (?), En*crin"i*tal (?), } a. (Paleon.) Relating to encrinites; containing encrinites, as certain kinds of limestone.

encrinite.c: Encrinite En"cri*nite (?), n. [Gr.? in +? a lily: cf. F. encrinite.] (Paleon.) A fossil crinoid, esp. one belonging to, or resembling, the genus Encrinus. Sometimes used in a general sense for any crinoid.

encrinitical.c: Encrinitical Encrinitic { En`cri*nit"ic (?), En`cri*nit"ic*al (?), } a. (Paleon.) Pertaining to encrinites; encrinal.

encrinoidea.c: Encrinoidea ‖En`cri*noid"e*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Encrinus and -oid.] (Zoöl.) That order of the Crinoidea which includes most of the living and many fossil forms, having jointed arms around the margin of the oral disk; -- also called Brachiata and Articulata. See Illusts. under Comatula and Crinoidea.

encrinus.c: Encrinus ‖En"cri*nus (?), n.; pl. Encrini (#). [NL. See Encrinite.] (Paleon.) A genus of fossil encrinoidea, from the Mesozoic rocks.

encroach.c: Encroach En*croach" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Encroached (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Encroaching.] [OF. encrochier to perch, prop., to hook, fasten a hook (perh. confused with acrochier, F. accrocher, to hook, get hold of, E. accroach); pref. en- (L. in) + F. croc hook. See Crook, and cf. Accroach.] To enter by gradual steps or by stealth into the possessions or rights of another; to trespass; to intrude; to trench; -- commonly with on or upon; as, to encroach on a neighbor; to encroach on the highway.

encroacher.c: Encroacher En*croach"er (?), n. One who by gradual steps enters on, and takes possession of, what is not his own.

encroachingly.c: Encroachingly En*croach"ing*ly, adv. By way of encroachment.

encroachment.c: Encroachment En*croach"ment (?), n. 1. The act of entering gradually or silently upon the rights or possessions of another; unlawful intrusion.

encrust.c: encrust en*crust" (?), v. t. To incrust. See Incrust.

encrustment.c: encrustment en*crust"ment (?), n. That which is formed as a crust; incrustment; incrustation.

encumber.c: Encumber En*cum"ber (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Encumbered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Encumbering.] [F. encombrer; pref. en- (L. in) + OF. combrer to hinder. See Cumber, and cf. Incumber.] [Written also incumber.] 1. To impede the motion or action of, as with a burden; to retard with something superfluous; to weigh down; to obstruct or embarrass; as, his movements were encumbered by his mantle; his mind is encumbered with useless learning.

encumbrance.c: Encumbrance En*cum"brance (?), n. [Cf. OF. encombrance. Cf. Incumbrance.] 1. That which encumbers; a burden which impedes action, or renders it difficult and laborious; a clog; an impediment. See Incumbrance.

encurtain.c: Encurtain En*cur"tain (?), v. t. To inclose with curtains.

ency.c: -ency -en*cy (?). [L. -entia.] A noun suffix having much the same meaning as -ence, but more commonly signifying the quality or state; as, emergency, efficiency. See -ancy.

encyclical.c: Encyclical Encyclic { En*cyc"lic (?), En*cyc"li*cal (?), } a. [L. encyclios of a circle, general, Gr.?;? in +? circle: cf. F. encyclique. See Cycle.] Sent to many persons or places; intended for many, or for a whole order of men; general; circular; as, an encyclical letter of a council, of a bishop, or the pope.
Encyclical Encyclic { En*cyc"lic, En*cyc"li*cal, } n. An encyclical letter, esp. one from a pope. Shipley.

encyclopaedia.c: Encyclopaedia Encyclopedia { En*cy`clo*pe"di*a, En*cy`clo*pæ"di*a } (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, for??, instruction in the circle of arts and sciences: cf. F. encyclopédie. See Cyclopedia, and Encyclical.] [Formerly written encyclopædy and encyclopedy.] The full circle of arts and sciences; a comprehensive summary of knowledge, or of a branch of knowledge; esp., a work in which the various branches of science or art are discussed separately, and usually in alphabetical order; a cyclopedia.

encyclopedian.c: Encyclopedian En*cy`clo*pe"di*an (?), a. Embracing the whole circle of learning, or a wide range of subjects.

encyclopedical.c: Encyclopedical Encyclopedic { En*cy`clo*ped"ic (?), En*cy`clo*ped"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. encyclopédique.] Pertaining to, or of the nature of, an encyclopedia; broad in scope or content; embracing a wide range of subjects; as, a person having encyclopedic knowledge of a subject. [Also spelled encyclopaedic.]

encyclopedism.c: Encyclopedism En*cy`clo*pe"dism (?), n. The art of writing or compiling encyclopedias; also, possession of the whole range of knowledge; encyclopedic learning.

encyclopedist.c: Encyclopedist En*cy`clo*pe"dist (?), n. [Cf. F. encyclopédiste.] The compiler of an encyclopedia, or one who assists in such compilation; also, one whose knowledge embraces the whole range of the sciences.

encyst.c: Encyst En*cyst" (?), v. t. To inclose in a cyst.

encysted.c: Encysted En*cyst"ed (?), a. Inclosed in a cyst, or a sac, bladder, or vesicle; as, an encysted tumor.

encystment.c: Encystment En*cyst"ment (?), n. 1. (Biol.) A process which, among some of the lower forms of life, precedes reproduction by budding, fission, spore formation, etc.

end.c: End End (ĕnd), n. [OE. & AS. ende; akin to OS. endi, D. einde, eind, OHG. enti, G. ende, Icel. endir, endi, Sw. ände, Dan. ende, Goth. andeis, Skr. anta. √208. Cf. Ante-, Anti-, Answer.] 1. The extreme or last point or part of any material thing considered lengthwise (the extremity of breadth being side); hence, extremity, in general; the concluding part; termination; close; limit; as, the end of a field, line, pole, road; the end of a year, of a discourse; put an end to pain; -- opposed to beginning, when used of anything having a first part.
End End (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ended; p. pr. & vb. n. Ending.] 1. To bring to an end or conclusion; to finish; to close; to terminate; as, to end a speech. “I shall end this strife.” Shak.
End End, v. i. To come to the ultimate point; to be finished; to come to a close; to cease; to terminate; as, a voyage ends; life ends; winter ends.
End- Endo- { En"do- (?), End- (?) }. [Gr. 'e`ndon within, fr.? in. See In.] A combining form signifying within; as, endocarp, endogen, endocuneiform, endaspidean.
End of the dictionary. Last entry: Zythum.

endable.c: Endable End"a*ble (?), a. That may be ended; terminable.

endamage.c: Endamage En*dam"age (?; 48), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Endamaged (?; 48); p. pr. & vb. n. Endamaging (?).] [Pref. en- + damage: cf. F. endommager.] To bring loss or damage to; to harm; to injure. [R.]

endamageable.c: Endamageable En*dam"age*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being damaged, or injured; damageable. [Obs.]

endamagement.c: Endamagement En*dam"age*ment (?), n. [Cf. F. endommagement.] Damage; injury; harm. [Obs.] Shak.

endamnify.c: Endamnify En*dam"ni*fy (?), v. t. To damnify; to injure. [R.] Sandys.

endanger.c: Endanger En*dan"ger (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Endangered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Endangering.] 1. To put to hazard; to bring into danger or peril; to expose to loss or injury; as, to endanger life or peace.

endark.c: Endark En*dark" (?), v. t. To darken. [Obs.] Feltham.

endaspidean.c: Endaspidean En`das*pid"e*an (?), a. [Endo- + Gr.?,?, a shield.] (Zoöl.) Having the anterior scutes extending around the tarsus on the inner side; -- said of certain birds.

endazzle.c: Endazzle En*daz"zle (?), v. t. To dazzle. [Obs.] “Endazzled eyes.” Milton.

endear.c: Endear En*dear" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Endeared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Endearing.] 1. To make dear or beloved. “To be endeared to a king.” Shak.

endearedly.c: Endearedly En*dear"ed*ly (?), adv. With affection or endearment; dearly.

endearedness.c: Endearedness En*dear"ed*ness, n. State of being endeared.

endearing.c: Endearing En*dear"ing, a. Making dear or beloved; causing love. -- En*dear"ing*ly, adv.

endearment.c: Endearment En*dear"ment (?), n. The act of endearing or the state of being endeared; also, that which manifests, excites, or increases, affection. “The great endearments of prudent and temperate speech.” Jer. Taylor.

endeavor.c: Endeavor En*deav"or (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Endeavored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Endeavoring.] [OE. endevor; pref. en- + dever, devoir, duty, F. devoir: cf. F. se mettre en devoir de faire quelque chose to try to do a thing, to go about it. See Devoir, Debt.] [Written also endeavour.] To exert physical or intellectual strength for the attainment of; to use efforts to effect; to strive to achieve or reach; to try; to attempt.
Endeavor En*deav"or, v. i. To exert one's self; to work for a certain end.
Endeavor En*deav"or, n. [Written also endeavour.] An exertion of physical or intellectual strength toward the attainment of an object; a systematic or continuous attempt; an effort; a trial.

endeavorer.c: Endeavorer En*deav"or*er (?), n. One who makes an effort or attempt. [Written also endeavourer.]

endeavorment.c: Endeavorment En*deav"or*ment (?), n. Act of endeavoring; endeavor. [Obs.] Spenser.

endecagon.c: Endecagon En*dec"a*gon (?), n. [See Hendecagon.] (Geom.) A plane figure of eleven sides and angles.

endecagynous.c: Endecagynous En`de*cag"y*nous (?), a. [Gr.? eleven +? female.] (Bot.) Having eleven pistils; as, an endecagynous flower.

endecane.c: Endecane En"de*cane (?), n. [Gr.? eleven.] (Chem.) One of the higher hydrocarbons of the paraffin series, C11H24, found as a constituent of petroleum. [Written also hendecane.]

endecaphyllous.c: Endecaphyllous En`de*caph"yl*lous (?), a. [Gr.? eleven +? leaf.] (Bot.) Composed of eleven leaflets; -- said of a leaf.

endeictic.c: Endeictic En*deic"tic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to point out, show;? in +? to show.] Serving to show or exhibit; as, an endeictic dialogue, in the Platonic philosophy, is one which exhibits a specimen of skill. Enfield.

endeixis.c: Endeixis ‖En*deix"is (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? indication. See Endeictic.] (Med.) An indication.

endemical.c: Endemical Endemic { En*de"mic (?), En*de"mic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?,?;? +? the people: cf. F. endémique.] (Med.) 1. Peculiar to a district or particular locality, or class of persons; as, an endemic disease.

endemically.c: Endemically En*dem"ic*al*ly, adv. In an endemic manner.

endemiology.c: Endemiology En*dem`i*ol"o*gy (?), n. The science which treats of endemic affections.

endenization.c: Endenization En*den`i*za"tion (?), n. The act of naturalizing. [R.]

endenizen.c: Endenizen En*den"i*zen (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + denizen. Cf. Indenizen.] To admit to the privileges of a denizen; to naturalize. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

ender.c: Ender End"er (?), n. One who, or that which, makes an end of something; as, the ender of my life.

endermic.c: Endermic En*der"mic (?), a. [Gr.? in +? skin.] (Med.) Acting through the skin, or by direct application to the skin.

endermically.c: Endermically En*der"mic*al*ly (?), adv. By the endermic method; as, applied endermically.

enderon.c: Enderon ‖En"de*ron (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? in +? skin.] (Anat.) The deep sensitive and vascular layer of the skin and mucous membranes. -- En`de*ron"ic, a.

endiaper.c: Endiaper En*di"a*per (?), v. t. [See Diaper.] To decorate with a diaper pattern.

ending.c: Ending End"ing (?), n. 1. Termination; concluding part; result; conclusion; destruction; death.

endite.c: Endite En*dite (?), v. t. See Indite. Spenser.

endive.c: Endive En"dive (?), n. [F. endive (cf. Pr., Sp. Pg., & It. endivia), fr. a deriv. of L. intibus, intybus, endive.] (Bot.) A composite herb (Cichorium Endivia). Its finely divided and much curled leaves, when blanched, are used for salad.

endless.c: Endless End"less (?), a. [AS. endeleás. See End.] 1. Without end; having no end or conclusion; perpetual; interminable; -- applied to length, and to duration; as, an endless line; endless time; endless bliss; endless praise; endless clamor.

endlessly.c: Endlessly End"less*ly, adv. In an endless manner.

endlessness.c: Endlessness End"less*ness, n. [AS. endeleásnys.] The quality of being endless; perpetuity.

endlong.c: Endlong End"long` (?; 115), adv. & prep. [Cf. Along.] Lengthwise; along. [Archaic]

endmost.c: Endmost End"most` (?), a. Farthest; remotest; at the very end. Tylor.

endoblast.c: Endoblast En"do*blast (?), n. [Endo- + -blast.] (Biol.) Entoblast; endoplast. See Nucleus,

endoblastic.c: Endoblastic En`do*blas"tic (?), a. (Biol.) Relating to the endoblast; as, the endoblastic layer.

endocardial.c: Endocardial Endocardiac { En`do*car"di*ac (?), En`do*car"di*al (?), } a. 1. Pertaining to the endocardium.

endocarditis.c: Endocarditis ‖En`do*car*di"tis (?), n. [NL. See -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the endocardium.

endocardium.c: Endocardium ‖En`do*car"di*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`ndon within + kardi`a heart.] (Anat.) The membrane lining the cavities of the heart.

endocarp.c: Endocarp En"do*carp (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? fruit: cf. F. endocarpe.] (Bot.) The inner layer of a ripened or fructified ovary.

endochondral.c: Endochondral En`do*chon"dral (?), a. [Endo- + Gr.? cartilage.] (Physiol.) Growing or developing within cartilage; -- applied esp. to developing bone.

endochrome.c: Endochrome En"do*chrome (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? color.] (Bot.) The coloring matter within the cells of plants, whether green, red, yellow, or any other color.

endoctrine.c: Endoctrine En*doc"trine (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + doctrine.] To teach; to indoctrinate. [Obs.] Donne.

endocyst.c: Endocyst En"do*cyst (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? bladder, a bag.] (Zoöl.) The inner layer of the cells of Bryozoa.

endoderm.c: Endoderm En"do*derm (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? skin.] (Biol.) (a) The inner layer of the skin or integument of an animal. (b) The innermost layer of the blastoderm and the structures derived from it; the hypoblast; the entoblast. See Illust. of Ectoderm.

endodermic.c: Endodermic Endodermal { En`do*der"mal (?), En`do*der"mic (?), } a. (Biol.) Of or pertaining to the endoderm.

endodermis.c: Endodermis ‖En`do*der"mis (?), n. [NL. See Endoderm.] (Bot.) A layer of cells forming a kind of cuticle inside of the proper cortical layer, or surrounding an individual fibrovascular bundle.

endogamous.c: Endogamous En*dog"a*mous (?), a. [Endo- + Gr.? marriage.] Marrying within the same tribe; -- opposed to exogamous.

endogamy.c: Endogamy En*dog"a*my (?), n. Marriage only within the tribe; a custom restricting a man in his choice of a wife to the tribe to which he belongs; -- opposed to exogamy.

endogen.c: Endogen En"do*gen (?), n. [Endo- + -gen: cf. F. endogène.] (Bot.) A plant which increases in size by internal growth and elongation at the summit, having the wood in the form of bundles or threads, irregularly distributed throughout the whole diameter, not forming annual layers, and with no distinct pith. The leaves of the endogens have, usually, parallel veins, their flowers are mostly in three, or some multiple of three, parts, and their embryos have but a single cotyledon, with the first leaves alternate. The endogens constitute one of the great primary classes of plants, and included all palms, true lilies, grasses, rushes, orchids, the banana, pineapple, etc. See Exogen.

endogenous.c: Endogenous En*dog"e*nous (?), a. 1. (Bot.) Increasing by internal growth and elongation at the summit, instead of externally, and having no distinction of pith, wood, and bark, as the rattan, the palm, the cornstalk.

endogeny.c: Endogeny En*dog"e*ny (?), n. [See Endogenesis.] (Biol.) Growth from within; multiplication of cells by endogenous division, as in the development of one or more cells in the interior of a parent cell.

endognath.c: Endognath En"dog*nath (ĕn"dŏg*năth), n. [Endo- + Gr. gna`qos the jaw.] (Zoöl.) The inner or principal branch of the oral appendages of Crustacea. See Maxilla.

endognathal.c: Endognathal En*dog"na*thal (?), a. (Zoöl.) Pertaining to the endognath.

endolymph.c: Endolymph En"do*lymph (?), n. [Endo- + lymph: cf. F. endolymphe.] (Anat.) The watery fluid contained in the membranous labyrinth of the internal ear.

endolymphangial.c: Endolymphangial En"do*lym*phan"gi*al (?), a. [Endo- + lymphangial.] (Anat.) Within a lymphatic vessel.

endolymphatic.c: Endolymphatic En"do*lym*phat"ic (?), a. [Endo- + lymphatic.] (Anat.) (a) Pertaining to, or containing, endolymph; as, the endolymphatic duct. (b) Within a lymphatic vessel; endolymphangial.

endome.c: Endome En*dome" (?), v. t. To cover as with a dome.

endometritis.c: Endometritis ‖En`do*me*tri"tis (?), n. [NL. See Endometrium, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the endometrium.

endometrium.c: Endometrium ‖En`do*me"tri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`ndon within + mh`tra the womb.] (Anat.) The membrane lining the inner surface of the uterus, or womb.

endomorph.c: Endomorph En"do*morph (?), n. [Endo- + Gr. morfh` form.] (Min.) A crystal of one species inclosed within one of another, as one of rutile inclosed in quartz.

endomysium.c: Endomysium ‖En`do*my"si*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`ndon within + my^s a muscle.] (Anat.) The delicate bands of connective tissue interspersed among muscular fibers.

endoneurium.c: Endoneurium ‖En`do*neu"ri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`ndon within +? a sinew, nerve.] (Anat.) The delicate bands of connective tissue among nerve fibers.

endoparasite.c: Endoparasite En`do*par"a*site (?), n. [Endo- + parasite.] (Zoöl.) Any parasite which lives in the internal organs of an animal, as the tapeworms, Trichina, etc.; -- opposed to ectoparasite. See Entozoön. -- En`do*par`a*sit"ic (#), a.

endophloeum.c: Endophloeum ‖En`do*phlœ"um (ĕn`dō*flē"ŭm), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`ndon within + floio`s bark.] (Bot.) The inner layer of the bark of trees.

endophragma.c: Endophragma ‖En`do*phrag"ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`ndon + fra`gma a fence.] (Zoöl.) A chitinous structure above the nervous cord in the thorax of certain Crustacea.

endophragmal.c: Endophragmal En`do*phrag"mal (?), a. (Zoöl.) Of or pertaining to the endophragma.

endophyllous.c: Endophyllous En*doph"yl*lous (?), a. [Endo- + Gr. fy`llon leaf.] (Bot.) Wrapped up within a leaf or sheath.

endoplasm.c: Endoplasm En"do*plasm (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? anything formed or molded.] (Biol.) The protoplasm in the interior of a cell.

endoplasma.c: Endoplasma ‖En`do*plas"ma (?), n. [NL. See Endoplasm.] (Biol.) Same as Entoplasm and Endosarc.

endoplast.c: Endoplast En"do*plast (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? to form.] (Biol.) See Nucleus.

endoplastica.c: Endoplastica ‖En`do*plas"ti*ca (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? within +? plastic.] (Zoöl.) A group of Rhizopoda having a distinct nucleus, as the amœba.

endoplastule.c: Endoplastule En`do*plas"tule (?; 135), n. [A dim. fr. endo- + Gr.? to mold.] (Biol.) See Nucleolus.

endopleura.c: Endopleura ‖En`do*pleu"ra, n. [NL., fr. Gr.? within +? rib, side. See Pleura.] (Bot.) The inner coating of a seed. See Tegmen.

endopleurite.c: Endopleurite En`do*pleu"rite (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? a rib.] (Zoöl.) The portion of each apodeme developed from the interepimeral membrane in certain crustaceans.

endopodite.c: Endopodite En*dop"o*dite (?), n. [Endo- + Gr. poy`s, podo`s, a foot.] (Zoöl.) The internal or principal branch of the locomotive appendages of Crustacea. See Maxilliped.

endorhiza.c: Endorhiza ‖En`do*rhi"za (?), n.; pl. Endorhizæ (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? within +? root.] (Bot.) Any monocotyledonous plant; -- so named because many monocotyledons have an endorhizal embryo.

endorhizous.c: Endorhizous Endorhizal { En`do*rhi"zal (?), En`do*rhi"zous (?), } a. (Bot.) Having the radicle of the embryo sheathed by the cotyledon, through which the embryo bursts in germination, as in many monocotyledonous plants.

endorse.c: Endorse En*dorse" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Endorsed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Endorsing.] [Formerly endosse, fr. F. endosser to put on the back, to endorse; pref. en- (L. in) + dos back, L. dorsum. See Dorsal, and cf. Indorse.] Same as Indorse.
Endorse En*dorse", n. (Her.) A subordinary, resembling the pale, but of one fourth its width (according to some writers, one eighth).

endorsement.c: Endorsement En*dorse"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. endossement.] Same as Indorsement.

endosarc.c: Endosarc En"do*sarc (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.?,?, flesh.] (Biol.) The semifluid, granular interior of certain unicellular organisms, as the inner layer of sarcode in the amœba; entoplasm; endoplasta.

endoscope.c: Endoscope En"do*scope (?), n. [Endo- + -scope.] (Med.) An instrument for examining the interior of the body, consisting of a flexible tube with lenses and optical fibers permitting illumination of the interior site to be inspected, and visualization of the interior site from outside the body; it often has small surgical instruments attached to the end and manipulable from the outside, permitting biopsy or surgery. It is used as a non-invasive or minimally invasive tool for diagnosis or treatment, especially in organs having an external opening such as the rectum, the urethra, and the bladder.

endoscopy.c: Endoscopy En*dos"co*py (?), n. (Med.) The art or process of examination or treatment by means of an endoscope.

endoskeletal.c: Endoskeletal En`do*skel"e*tal (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or connected with, the endoskeleton; as, endoskeletal muscles.

endoskeleton.c: Endoskeleton En`do*skel"e*ton (?), n. [Endo- + skeleton.] (Anat.) The bony, cartilaginous, or other internal framework of an animal, as distinguished from the exoskeleton.

endosmometer.c: Endosmometer En`dos*mom"e*ter (?), n. [Endosmose + -meter.] (Physics) An instrument for measuring the force or amount of endosmotic action.

endosmometric.c: Endosmometric En*dos`mo*met"ric (?), a. Pertaining to, or designed for, the measurement of endosmotic action.

endosmosis.c: Endosmosis Endosmose { En"dos*mose` (?), En`dos*mo"sis (?), } n. [NL. endosmosis, fr. Gr. 'e`ndon within +? a thrusting, impulsion, fr.? to push: cf. F. endosmose.] (Physics) The transmission of a fluid or gas from without inward in the phenomena, or by the process, of osmose.

endosmotic.c: Endosmotic En`dos*mot"ic (?), a. Pertaining to endosmose; of the nature endosmose; osmotic. Carpenter.

endosperm.c: Endosperm En"do*sperm (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? seed.] (Bot.) The albumen of a seed; -- limited by recent writers to that formed within the embryo sac.

endospermic.c: Endospermic En`do*sper"mic (?), a. (Bot.) Relating to, accompanied by, or containing, endosperm.

endospore.c: Endospore En"do*spore (?), n. [Endo- + spore.] (Bot.) The thin inner coat of certain spores.

endosporous.c: Endosporous En`do*spor"ous (?), a. (Bot.) Having the spores contained in a case; -- applied to fungi.

endoss.c: Endoss En*doss" (?; 115), v. t. [F. endosser. See Endorse.] To put upon the back or outside of anything; -- the older spelling of endorse. [Obs.] Spenser.

endosteal.c: Endosteal En*dos"te*al (?), a. (Physiol.) Relating to endostosis; as, endosteal ossification.

endosternite.c: Endosternite En`do*ster"nite (?), n. [Endo- + sternum.] (Zoöl.) The part of each apodeme derived from the intersternal membrane in Crustacea and insects.

endosteum.c: Endosteum ‖En*dos"te*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? +? a bone.] (Anat.) The layer of vascular connective tissue lining the medullary cavities of bone.

endostoma.c: Endostoma ‖En*dos"to*ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? +?,?, the mouth.] (Zoöl.) A plate which supports the labrum in certain Crustacea.

endostome.c: Endostome En"do*stome (?), n. [See Endostoma.] 1. (Bot.) The foramen or passage through the inner integument of an ovule.

endostosis.c: Endostosis En`dos*to"sis (?), n. [NL. See Endo-, and Ostosis.] (Physiol.) A process of bone formation in which ossification takes place within the substance of the cartilage.

endostyle.c: Endostyle En"do*style (?), n. [Endo- + Gr.? a pillar.] (Zoöl.) A fold of the endoderm, which projects into the blood cavity of ascidians. See Tunicata.

endotheca.c: Endotheca ‖En`do*the"ca (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'e`ndon within + qh`kh a case, box, fr.? to place.] (Zoöl.) The tissue which partially fills the interior of the interseptal chambers of most madreporarian corals. It usually consists of a series of oblique tranverse septa, one above another. -- En`do*the"cal (#), a.

endothecium.c: Endothecium ‖En`do*the"ci*um (?), n. [NL. See Endotheca.] (Bot.) The inner lining of an anther cell.

endothelial.c: Endothelial En`do*the"li*al (?), a. (Anat.) Of, or relating to, endothelium.

endothelium.c: Endothelium ‖En`do*the"li*um (?), n.; pl. Endothelia (#). [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`ndon within +? nipple.] (Anat.) The thin epithelium lining the blood vessels, lymphatics, and serous cavities. See Epithelium.

endothermic.c: Endothermic En`do*ther"mic (?), a. [Pref. endo- + thermic.] (Chem.) Designating, or pert. to, a reaction which occurs with absorption of heat; formed by such a reaction; as, an endothermic substance; -- opposed to exothermic.

endothorax.c: Endothorax En`do*tho"rax (?), n. [Endo- + thorax.] (Zoöl.) An internal process of the sternal plates in the thorax of insects.

endow.c: Endow En*dow" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Endowed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Endowing.] [OF. endouer; pref. en- (L. in) + F. douer to endow, L. dotare. See Dower, and cf. 2d Endue.] 1. To furnish with money or its equivalent, as a permanent fund for support; to make pecuniary provision for; to settle an income upon; especially, to furnish with dower; as, to endow a wife; to endow a public institution.

endower.c: Endower En*dow"er (?), v. t. [Cf. OF. endouairer. See Dower, Endow.] To endow. [Obs.] Waterhouse.

endowment.c: Endowment En*dow"ment (?), n. 1. The act of bestowing a dower, fund, or permanent provision for support.

endozoa.c: Endozoa ‖En`do*zo"a (ĕn`do*zō"ȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. 'e`ndon within + zw^,on an animal.] (Zoöl.) See Entozoa.

endrudge.c: Endrudge En*drudge" (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + drudge.] To make a drudge or slave of. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

endue.c: Endue En*due" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Endued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enduing.] [L. induere, prob. confused with E. endow. See Indue.] To invest. Latham.
Endue En*due", v. t. An older spelling of Endow. Tillotson.

enduement.c: Enduement En*due"ment (?), n. Act of enduing; induement.

endurable.c: Endurable En*dur"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. endurable. See Endure.] Capable of being endured or borne; sufferable. Macaulay. -- En*dur"a*ble*ness, n.

endurably.c: Endurably En*dur"a*bly, adv. In an endurable manner.

endurance.c: Endurance En*dur"ance (?), n. [Cf. OF. endurance. See Endure.] 1. A state or quality of lasting or duration; lastingness; continuance.

endurant.c: Endurant En*dur"ant (?), a. Capable of enduring fatigue, pain, hunger, etc.

endure.c: Endure En*dure" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Endured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enduring (?).] [F. endurer; pref. en- (L. in) + durer to last. See Dure, v. i., and cf. Indurate.] 1. To continue in the same state without perishing; to last; to remain.

Endure En*dure", v. t. 1. To remain firm under; to sustain; to undergo; to support without breaking or yielding; as, metals endure a certain degree of heat without melting; to endure wind and weather.

endurement.c: Endurement En*dure"ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. endurement.] Endurance. [Obs.] South.

endurer.c: Endurer En*dur"er (?), n. One who, or that which, endures or lasts; one who bears, suffers, or sustains.

enduring.c: Enduring En*dur"ing, a. Lasting; durable; long-suffering; as, an enduring disposition. “A better and enduring substance.” Heb. x. 34. -- En*dur"ing*ly, adv. T. Arnold. -- En*dur"ing*ness, n.

endwise.c: Endwise Endways { End"ways` (?), End"wise (?), } adv. 1. On end; erectly; in an upright position.

endyma.c: Endyma ‖En"dy*ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a garment.] (Anat.) See Ependyma.

endysis.c: Endysis ‖En"dy*sis (?), n.; pl. Endyses (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? a putting on, fr.? to put on.] (Biol.) The act of developing a new coat of hair, a new set of feathers, scales, etc.; -- opposed to ecdysis.

enecate.c: Enecate En"e*cate (?), v. t. [L. enecatus, p. p. of enecare; e out, utterly + necare to kill.] To kill off; to destroy. [Obs.] Harvey.

enema.c: Enema En"e*ma (?), n.; pl. L. Enemata (#). [L. enema, Gr.?, fr.? to send in;? in +? to send.] (Med.) An injection, or clyster, thrown into the rectum as a medicine, or to impart nourishment. Hoblyn.

enemy.c: Enemy En"e*my (?), n.; pl. Enemies (#). [OF. enemi, F. ennemi, from L. inimicus; in- (negative) + amicus friend. See Amicable.] One hostile to another; one who hates, and desires or attempts the injury of, another; a foe; an adversary; as, an enemy of or to a person; an enemy to truth, or to falsehood.

enepidermic.c: Enepidermic En*ep`i*der"mic (?), a. [Pref. en- (Gr.?) + epidermic.] (Med.) Applied to the skin without friction; -- said of medicines.

energetical.c: Energetical Energetic { En`er*get"ic (?), En`er*get"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?, fr.? to work, be active, fr.? active. See Energy.] 1. Having energy or energies; possessing a capacity for vigorous action or for exerting force; active. “A Being eternally energetic.” Grew.

energetics.c: Energetics En`er*get"ics (?), n. That branch of science which treats of the laws governing the physical or mechanical, in distinction from the vital, forces, and which comprehends the consideration and general investigation of the whole range of the forces concerned in physical phenomena. [R.]

energical.c: Energical Energic { En*er"gic (?), En*er"gic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. énergique.] 1. In a state of action; acting; operating.

energize.c: Energize En"er*gize (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Energized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Energizing (?).] [From Energy.] To use strength in action; to act or operate with force or vigor; to act in producing an effect.
Energize En"er*gize, v. t. To give strength or force to; to make active; to alacrify; as, to energize the will.

energizer.c: Energizer En"er*gi`zer (?), n. One who, or that which, gives energy, or acts in producing an effect.

energizing.c: energizing en"er*gi`zing (?), a. 1. imparting or capable of imparting vitality and energy. [wns=1]

energumen.c: Energumen En`er*gu"men (?), n. [L. energumenos, fr. Gr.? possessed by an evil spirit, from?: cf. F. énergumène. See Energetic.] (Eccl. Antiq.) One possessed by an evil spirit; a demoniac.

energy.c: Energy En"er*gy (?), n.; pl. Energies (#). [F. énergie, LL. energia, fr. Gr.?, fr.? active;? in +? work. See In, and Work.] 1. Internal or inherent power; capacity of acting, operating, or producing an effect, whether exerted or not; as, men possessing energies may suffer them to lie inactive.

enervate.c: Enervate E*ner"vate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enervated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enervating.] [L. enervatus, p. p. of enervare, fr. enervis nerveless, weak; e out + nervus nerve. See Nerve.] To deprive of nerve, force, strength, or courage; to render feeble or impotent; to make effeminate; to impair the moral powers of.
Enervate E*ner"vate (?), a. [L. enervatus, p. p.] Weakened; weak; without strength of force. Pope.

enervation.c: Enervation En`er*va"tion (?), n. [L. enervatio: cf. F. énervation.] 1. The act of weakening, or reducing strength.

enervative.c: Enervative E*ner"va*tive (?), a. Having power, or a tendency, to enervate; weakening. [R.]

enerve.c: Enerve E*nerve" (?), v. t. [Cf. F. énerver. See Enervate.] To weaken; to enervate. [Obs.] Milton.

enervous.c: Enervous E*nerv"ous (?), a. [L. enervis, enervus.] Lacking nerve or force; enervated. [R.]

enface.c: Enface En*face" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enfaced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enfacing.] [Pref. en- + face.] 1. To write or print on the face of (a draft, bill, etc.); as, to enface drafts with memoranda.

enfamish.c: Enfamish En*fam"ish (?), v. t. To famish; to starve.

enfect.c: Enfect En*fect" (?), a. [See Infect, a.] Contaminated with illegality. [Obs.] Chaucer.

enfeeble.c: Enfeeble En*fee"ble (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enfeebled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enfeebling (?).] [OF. enfeblir, enfeiblir; pref. en- (L. in) + feble, F. faible, feeble. See Feeble.] To make feeble; to deprive of strength; to reduce the strength or force of; to weaken; to debilitate.

enfeeblement.c: Enfeeblement En*fee"ble*ment (?), n. The act of weakening; enervation; weakness.

enfeebler.c: Enfeebler En*fee"bler (?), n. One who, or that which, weakens or makes feeble.

enfeeblish.c: Enfeeblish En*fee"blish, v. i. To enfeeble. [Obs.] Holland.

enfeloned.c: Enfeloned En*fel"oned (?), a. [Pref. en- + felon: cf. OF. enfelonner.] Rendered fierce or frantic. [Obs.] “Like one enfeloned or distraught.” Spenser.

enfeoff.c: Enfeoff En*feoff" (?; see Feoff, 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enfeoffed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enfeoffing.] [Pref. en- + feoff, fief: cf. LL. infeofare, OF. enfeffer, enfeofer.] 1. (Law) To give a feud, or right in land, to; to invest with a fief or fee; to invest (any one) with a freehold estate by the process of feoffment. Mozley & W.

enfeoffment.c: Enfeoffment En*feoff"ment (?), n. (Law) (a) The act of enfeoffing. (b) The instrument or deed by which one is invested with the fee of an estate.

enfester.c: Enfester En*fes"ter (?), v. t. To fester. [Obs.] “Enfestered sores.” Davies (Holy Roode).

enfetter.c: Enfetter En*fet"ter (?), v. t. To bind in fetters; to enchain. “Enfettered to her love.” Shak.

enfever.c: Enfever En*fe"ver (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + fever: cf. F. enfiévrer.] To excite fever in. [R.] A. Seward.

enfierce.c: Enfierce En*fierce" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enfierced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enfiercing (?).] To make fierce. [Obs.] Spenser.

enfilade.c: Enfilade En`fi*lade" (?; 277), n. [F., fr. enfiler to thread, go trough a street or square, rake with shot; pref. en- (L. in) + fil thread. See File a row.] 1. A line or straight passage, or the position of that which lies in a straight line. [R.]

Enfilade En`fi*lade", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enfiladed; p. pr. & vb. n. Enfilading.] (Mil.) To pierce, scour, or rake with shot in the direction of the length of, as a work, or a line of troops. Campbell.

enfiled.c: Enfiled En*filed" (?), p. a. [F. enfiler to pierce, thread.] (Her.) Having some object, as the head of a man or beast, impaled upon it; as, a sword which is said to be “enfiled of” the thing which it pierces.

enfire.c: Enfire En*fire" (?), v. t. To set on fire. [Obs.] Spenser.

enflesh.c: Enflesh En*flesh" (?), v. t. To clothe with flesh. [Obs.]

enfleurage.c: Enfleurage ‖En`fleu`rage" (?), n. [F., fr. en- (L. in) + fleur flower.] A process of extracting perfumes by exposing absorbents, as fixed oils or fats, to the exhalations of the flowers. It is used for plants whose volatile oils are too delicate to be separated by distillation.

enflower.c: Enflower En*flow"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enflowered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enflowering.] To cover or deck with flowers. [Poetic]

enfold.c: Enfold En*fold" (?), v. t. To infold. See Infold.

enfoldment.c: Enfoldment En*fold"ment (?), n. The act of infolding. See Infoldment.

enforce.c: Enforce En*force" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enforced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enforcing (?).] [OF. enforcier to strengthen, force, F. enforcir; pref. en- (L. in) + F. force. See Force.] 1. To put force upon; to force; to constrain; to compel; as, to enforce obedience to commands.
Enforce En*force (?), v. i. 1. To attempt by force. [Obs.]

enforceable.c: Enforceable En*force"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being enforced.

enforced.c: Enforced En*forced" (?), a. Compelled; forced; not voluntary. “Enforced wrong.” “Enforced smiles.” Shak. -- En*for"ced*ly, adv. Shak.

enforcement.c: Enforcement En*force"ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. enforcement.] 1. The act of enforcing; compulsion.

enforcible.c: Enforcible En*for"ci*ble (?), a. That may be enforced.

enforcive.c: Enforcive En*for"cive (?), a. Serving to enforce or constrain; compulsive. Marsion. -- En*for"cive*ly, adv.

enforest.c: Enforest En*for"est (?), v. t. To turn into a forest.

enform.c: Enform En*form" (?), v. t. [F. enformer. See Inform.] To form; to fashion. [Obs.] Spenser.

enfouldred.c: Enfouldred En*foul"dred (?), a. [Pref. en- + OF. fouldre, foldre, lightning, F. foudre, L. fulgur.] Mixed with, or emitting, lightning. [Obs.] “With foul enfouldred smoke.” Spenser.

enframe.c: Enframe En*frame" (?), v. t. To inclose, as in a frame.

enfranchise.c: Enfranchise En*fran"chise (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enfranchised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enfranchising (?).] [Pref. en- + franchise: cf. F. enfranchir.] 1. To set free; to liberate from slavery, prison, or any binding power. Bacon.

enfranchisement.c: Enfranchisement En*fran"chise*ment (?), n. 1. Releasing from slavery or custody. Shak.

enfree.c: Enfree En*free" (?), v. t. To set free. [Obs.] “The enfreed Antenor.” Shak.

enfreedom.c: Enfreedom En*free"dom (?), v. t. To set free. [Obs.] Shak.

enfreeze.c: Enfreeze En*freeze" (?), v. t. To freeze; to congeal. [Obs.]

enfroward.c: Enfroward En*fro"ward (?), v. t. To make froward, perverse, or ungovernable. [Obs.] Sir E. Sandys.

engage.c: Engage En*gage" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engaged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engaging (?).] [F. engager; pref. en- (L. in) + gage pledge, pawn. See Gage.] 1. To put under pledge; to pledge; to place under obligations to do or forbear doing something, as by a pledge, oath, or promise; to bind by contract or promise. “I to thee engaged a prince's word.” Shak.
Engage En*gage", v. i. 1. To promise or pledge one's self; to enter into an obligation; to become bound; to warrant.

engagedly.c: Engagedly En*ga"ged*ly (?), adv. With attachment; with interest; earnestly.

engagedness.c: Engagedness En*ga"ged*ness, n. The state of being deeply interested; earnestness; zeal.

engagement.c: Engagement En*gage"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. engagement.] 1. The act of engaging, pledging, enlisting, occupying, or entering into contest.

engager.c: Engager En*ga"ger (?), n. One who enters into an engagement or agreement; a surety.

engaging.c: Engaging En*ga"ging (?), a. Tending to draw the attention or affections; attractive; as, engaging manners or address. -- En*ga"ging*ly, adv. -- En*ga"ging*ness, n.

engallant.c: Engallant En*gal"lant (?), v. t. To make a gallant of. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

engaol.c: Engaol En*gaol" (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + gaol: cf. OF. engaoler, engeoler. See Gaol, and cf. Enjail.] To put in jail; to imprison. [Obs.] Shak.

engarboil.c: Engarboil En*gar"boil (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + garboil.] To throw into disorder; to disturb. [Obs.] “To engarboil the church.” Bp. Montagu.

engarland.c: Engarland En*gar"land (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + garland: cf. F. enguirlander.] To encircle with a garland, or with garlands. Sir P. Sidney.

engarrison.c: Engarrison En*gar"ri*son (?), v. t. To garrison; to put in garrison, or to protect by a garrison. Bp. Hall.

engastrimuth.c: Engastrimuth En*gas"tri*muth (?), n. [Gr.?;? in +? belly +? to speak: cf. F. engastrimythe.] An ventriloquist. [Obs.]

engender.c: Engender En*gen"der (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engendered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engendering.] [F. engender, L. ingenerare; in + generare to beget. See Generate, and cf. Ingenerate.] 1. To produce by the union of the sexes; to beget. [R.]
Engender En*gen"der, v. i. 1. To assume form; to come into existence; to be caused or produced.
Engender En*gen"der (?), n. One who, or that which, engenders.

engendrure.c: Engendrure En`gen*drure" (?), n. [OF. engendreure.] The act of generation. [Obs.] Chaucer.

engild.c: Engild En*gild" (?), v. t. To gild; to make splendent.

engine.c: Engine En"gine (ĕn"jĭn), n. [F. engin skill, machine, engine, L. ingenium natural capacity, invention; in in + the root of gignere to produce. See Genius, and cf. Ingenious, Gin a snare.] 1. Natural capacity; ability; skill. [Obs.]
Engine En"gine, v. t. 1. To assault with an engine. [Obs.]

engineer.c: Engineer En`gi*neer" (?), n. [OE. enginer: cf. OF. engignier, F. ingénieur. See Engine, n.] 1. A person skilled in the principles and practice of any branch of engineering; as, a civil engineer; an electronic engineer; a chemical engineer. See under Engineering, n.

Engineer En`gi*neer" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engineered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engineering.] 1. To lay out or construct, as an engineer; to perform the work of an engineer on; as, to engineer a road. J. Hamilton.

engineering.c: Engineering En`gi*neer"ing, n. Originally, the art of managing engines; in its modern and extended sense, the art and science by which the properties of matter are made useful to man, whether in structures, machines, chemical substances, or living organisms; the occupation and work of an engineer. In the modern sense, the application of mathematics or systematic knowledge beyond the routine skills of practise, for the design of any complex system which performs useful functions, may be considered as engineering, including such abstract tasks as designing software (software engineering).

engineman.c: Engineman En"gine*man (?), n.; pl. Enginemen (?). A man who manages, or waits on, an engine.

enginer.c: Enginer En"gin*er (?), n. [See Engineer.] A contriver; an inventor; a contriver of engines. [Obs.] Shak.

enginery.c: Enginery En"gine*ry (?), n. 1. The act or art of managing engines, or artillery. Milton.

enginesized.c: Engine-sized En"gine-sized` (?), a. Sized by a machine, and not while in the pulp; -- said of paper. Knight.

enginetype.c: Engine-type generator En"gine-type` gen"er*a`tor. (Elec.) A generator having its revolving part carried on the shaft of the driving engine.

enginous.c: Enginous En"gi*nous (?), a. [OF. engignos. See Ingenious.] 1. Pertaining to an engine. [Obs.]

engird.c: Engird En*gird" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engirded or Engirt (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engirding.] [Pref. en- + gird. Cf. Ingirt.] To gird; to encompass. Shak.

engirdle.c: Engirdle En*gir"dle (?), v. t. To surround as with a girdle; to girdle.

engirt.c: Engirt En*girt" (?), v. t. To engird. [R.] Collins.

engiscope.c: Engiscope En"gi*scope (?), n. [Gr.? near + -scope.] (Opt.) A kind of reflecting microscope. [Obs.]

englaimed.c: Englaimed En*glaimed" (?), a. [OE. engleimen to smear, gleim birdlime, glue, phlegm.] Clammy. [Obs.]

engle.c: Engle En"gle (?), n. [OE. enghle to coax or cajole. Cf. Angle a hook, one easily enticed, a gull, Ingle.] A favorite; a paramour; an ingle. [Obs.] B. Jonson.
Engle En"gle, v. t. To cajole or coax, as favorite. [Obs.]

english.c: English Eng"lish (?), a. [AS. Englisc, fr. Engle, Angle, Engles, Angles, a tribe of Germans from the southeast of Sleswick, in Denmark, who settled in Britain and gave it the name of England. Cf. Anglican.] Of or pertaining to England, or to its inhabitants, or to the present so-called Anglo-Saxon race.
English Eng"lish, n. 1. Collectively, the people of England; English people or persons.
English Eng"lish, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Englished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Englishing.] 1. To translate into the English language; to Anglicize; hence, to interpret; to explain.

englishable.c: Englishable Eng"lish*a*ble (?), a. Capable of being translated into, or expressed in, English.

englishism.c: Englishism Eng"lish*ism (?), n. 1. A quality or characteristic peculiar to the English. M. Arnold.

englishman.c: Englishman Eng"lish*man (-main), n.; pl. Englishmen (-mein). A native or a naturalized inhabitant of England.

englishry.c: Englishry Eng"lish*ry (?), n. 1. The state or privilege of being an Englishman. [Obs.] Cowell.

englishwoman.c: Englishwoman Eng"lish*wom`an (?), n.; pl. Englishwomen (?). Fem. of Englishman. Shak.

engloom.c: Engloom En*gloom" (?), v. t. To make gloomy. [R.]

englue.c: Englue En*glue" (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + glue: cf. F. engluer to smear with birdlime.] To join or close fast together, as with glue; as, a coffer well englued. Gower.

englut.c: Englut En*glut" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Englutted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Englutting (?).] [Pref. en- + glut: cf. F. engloutir.] 1. To swallow or gulp down. [Obs.] Shak.

engore.c: Engore En*gore" (?), v. t. 1. To gore; to pierce; to lacerate. [Obs.]

engorge.c: Engorge En*gorge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engorged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engorging (?).] [Pref. en- + gorge: cf. F. engorger to obstruct, cram.] 1. To gorge; to glut. Mir. for Mag.
Engorge En*gorge", v. i. To feed with eagerness or voracity; to stuff one's self with food. Beaumont.

engorged.c: Engorged En*gorged" (?), p. a. 1. Swallowed with greediness, or in large draughts.

engorgement.c: Engorgement En*gorge"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. engorgement.] 1. The act of swallowing greedily; a devouring with voracity; a glutting.

engouled.c: Engouled En*gouled" (?), a. (Her.) Partly swallowed; disappearing in the jaws of anything; as, an infant engouled by a serpent; said also of an ordinary, when its two ends to issue from the mouths of lions, or the like; as, a bend engouled.

engoulee.c: Engoulee ‖En`gou`lée" (?), a. [F., p. p. of engouler to swallow up; pref. en- (L. in) + gueule mouth.] (Her.) Same as Engouled.

engraff.c: Engraff En*graff" (?), v. t. [See Ingraft.] To graft; to fix deeply. [Obs.]

engraft.c: Engraft En*graft" (?), v. t. See Ingraft. Shak.

engraftment.c: Engraftment Engraftation { En`graf*ta"tion (?), En*graft"ment (?), } n. The act of ingrafting; ingraftment. [R.]

engrail.c: Engrail En*grail" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engrailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engrailing.] [F. engrêler; pref. en- (L. in) + grêle hail. See Grail gravel.] 1. To variegate or spot, as with hail.
Engrail En*grail", v. i. To form an edging or border; to run in curved or indented lines. Parnell.

engrailed.c: Engrailed En*grailed" (?), a. (Her.) Indented with small concave curves, as the edge of a bordure, bend, or the like.

engrailment.c: Engrailment En*grail"ment (?), n. 1. The ring of dots round the edge of a medal, etc. Brande & C.

engrain.c: Engrain En*grain" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engrained (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engraining.] [Pref. en- + grain. Cf. Ingrain.] 1. To dye in grain, or of a fast color. See Ingrain.

engrapple.c: Engrapple En*grap"ple (?), v. t. & i. To grapple. [Obs.]

engrasp.c: Engrasp En*grasp" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engrasped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engrasping.] To grasp; to grip. [R.] Spenser.

engrave.c: Engrave En*grave", v. t. [Pref. en- + grave a tomb. Cf. Engrave to carve.] To deposit in the grave; to bury. [Obs.] “Their corses to engrave.” Spenser.
Engrave En*grave" (?), v. t. [imp. Engraved (?); p. p. Engraved or Engraven (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engraving.] [Pref. en- + grave to carve: cf. OF. engraver.] 1. To cut in; to make by incision. [Obs.]

engraved.c: Engraved En*graved" (?), a. 1. Made by engraving or ornamented with engraving.

engraver.c: Engraver En*grav"er (?), n. One who engraves; a person whose business it is to produce engraved work, especially on metal or wood.

engravery.c: Engravery En*grav"er*y (?), n. The trade or work of an engraver. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

engraving.c: Engraving En*grav"ing, n. 1. The act or art of producing upon hard material incised or raised patterns, characters, lines, and the like; especially, the art of producing such lines, etc., in the surface of metal plates or blocks of wood. Engraving is used for the decoration of the surface itself; also, for producing an original, from which a pattern or design may be printed on paper.

engregge.c: Engregge En*greg"ge (?), v. t. [OF. engregier, from (assumed) LL. ingreviare; in + (assumed) grevis heavy, for L. gravis. Cf. Aggravate.] To aggravate; to make worse; to lie heavy on. [Obs.] Chaucer.

engrieve.c: Engrieve En*grieve" (?), v. t. To grieve. [Obs.] Spenser.

engross.c: Engross En*gross" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engrossed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engrossing.] [F., fr. pref. en- (L. in) + gros gross, grosse, n., an engrossed document: cf. OF. engrossir, engroissier, to make thick, large, or gross. See Gross.] 1. To make gross, thick, or large; to thicken; to increase in bulk or quantity. [Obs.]

engrosser.c: Engrosser En*gross"er (?), n. 1. One who copies a writing in large, fair characters.

engrossment.c: Engrossment En*gross"ment (?), n. 1. The act of engrossing; as, the engrossment of a deed.

enguard.c: Enguard En*guard" (?), v. t. To surround as with a guard. [Obs.] Shak.

engulf.c: Engulf En*gulf" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Engulfed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Engulfing.] [Pref. en- + gulf: cf. OF. engolfer. Cf. Ingulf.] To absorb or swallow up as in a gulf.

engulfment.c: Engulfment En*gulf"ment (?), n. A swallowing up as if in a gulf. [R.]

enhalo.c: Enhalo En*ha"lo (?), v. t. To surround with a halo.

enhance.c: Enhance En*hance" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enhanced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enhancing (?).] [Norm. F. enhauncer, enhaucer, OF. enhaleier, enhaucier; pref. en- (L. in) + haucier to lift, raise up, from an assumed L. altiare, fr. L. altus high; cf. Pr. enansar, enanzar, to advance, exalt, and E. advance. See Altitude, and cf. Hawser.] 1. To raise or lift up; to exalt. [Obs.] Wyclif.
Enhance En*hance", v. i. To be raised up; to grow larger; as, a debt enhances rapidly by compound interest.

enhancement.c: Enhancement En*hance"ment (?), n. The act of increasing, or state of being increased; augmentation; aggravation; as, the enhancement of value, price, enjoyments, crime.

enhancer.c: Enhancer En*han"cer (?), n. One who enhances; one who, or that which, raises the amount, price, etc.

enharbor.c: Enharbor En*har"bor (?), v. t. To find harbor or safety in; to dwell in or inhabit. W. Browne.

enharden.c: Enharden En*hard"en (?), v. t. [Pref. en- + harden: cf. F. enhardir to embolden.] To harden; to embolden. [Obs.] Howell.

enharmonical.c: Enharmonical Enharmonic { En`har*mon"ic (ĕn`hȧr*mŏn"ĭk), En`har*mon"ic*al (ĕn`hȧr*mŏn"ĭ*kail), } a. [Gr. 'enarmoniko`s, 'enarmo`nios fitting, accordant; 'en in + "armoni`a harmony: cf. F. enharmonique.]

enharmonically.c: Enharmonically En`har*mon"ic*al*ly (?), adv. In the enharmonic style or system; in just intonation.

enhearten.c: Enhearten En*heart"en (?), v. t. To give heart to; to fill with courage; to embolden.

enhedge.c: Enhedge En*hedge" (?), v. t. To surround as with a hedge. [R.] Vicars.

enhort.c: Enhort En*hort" (?), v. t. [OF. enhorter, enorter, L. inhortari. Cf. Exhort.] To encourage. [Obs.] “To enhort the people.” Chaucer.

enhunger.c: Enhunger En*hun"ger (?), v. t. To make hungry.

enhydros.c: Enhydros ‖En*hy"dros (?), n. [NL. See Enhydrous.] (Min.) A variety of chalcedony containing water.

enhydrous.c: Enhydrous En*hy"drous (?), a. [Gr.?;? in +? water.] Having water within; containing fluid drops; -- said of certain crystals.

enigma.c: enigma e*nig"ma (e*nĭg"mȧ), n.; pl. enigmas (e*nĭg"mȧz). [L. aenigma, Gr. a'i`nigma, fr. a'ini`ssesqai to speak darkly, fr. a'i^nos tale, fable.] 1. A dark, obscure, or inexplicable saying; a riddle; a statement, the hidden meaning of which is to be discovered or guessed.

enigmatical.c: Enigmatical Enigmatic { E`nig*mat"ic (?; 277), E`nig*mat"ic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. énigmatique.] Relating to or resembling an enigma; not easily explained or accounted for; darkly expressed; not clear to the understanding; obscure; puzzling; as, an enigmatical answer; I didn't grasp the meaning of that enigmatical comment until much later; prophetic texts so enigmatical that their meaning has been disputed for centuries.

enigmatist.c: Enigmatist E*nig"ma*tist (?), n. [Gr.?.] One who makes, or talks in, enigmas. Addison.

enigmatize.c: Enigmatize E*nig"ma*tize (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Enigmatized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enigmatizing (?).] To make, or talk in, enigmas; to deal in riddles.

enigmatology.c: Enigmatology Enigmatography { E*nig`ma*tog"ra*phy (?), E*nig`ma*tol"o*gy (?), } n. [Gr.?,?, an enigma + -graphy, -logy.] The art of making or of solving enigmas.

enisled.c: Enisled En*isled" (?), p. a. Placed alone or apart, as if on an island; severed, as an island. [R.] “In the sea of life enisled.” M. Arnold.

enjail.c: Enjail En*jail" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enjailed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enjailing.] [Pref. en- + jail. Cf. Engaol.] To put into jail; to imprison. [R.] Donne.

enjoin.c: Enjoin En*join" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enjoined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enjoining.] [F. enjoindre, L. injungere to join into, charge, enjoin; in + jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Injunction.] 1. To lay upon, as an order or command; to give an injunction to; to direct with authority; to order; to charge.
Enjoin En*join", v. t. To join or unite. [Obs.] Hooker.

enjoinment.c: Enjoinment En*join"ment (?), n. Direction; command; authoritative admonition. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

enjoy.c: Enjoy En*joy" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Enjoyed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Enjoying.] [OF. enjoier to receive with joy; pref. en- (L. in) + OF. & F. joie joy: cf. OF. enjoir to enjoy. See Joy.] 1. To take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession or experience of; to feel or perceive with pleasure; to be delighted with; as, to enjoy the dainties of a feast; to enjoy conversation.
