epicyclical.c: epicyclical epicyclic ep`i*cyc"lic, ep`i*cyc"lic*al (?), a. Pertaining to, resembling, or having the motion of, an epicycle.

epicycloid.c: Epicycloid Ep`i*cy"cloid (?), n. [Epicycle + -oid: cf. F. épicycloïde.] (Geom.) A curve traced by a point in the circumference of a circle which rolls on the convex side of a fixed circle.

epicycloidal.c: Epicycloidal Ep`i*cy*cloid"al (?), a. Pertaining to the epicycloid, or having its properties.

epideictic.c: Epideictic Ep`i*deic"tic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to show forth, display; 'epi` +? to show. Cf. Epidictic.] Serving to show forth, explain, or exhibit; -- applied by the Greeks to a kind of oratory, which, by full amplification, seeks to persuade.

epidemical.c: Epidemical Epidemic { Ep`i*dem"ic (?), Ep`i*dem"ic*al (?), } a. [L. epidemus, Gr.?,?, among the people, epidemic;? in +? people: cf. F. épidémique. Cf. Demagogue.] 1. (Med.) Common to, or affecting at the same time, a large number in a community; -- applied to a disease which, spreading widely, attacks many persons at the same time; as, an epidemic disease; an epidemic catarrh, fever, etc. See Endemic.

epidemic.c: Epidemic Ep`i*dem"ic (?), n. [Cf. Epidemy.] 1. (Med.) An epidemic disease.

epidemically.c: Epidemically Ep`i*dem"ic*al*ly, adv. In an epidemic manner.

epidemiography.c: Epidemiography Ep`i*de`mi*og"ra*phy (?), n. [Epidemy + -graphy.] (Med.) A treatise upon, or history of, epidemic diseases.

epidemiological.c: epidemiological epidemiologic ep`i*de`mi*o*log"ic, ep`i*de`mi*o*log"ic*al (?), a. Connected with, or pertaining to, epidemiology; as, epidemiological studies.

epidemiologist.c: epidemiologist ep`i*de`mi*ol"o*gist (?), n. A person skilled in epidemiology.

epidemiology.c: epidemiology ep`i*de`mi*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Epidemy + -logy.] (Med.) That branch of medicine which studies the incidence and distribution of disease in a population, and uses such information to find the causes, modes of transmission, and methods for control of disease.

epidemy.c: Epidemy Ep"i*dem`y (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.?: cf. F. épidémie. See Epidemic.] (Med.) An epidemic disease. Dunglison.

epiderm.c: Epiderm Ep"i*derm (?), n. [Cf. F. épiderme. See Epidermis.] (Anat.) The epidermis.

epidermal.c: Epidermal Ep`i*der"mal (?), a. Of or pertaining to the epidermis; epidermic; cuticular.

epidermatoid.c: Epidermatoid Ep`i*der"ma*toid (?), a. [Gr. 'epi` upon + de`rma, -atos, skin + -oid. Cf. Epidermoid.] (Anat.) Epidermoid. Owen.

epidermic.c: Epidermic Ep`i*der"mic (?), a. [Cf. F. épidermique.] Epidermal; connected with the skin or the bark.

epidermis.c: Epidermis Ep`i*der"mis (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?;? over +? skin, fr.? to skin. See Tear, v. t.] 1. (Anat.) The outer, nonsensitive layer of the skin; cuticle; scarfskin. See Dermis.

epidermoid.c: Epidermoid Ep`i*der"moid (?), a. [Cf. F. épidermoïde.] (Anat.) Like epidermis; pertaining to the epidermis.

epidictical.c: Epidictical Epidictic { Ep`i*dic"tic (?), Ep`i*dic"tic*al (?), } a. [L. epidictius. See Epideictic.] Serving to explain; demonstrative.

epididymis.c: Epididymis ‖Ep`i*did"y*mis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?; 'epi` upon +? testicle.] (Anat.) An oblong vermiform mass on the dorsal side of the testicle, composed of numerous convolutions of the excretory duct of that organ. -- Ep`i*did"y*mal (#), a.

epididymitis.c: Epididymitis ‖Ep`i*did`y*mi"tis (?), n. [NL. See Epididymis, and -itis.] (Med.) Inflammation of the epididymis, one of the common results of gonorrhea.

epidote.c: Epidote Ep"i*dote (?), n. [Gr.? to give besides;? over +? to give: cf. F. épidote. So named from the enlargement of the base of the primary, in some of the secondary forms.] (Min.) A mineral, commonly of a yellowish green (pistachio) color, occurring granular, massive, columnar, and in monoclinic crystals. It is a silicate of alumina, lime, and oxide of iron, or manganese.

epidotic.c: Epidotic Ep`i*dot"ic (?),, a. Related to, resembling, or containing epidote; as, an epidotic granite.

epigaea.c: Epigaea ‖Ep`i*gæ"a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +? earth.] (Bot.) An American genus of plants, containing but a single species (E. repens), the trailing arbutus.

epigaeous.c: Epigaeous Ep`i*gæ"ous (?), a. [Gr.?. See Epigæa, and cf. Epigee.] (Bot.) Growing on, or close to, the ground.

epigastric.c: Epigastric Ep`i*gas"tric (?), a. [Gr.? over the belly; 'epi` upon +? belly: cf. F. épigastrique.] 1. (Anat.) Pertaining to the epigastrium, or to the epigastric region.

epigastrium.c: Epigastrium Ep`i*gas"tri*um (?), n. [NL., from Gr.?.] (Anat.) The upper part of the abdomen.

epigee.c: Epigee Ep"i*gee (?), n. [NL. epigeum, fr. Gr.? upon the earth. See Epigæa.] See Perigee. [Obs.]

epigene.c: Epigene Ep"i*gene (?), a. [Pref. epi- + Gr. gi`gnesqai to be born, grow.] 1. (Crystallog.) Foreign; unnatural; unusual; -- said of forms of crystals not natural to the substances in which they are found.

epigenesis.c: Epigenesis Ep`i*gen"e*sis (?), n. [Pref. epi- + genesis.] (Biol.) The theory of generation which holds that the germ is created entirely new, not merely expanded, by the procreative power of the parents. It is opposed to the theory of evolution, also to syngenesis.

epigenesist.c: Epigenesist Ep`i*gen"e*sist (?), n. (Biol.) One who believes in, or advocates the theory of, epigenesis.

epigenetic.c: Epigenetic Ep`i*ge*net"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the epigenesis; produced according to the theory of epigenesis.

epiglottic.c: Epiglottic Ep`i*glot"tic (?), a. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or connected with, the epiglottis.

epiglottis.c: Epiglottis Ep`i*glot"tis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?; 'epi` upon +?,?, tongue. See Glottis.] (Anat.) A cartilaginous lidlike appendage which closes the glottis while food or drink is passing while food or drink is passing through the pharynx.

epignathous.c: Epignathous E*pig"na*thous (?), a. [Epi- + Gr. gna`qos the jaw.] (Zoöl.) Hook-billed; having the upper mandible longer than the lower.

epigram.c: Epigram Ep"i*gram (?), n. [L. epigramma, fr. Gr.? inscription, epigram, fr.? to write upon, 'epi` upon +? to write: cf. F. épigramme. See Graphic.] 1. A short poem treating concisely and pointedly of a single thought or event. The modern epigram is so contrived as to surprise the reader with a witticism or ingenious turn of thought, and is often satirical in character.

epigrammatical.c: Epigrammatical Epigrammatic { Ep`i*gram*mat"ic (?), Ep`i*gram*mat"ic*al (?), }[L. epigrammaticus: cf. F. épigrammatique.] 1. Writing epigrams; dealing in epigrams; as, an epigrammatical poet.

epigrammatically.c: Epigrammatically Ep`i*gram*mat"ic*al*ly, adv. In the way of epigram; in an epigrammatic style.

epigrammatist.c: Epigrammatist Ep`i*gram"ma*tist (?), n. [L. epigrammatista: cf. F. épigrammatiste.] One who composes epigrams, or makes use of them.

epigrammatize.c: Epigrammatize Ep`i*gram"ma*tize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Epigrammatized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Epigrammatizing (?).] To represent by epigrams; to express by epigrams.

epigrammatizer.c: Epigrammatizer Ep`i*gram"ma*ti`zer (?), n. One who writes in an affectedly pointed style.

epigrammist.c: Epigrammist Ep"i*gram`mist (?), n. An epigrammatist. Jer. Taylor.

epigraph.c: Epigraph Ep"i*graph (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.?: cf. F. épigraphe. See Epigram.] 1. Any inscription set upon a building; especially, one which has to do with the building itself, its founding or dedication.

epigraphical.c: Epigraphical Epigraphic { Ep`i*graph"ic (?), Ep`i*graph"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to epigraphs or to epigraphy; as, an epigraphic style; epigraphical works or studies.

epigraphics.c: Epigraphics Ep`i*graph"ics (?), n. The science or study of epigraphs.

epigraphist.c: Epigraphist E*pig"ra*phist (?), n. A student of, or one versed in, epigraphy.

epigraphy.c: Epigraphy E*pig"ra*phy (?), n. The science of inscriptions; the art of engraving inscriptions or of deciphering them.

epigynous.c: Epigynous E*pig"y*nous (?), a. [Pref. epi- + Gr.? woman, female: cf. F. épigyne.] (Bot.) Adnate to the surface of the ovary, so as to be apparently inserted upon the top of it; -- said of stamens, petals, sepals, and also of the disk.

epihyal.c: Epihyal Ep`i*hy"al (?), n. [Pref. epi- + the Greek letter?.] (Anat.) A segment next above the ceratohyal in the hyoidean arch.

epilepsy.c: Epilepsy Ep"i*lep`sy (?), n. [L. epilepsia, Gr.? a seizure, the “falling sickness,” fr.? to take besides, seize, attack; 'epi` upon, besides +? to take: cf. F. épilepsie. Cf. Catalepsy.] (Med.) The “falling sickness,” so called because the patient falls suddenly to the ground; a disease characterized by paroxysms (or fits) occurring at interval and attended by sudden loss of consciousness, and convulsive motions of the muscles. Dunglison.

epileptic.c: Epileptic Ep`i*lep"tic (?), a. [L. epilepticus, Gr.?: cf. F. épileptique.] Pertaining to, affected with, or of the nature of, epilepsy.
Epileptic Ep`i*lep"tic, n. 1. One affected with epilepsy.

epileptogenous.c: Epileptogenous Ep`i*lep*tog"e*nous (?), a. [Gr. 'epi`lhptos epileptic + -genous.] (Med.) Producing epilepsy or epileptoid convulsions; -- applied to areas of the body or of the nervous system, stimulation of which produces convulsions.

epileptoid.c: Epileptoid Ep`i*lep"toid (?), a. [Gr. 'epi`lhptos + -oid.] (Med.) Resembling epilepsy; as, epileptoid convulsions.

epilogation.c: Epilogation Ep`i*lo*ga"tion (?), n. [LL. epilogatio.] A summing up in a brief account. [Obs.] Udall.

epilogical.c: Epilogical Epilogic { Ep`i*log"ic (?), Ep`i*log"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr. 'epilogiko`s.] Of or pertaining to an epilogue.

epilogism.c: Epilogism E*pil"o*gism (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? to reckon over, to deliver an epilogue; 'epi` upon +? to count, reckon. See Epilogue.] Enumeration; computation. [R.] J. Gregory.

epilogistic.c: Epilogistic Ep`i*lo*gis"tic (?), a. [Cf. Gr.? calculating. See Epilogism.] Of or pertaining to epilogue; of the nature of an epilogue. T. Warton.

epilogize.c: Epilogize E*pil"o*gize (?), v. i. & t. [See Epilogism.] To speak an epilogue to; to utter as an epilogue.

epilogue.c: Epilogue Ep"i*logue (?; 115), n. [F. épilogue, L. epilogus, fr. Gr.? conclusion, fr.? to say in addition; 'epi` upon, besides +? to say. See Legend.] 1. (Drama) A speech or short poem addressed to the spectators and recited by one of the actors, after the conclusion of the play.

epiloguize.c: epiloguize ep"i*lo*guize (?), v. i. & t. Same as epilogize.

epimachus.c: Epimachus ‖E*pim"a*chus (e*pĭm"ȧ*kŭs), prop. n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi`machos equipped for battle; 'epi` for + ma`chh battle.] (Zoöl.) A genus of highly ornate and brilliantly colored birds of Australia, allied to the birds of Paradise.

epimeral.c: Epimeral E*pim"er*al (?), a. (Zoöl.) Pertaining to the epimera.

epimere.c: Epimere Ep"i*mere (?), n. [Epi- + -mere.] (Biol.) One of the segments of the transverse axis, or the so called homonymous parts; as, for example, one of the several segments of the extremities in vertebrates, or one of the similar segments in plants, such as the segments of a segmented leaf. Syd. Soc. Lex.

epimeron.c: Epimeron ‖E*pim"e*ron (?), n.; pl. Epimera (#). [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +? a part.] (Zoöl.) (a) In crustaceans: The part of the side of a somite external to the basal joint of each appendage. See Illust. under Crustacea. (b) In insects: The lateral piece behind the episternum. [Written also epimerum.]

epinastic.c: Epinastic Ep`i*nas"tic (?), a. [Pref. epi- + Gr.? pressed close.] (Physiol.) A term applied to that phase of vegetable growth in which an organ grows more rapidly on its upper than on its under surface. See Hyponastic.

epineural.c: Epineural Ep`i*neu"ral (?), a. [Pref. epi- + neural.] (Anat.) Arising from the neurapophysis of a vertebra.

epineurium.c: Epineurium ‖Ep`i*neu"ri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +? a nerve.] (Anat.) The connective tissue framework and sheath of a nerve which bind together the nerve bundles, each of which has its own special sheath, or perineurium.

epinglette.c: Epinglette ‖Ep`in*glette" (?), n. [F.] (Mil.) An iron needle for piercing the cartridge of a cannon before priming.

epinicial.c: Epinicial Ep`i*ni"cial (?), a. [See Epinicion.] Relating to victory. “An epinicial song.” T. Warton.

epinicion.c: Epinicion Ep`i*ni"cion (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?, fr.? belonging to victory; 'epi` upon, to +? victory: cf. L. epinicium.] A song of triumph. [Obs.] T. Warton.

epiornis.c: Epiornis Ep`i*or"nis (?), n. [NL.: cf. F. épiornis. See Æpyornis.] (Zoöl.) One of the gigantic ostrichlike birds of the genus Æpiornis, only recently extinct. Its remains have been found in Madagascar. [Written also Æpyornis.]

epiotic.c: Epiotic Ep`i*o"tic (?), n. [Pref. epi- + Gr.?, gen.?, ear.] (Anat.) The upper and outer element of periotic bone, -- in man forming a part of the temporal bone.

epipedometry.c: Epipedometry Ep`i*pe*dom"e*try (?), n. [Gr. 'epi`pedos on the ground, level ('epi` + pe`don ground) + -metry.] (Geom.) The mensuration of figures standing on the same base. [Obs.]

epiperipheral.c: Epiperipheral Ep`i*pe*riph"er*al (?), a. [Pref. epi- + peripheral.] (Physiol.) Connected with, or having its origin upon, the external surface of the body; -- especially applied to the feelings which originate at the extremities of nerves distributed on the outer surface, as the sensation produced by touching an object with the finger; -- opposed to entoperipheral. H. Spenser.

epipetalous.c: Epipetalous Ep`i*pet"al*ous (?), a. [Pref. epi- + petal.] (Bot.) Borne on the petals or corolla.

epiphany.c: Epiphany E*piph"a*ny (?), n. [F. épiphanie, L. epiphania, Gr. 'epifa`nia (sc.?), for 'epifa`neia appearance, fr. 'epifai`nein to show forth; 'epi` + fai`nein to show. See Fancy.] 1. An appearance, or a becoming manifest.

epipharyngeal.c: Epipharyngeal Ep`i*phar`yn*ge"al (?), a. [Pref. epi- + pharyngeal.] (Anat.) Pertaining to the segments above the epibranchial in the branchial arches of fishes. -- n. An epipharyngeal bone or cartilage.

epipharynx.c: Epipharynx Ep`i*phar"ynx (?), n. [Epi- + pharynx.] (Zoöl.) A structure which overlaps the mouth of certain insects.

epiphonema.c: Epiphonema ‖Ep`i*pho*ne"ma (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. 'epifw`nhma, fr. 'epifwnei^n to mention; 'epi` + fwnei^n to speak.] (Rhet.) An exclamatory sentence, or striking reflection, which sums up or concludes a discourse.

epiphora.c: Epiphora ‖E*piph"o*ra (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. 'epifora`, fr. 'epife`rein to bring to or upon; 'epi` + fe`rein to bring.] 1. (Med.) The watery eye; a disease in which the tears accumulate in the eye, and trickle over the cheek.

epiphragm.c: Epiphragm Ep"i*phragm (?), n. [Gr.? a covering, lid, fr.? to block up.] (Zoöl.) A membranaceous or calcareous septum with which some mollusks close the aperture of the shell during the time of hibernation, or estivation.

epiphyllospermous.c: Epiphyllospermous Ep`i*phyl`lo*sper"mous (?), a. [Gr. 'epi` + fy`llon leaf + spe`rma seed.] (Bot.) Bearing fruit on the back of the leaves, as ferns. Harris (1710).

epiphyllous.c: Epiphyllous E*piph"yl*lous (?), a. [Gr. 'epi` + fy`llon leaf.] (Bot.) Growing upon, or inserted into, the leaf.

epiphyllum.c: Epiphyllum ‖Ep`i*phyl"lum (?), n. [NL.] (Bot.) A genus of cactaceous plants having flattened, jointed stems, and petals united in a tube. The flowers are very showy, and several species are in cultivation.

epiphysial.c: Epiphysial Epiphyseal { Ep`i*phys"e*al (?), Ep`i*phys"i*al (?), } (Anat.) Pertaining to, or having the nature of, an epiphysis.

epiphysis.c: Epiphysis ‖E*piph"y*sis (?), n.; pl. Epiphyses (#). [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi`fysis, fr. 'epify`ein to grow upon; 'epi` upon + fy`ein to grow.] (Anat.) (a) The end, or other superficial part, of a bone, which ossifies separately from the central portion, or diaphysis. (b) The cerebral epiphysis, or pineal gland. See Pineal gland, under Pineal.

epiphytal.c: Epiphytal E*piph"y*tal (?), a. (Bot.) Pertaining to an epiphyte.

epiphyte.c: Epiphyte Ep"i*phyte (?), n. [Gr. 'epi` upon + fyto`n plant,? to grow: cf. F. épiphyte.] 1. (Bot.) An air plant which grows on other plants, but does not derive its nourishment from them. See Air plant.

epiphytical.c: Epiphytical Epiphytic { Ep`i*phyt"ic (?), Ep`i*phyt"ic*al (?), } a. (Bot.) Pertaining to, or having the nature of, an epiphyte. -- Ep`i*phyt"ic*al*ly, adv.

epiplastron.c: Epiplastron Ep`i*plas"tron (?), n.; pl. Epiplastra (#). [Pref. epi- + plastron.] (Anat.) One of the first pair of lateral plates in the plastron of turtles.

epipleural.c: Epipleural Ep`i*pleu"ral (?), a. [Pref. epi- + pleural.] (Anat.) Arising from the pleurapophysis of a vertebra. Owen.

epiplexis.c: Epiplexis ‖Ep`i*plex"is (?), n. [L., reproof, fr. Gr.?, fr.? to strike at, reprove; 'epi` +? to strike.] (Rhet.) A figure by which a person seeks to convince and move by an elegant kind of upbraiding.

epiploce.c: Epiploce ‖E*pip"lo*ce (?), n. [L., connection, from Gr.? a plaiting together, fr.? to plait or braid in; 'epi` upon +? to twist, plait.] (Rhet.) A figure by which one striking circumstance is added, in due gradation, to another; climax; e. g., “He not only spared his enemies, but continued them in employment; not only continued, but advanced them.” Johnson.

epiploic.c: Epiploic Ep`i*plo"ic (?), a. Relating to the epiploön.

epiploon.c: Epiploon ‖E*pip"lo*ön (?), n.; pl. Epiploa (#). [NL., fr. Gr.?.] (Anat.) See Omentum.

epipodial.c: Epipodial Ep`i*po"di*al (?), a. 1. (Anat.) Pertaining to the epipodialia or the parts of the limbs to which they belong.

epipodiale.c: Epipodiale ‖Ep`i*po`di*a"le (?), n.; pl. Epipodialia (#). [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +?, dim. of?,?, foot.] (Anat.) One of the bones of either the forearm or shank, the epipodialia being the radius, ulna, tibia, and fibula.

epipodite.c: Epipodite E*pip"o*dite (?), n. [See Epipodium.] (Zoöl.) The outer branch of the legs in certain Crustacea. See Maxilliped.

epipodium.c: Epipodium ‖Ep`i*po"di*um (?), n.; pl. Epipodia (#). [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +?,?, foot.] (Zoöl.) One of the lateral lobes of the foot in certain gastropods.

epipolic.c: Epipolic Ep`i*pol"ic (?), a. (Opt.) Producing, or relating to, epipolism or fluorescence. [R.]

epipolism.c: Epipolism E*pip"o*lism (?), n. [Gr.? a surface; 'epi` + pe`lein to be.] (Opt.) See Fluorescence. [R.] Sir J. Herschel.

epipolized.c: Epipolized E*pip"o*lized (?), a. Changed to the epipolic condition, or that in which the phenomenon of fluorescence is presented; produced by fluorescence; as, epipolized light. [R.] Stokes.

epipteric.c: Epipteric Ep`ip*ter"ic (?), a. [Pref. epi- + Gr.? wing. So called because above the wing of the sphenoid.] (Anat.) Pertaining to a small Wormian bone sometimes present in the human skull between the parietal and the great wing of the sphenoid. -- n. The epipteric bone.

epipterygoid.c: Epipterygoid Ep`ip*ter"y*goid (?), a. [Pref. epi- + pterygoid.] (Anat.) Situated upon or above the pterygoid bone. -- n. An epipterygoid bone or cartilage; the columella in the skulls of many lizards.

epipubic.c: Epipubic Ep`i*pu"bic (?), a. Relating to the epipubis.

epipubis.c: Epipubis ‖Ep`i*pu"bis (?), n.; pl. Epipubes (#). [NL., epi- + pubis.] (Anat.) A cartilage or bone in front of the pubis in some amphibians and other animals.

episcopacy.c: Episcopacy E*pis"co*pa*cy (?), n. [See Episcopate.] Government of the church by bishops; church government by three distinct orders of ministers -- bishops, priests, and deacons -- of whom the bishops have an authority superior and of a different kind.

episcopal.c: Episcopal E*pis"co*pal (?), a. [L. episcopalis, fr. episcopus: cf. F. épiscopal. See Bishop.] 1. Governed by bishops; as, an episcopal church.

episcopalian.c: Episcopalian E*pis`co*pa"li*an (?), a. Pertaining to bishops, or government by bishops; episcopal; specifically, of or relating to the Protestant Episcopal Church.

Episcopalian E*pis`co*pa"li*an, n. One who belongs to an episcopal church, or adheres to the episcopal form of church government and discipline; a churchman; specifically, in the United States, a member of the Protestant Episcopal Church.

episcopalianism.c: Episcopalianism E*pis`co*pa"li*an*ism (?), n. The doctrine and usages of Episcopalians; episcopacy.

episcopally.c: Episcopally E*pis"co*pal*ly (?), adv. By episcopal authority; in an episcopal manner.

episcopate.c: Episcopate E*pis"co*pate (?), n. [L. episcopatus, fr. episcopus: cf. F. épiscopat. See Bishop.] 1. A bishopric; the office and dignity of a bishop.
Episcopate E*pis"co*pate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Episcopated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Episcopating.] To act as a bishop; to fill the office of a prelate. [Obs.]

episcopicide.c: Episcopicide E*pis"co*pi*cide (?), n. [L. episcopus bishop + caedere to kill.] The killing of a bishop.

episcopize.c: Episcopize E*pis"co*pize (?), v. t. To make a bishop of by consecration. Southey.
Episcopize E*pis"co*pize, v. i. To perform the duties of a bishop.

episcopy.c: Episcopy E*pis"co*py (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.?. See Bishop.] 1. Survey; superintendence. [Obs.] Milton.

episepalous.c: Episepalous Ep`i*sep"al*ous (?), a. [Pref. epi- + sepal.] (Bot.) Growing on the sepals or adnate to them.

episkeletal.c: Episkeletal Ep`i*skel"e*tal (?), a. [Pref. epi- + skeleletal.] (Anat.) Above or outside of the endoskeleton; epaxial.

episode.c: Episode Ep"i*sode (?), n. [Gr.? a coming in besides,? episode;? into, besides +? a coming in,? into +? way, cf. Skr. sad to go: cf. F. épisode.] (Rhet.) A separate incident, story, or action, introduced for the purpose of giving a greater variety to the events related; an incidental narrative, or digression, separable from the main subject, but naturally arising from it.

episodial.c: Episodial Ep`i*so"di*al (?), a. Pertaining to an episode; by way of episode; episodic.

episodical.c: Episodical Episodic { Ep`i*so"dic (?), Ep`i*so"dic*al (?), } a. [Cf. F. épisodique. See Episode.] Of or pertaining to an episode; adventitious. -- Ep`i*so"dic*al*ly, adv.

epispadias.c: Epispadias ‖Ep`i*spa"di*as (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +? to draw, rend.] (Med.) A deformity in which the urethra opens upon the top of the penis, instead of at its extremity.

epispastic.c: Epispastic Ep"i*spas"tic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to draw to, attract;? to +? to draw: cf. F. épispastique.] (Med.) Attracting the humors to the skin; exciting action in the skin; blistering.
Epispastic Ep"i*spas"tic, n. (Med.) An external application to the skin, which produces a puriform or serous discharge by exciting inflammation; a vesicatory.

episperm.c: Episperm Ep"i*sperm (?), n. [Pref. epi- + Gr.? seed: cf. F. épisperme.] (Bot.) The skin or coat of a seed, especially the outer coat. See Testa.

epispermic.c: Epispermic Ep`i*sper"mic (?), a. (Bot.) Pertaining, or belonging, to the episperm, or covering of a seed.

epispore.c: Epispore Ep"i*spore (?), n. [Pref. epi- + spore.] (Bot.) The thickish outer coat of certain spores.

epistaxis.c: Epistaxis ‖Ep`i*stax"is (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +? to drop.] (Med.) Bleeding at the nose.

epistemology.c: epistemology e*pis`te*mol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.? knowledge + -logy.] The theory or science of the method or grounds of knowledge.

episternal.c: Episternal Ep`i*ster"nal (?), a. (Anat. & Zoöl.) Of or pertaining to the episternum.

episternum.c: Episternum ‖Ep`i*ster"num (?), n.; pl. Episterna (#). [NL. See Epi-, and Sternum.] 1. (Anat.) (a) A median bone connected with the sternum, in many vertebrates; the interclavicle. (b) Same as Epiplastron.

epistilbite.c: Epistilbite Ep`i*stil"bite (?), n. [Pref. epi- + stilbite.] (Min.) A crystallized, transparent mineral of the Zeolite family. It is a hydrous silicate of alumina and lime.

epistle.c: Epistle E*pis"tle (?), n. [OE. epistle, epistel, AS. epistol, pistol, L. epistola, fr. Gr.? anything sent by a messenger, message, letter, fr.? to send to, tell by letter or message; 'epi` upon, to +? to dispatch, send; cf. OF. epistle, epistre, F. épître. See Stall.] 1. A writing directed or sent to a person or persons; a written communication; a letter; -- applied usually to formal, didactic, or elegant letters.
Epistle E*pis"tle, v. t. To write; to communicate in a letter or by writing. [Obs.] Milton.

epistler.c: Epistler E*pis"tler (?), n. 1. A writer of epistles, or of an epistle of the New Testament. M. Arnold.

epistolar.c: Epistolar E*pis"to*lar (?), a. Epistolary. Dr. H. More.

epistolary.c: Epistolary E*pis"to*la*ry (?), a. [L. epistolaris, fr. epistola: cf. F. épistolaire.] 1. Pertaining to epistles or letters; suitable to letters and correspondence; as, an epistolary style.

epistolean.c: Epistolean Ep`is*to"le*an (ĕp`ĭs*tō"lĕ*ain), n. One who writes epistles; a correspondent. Mary Cowden Clarke.

epistoler.c: Epistoler E*pis"to*ler (e*pĭs"to*lẽr), n. (Eccl.) One of the clergy who reads the epistle at the communion service; an epistler.

epistolet.c: Epistolet E*pis"to*let (e*pĭs"to*lĕt), n. A little epistle. Lamb.

epistolical.c: Epistolical Epistolic { Ep`is*tol"ic (?), Ep`is*tol"ic*al (?), } a. [L. epistolicus, Gr.?.] Pertaining to letters or epistles; in the form or style of letters; epistolary.

epistolize.c: Epistolize E*pis"to*lize (?), v. i. To write epistles.

epistolizer.c: Epistolizer E*pis"to*li`zer (?), n. A writer of epistles.

epistolographic.c: Epistolographic E*pis`to*lo*graph"ic (?), a. [Gr.?: cf. F. épistolographique.] Pertaining to the writing of letters; used in writing letters; epistolary.

epistolography.c: Epistolography E*pis`to*log"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr.? epistle + -graphy: cf. F. épistolographie.] The art or practice of writing epistles.

epistome.c: Epistome Epistoma { ‖E*pis"to*ma (?), Ep"i*stome (?), } n. [NL. epistoma, fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +?,?, mouth.] (Zoöl.) (a) The region between the antennæ and the mouth, in Crustacea. (b) A liplike organ that covers the mouth, in most Bryozoa. See Illust., under Entoprocta.

epistrophe.c: Epistrophe ‖E*pis"tro*phe (?), n. [L., from Gr.? a turning toward, return, fr.? to turn toward; 'epi` upon, to +? to turn.] (Rhet.) A figure in which successive clauses end with the same word or affirmation; e. g., “Are they Hebrews? so am I. Are they Israelites? so am I.” 2 Cor. xi. 22.

epistyle.c: Epistyle Ep"i*style (?), n. [L. epistylium, Gr.?; 'epi` upon +? column: cf. F. épistyle.] (Anc. Arch.) A massive piece of stone or wood laid immediately on the abacus of the capital of a column or pillar; -- now called architrave.

episyllogism.c: Episyllogism Ep`i*syl"lo*gism (?), n. [Pref. epi- + syllogism.] (Logic) A syllogism which assumes as one of its premises a proposition which was the conclusion of a preceding syllogism, called, in relation to this, the prosyllogism.

epitaph.c: Epitaph Ep"i*taph (?), n. [F. épitaphe, L. epitaphium a funeral oration, fr. Gr.?, orig. an adj., over or at a tomb; 'epi` upon +? tomb. Cf. Cenotaph.] 1. An inscription on, or at, a tomb, or a grave, in memory or commendation of the one buried there; a sepulchral inscription.
Epitaph Ep"i*taph, v. t. To commemorate by an epitaph. [R.]
Epitaph Ep"i*taph, v. i. To write or speak after the manner of an epitaph. [R.]

epitapher.c: Epitapher Ep"i*taph`er (?), n. A writer of epitaphs. Nash.

epitaphian.c: Epitaphian Epitaphial { Ep`i*taph"i*al (?), Ep`i*taph"i*an (?), } a. Relating to, or of the nature of, an epitaph.

epitaphic.c: Epitaphic Ep`i*taph"ic (?), a. Pertaining to an epitaph; epitaphian. -- n. An epitaph. Udall.

epitasis.c: Epitasis ‖E*pit"a*sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a stretching, fr.? to stretch upon or over; 'epi` upon +? to stretch.] 1. That part which embraces the main action of a play, poem, and the like, and leads on to the catastrophe; -- opposed to protasis.

epithalamic.c: Epithalamic Ep`i*tha*lam"ic (?), a. Belonging to, or designed for, an epithalamium.

epithalamium.c: Epithalamium Ep`i*tha*la"mi*um (?), n.; pl. Epithalamiums (#), L. Epithalamia (#). [L., fr. Gr.?, orig. an adj., nuptial; 'epi` upon, at +? bride chamber.] A nuptial song, or poem in honor of the bride and bridegroom.

epithalamy.c: Epithalamy Ep`i*thal"a*my (?), n.; pl. Epithalamies (?). Epithalamium. [R.] Donne.

epitheca.c: Epitheca ‖Ep`i*the"ca (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +? a case, box, fr.? to place.] (Zoöl.) A continuous and, usually, structureless layer which covers more or less of the exterior of many corals.

epithelial.c: Epithelial Ep`i*the"li*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to epithelium; as, epithelial cells; epithelial cancer.

epithelioid.c: Epithelioid Ep`i*the"li*oid (?), a. [Epithelium + -oid.] (Anat.) Like epithelium; as, epithelioid cells.

epithelioma.c: Epithelioma ‖Ep`i*the`li*o"ma (?), n. [NL. See Epithelium, and -oma.] (Med.) A malignant growth containing epithelial cells; -- called also epithelial cancer.

epithelium.c: Epithelium Ep`i*the"li*um (?), n.; pl. E. Epitheliums (#), L. Epithelia (#). [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon +? nipple.] (Anat.) The superficial layer of cells lining the alimentary canal and all its appendages, all glands and their ducts, blood vessels and lymphatics, serous cavities, etc. It often includes the epidermis (i. e., keratin-producing epithelial cells), and it is sometimes restricted to the alimentary canal, the glands and their appendages, -- the term endothelium being applied to the lining membrane of the blood vessels, lymphatics, and serous cavities.

epithem.c: Epithem Ep"i*them (?), n. [L. epithema, Gr.?, fr.? to lay or put on: cf. F. épithème. See Epithet.] (Med.) Any external topical application to the body, except ointments and plasters, as a poultice, lotion, etc.

epithema.c: Epithema ‖Ep`i*the"ma (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'epi` upon +? a case, box, fr.? to place.] (Zoöl.) A horny excrescence upon the beak of birds.

epithesis.c: Epithesis ‖E*pith"e*sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a putting on; 'epi` upon +? to place.] The addition of a letter at the end of a word, without changing its sense; as, numb for num, whilst for whiles.

epithet.c: Epithet Ep"i*thet (?), n. [L. epitheton, Gr.?, fr.? added, fr.? to add; 'epi` upon, to +? to put, place: cf. F. épithète. See Do.] 1. An adjective expressing some quality, attribute, or relation, that is properly or specially appropriate to a person or thing; as, a just man; a verdant lawn.
Epithet Ep"i*thet, v. t. To describe by an epithet. [R.]

epithetical.c: Epithetical Epithetic { Ep`i*thet"ic (?), Ep`i*thet"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.? added.] Pertaining to, or abounding with, epithets. “In epithetic measured prose.” Lloyd.

epithite.c: Epithite Ep"i*thite (?), n. [Gr.? impostor.] A lazy, worthless fellow; a vagrant. [Obs.] Mason.

epithumetical.c: Epithumetical Ep`i*thu*met"ic*al (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to long for, lust after; 'epi` + qymo`s soul, heart, desire.] Pertaining to sexual desire; sensual. Sir T. Browne.

epitithides.c: Epitithides Ep`i*tith"i*des (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? to place upon. See Epithet.] (Arch.) The uppermost member of the cornice of an entablature.

epitomator.c: Epitomator E*pit"o*ma`tor (?), n. [LL.] An epitomist. Sir W. Hamilton.

epitome.c: Epitome E*pit"o*me (?), n.; pl. Epitomes (#). [L., fr. Gr.? a surface incision, also, and abridgment, fr.? to cut into, cut short; 'epi` upon + te`mnein to cut: cf. F. épitome. See Tome.] 1. A work in which the contents of a former work are reduced within a smaller space by curtailment and condensation; a brief summary; an abridgement.

epitomist.c: Epitomist E*pit"o*mist (?), n. One who makes an epitome; one who abridges; an epitomizer. Milton.

epitomize.c: Epitomize E*pit"o*mize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Epitomized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Epitomizing.] 1. To make an epitome of; to shorten or abridge, as a writing or discourse; to reduce within a smaller space; as, to epitomize the works of Justin.

epitrite.c: Epitrite Ep"i*trite (?), n. [Gr.? containing an integer and one third (i. e.,, or in the ratio of 4 to 3); 'epi` upon, over +? the third: cf. L. epitritos, F. épitrite.] (Gr. & Lat. Pros.) A foot consisting of three long syllables and one short syllable.

epitrochlea.c: Epitrochlea ‖Ep`i*troch"le*a (?), n. [NL. See Epi-, and Trochlea.] (Anat.) A projection on the outer side of the distal end of the humerus; the external condyle.

epitrochlear.c: Epitrochlear Ep`i*troch"le*ar (?), a. Relating to the epitrochlea.

epitrochoid.c: Epitrochoid Ep`i*tro"choid (?), n. [Pref. epi- + Gr.? wheel + -oid.] (Geom.) A kind of curve. See Epicycloid, any Trochoid.

epitrope.c: Epitrope ‖E*pit"ro*pe (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.? reference, arbitration, fr.? to turn over, to give up, yield; 'epi` upon, over +? to turn.] (Rhet.) A figure by which permission is either seriously or ironically granted to some one, to do what he proposes to do; e. g., “He that is unjust, let him be unjust still.”

epizeuxis.c: Epizeuxis ‖Ep`i*zeux"is (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.? a fastening together, repetition, fr.? to fasten to or upon; 'epi` upon +? to join, yoke.] (Rhet.) A figure by which a word is repeated with vehemence or emphasis, as in the following lines: --

epizoic.c: Epizoic Ep`i*zo"ic (?), a. (Zoöl.) Living upon the exterior of another animal; ectozoic; -- said of external parasites.

epizoon.c: Epizoon ‖Ep`i*zo"ön (?), n.; pl. Epizoa (#). [NL., fr. Gr. 'epi` upon + zw^,on animal.] (Zoöl.) One of the artificial group of invertebrates of various kinds, which live parasitically upon the exterior of other animals; an ectozoön. Among them are the lice, ticks, many acari, the lerneans, or fish lice, and other crustaceans.

epizootic.c: Epizootic Ep`i*zo*öt"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. épizoötique.] 1. (Zoöl.) Of or pertaining to an epizoön.
Epizootic Epizooty { Ep`i*zo*öt"ic (?), Ep`i*zo"ö*ty (?) }, n. [F. épizoötie.] 1. A contagious disease which attacks many animals at the same time; an epizootic disease; an epidemic among animals.

epoch.c: Epoch Ep"och (ĕp"ŏk or ē"pŏk; 277), n. [LL. epocha, Gr. 'epochh` check, stop, an epoch of a star, an historical epoch, fr. 'epe`chein to hold on, check; 'epi` upon + 'e`chein to have, hold; akin to Skr. sah to overpower, Goth. sigis victory, AS. sigor, sige, G. sieg: cf. F. époque. See Scheme.] 1. A fixed point of time, established in history by the occurrence of some grand or remarkable event; a point of time marked by an event of great subsequent influence; as, the epoch of the creation; the birth of Christ was the epoch which gave rise to the Christian era.

epochal.c: Epochal Ep"o*chal (?), a. Belonging to an epoch; of the nature of an epoch. “Epochal points.” Shedd.

epode.c: Epode Ep"ode (?), n. [L. epodos, Gr.?, fr.?, adj., singing to, sung or said after, fr.? to sing to; 'epi` upon, to +? to sing: cf. F. épode. See Ode.] (Poet.) (a) The after song; the part of a lyric ode which follows the strophe and antistrophe, -- the ancient ode being divided into strophe, antistrophe, and epode. (b) A species of lyric poem, invented by Archilochus, in which a longer verse is followed by a shorter one; as, the Epodes of Horace. It does not include the elegiac distich.

epodic.c: Epodic E*pod"ic (?), a. [Gr.?.] Pertaining to, or resembling, an epode.

eponyme.c: Eponyme Eponym { Ep"o*nym, Ep"o*nyme } (?), n. [Cf. F. éponyme. See Eponymous.] 1. The hypothetical individual who is assumed as the person from whom any race, city, etc., took its name; as, Hellen is an eponym of the Hellenes.

eponymist.c: Eponymist E*pon"y*mist (?), n. One from whom a race, tribe, city, or the like, took its name; an eponym.

eponymous.c: Eponymous E*pon"y*mous (?), a. [Gr.?; 'epi` upon, to +? for? name.] Relating to an eponym; giving one's name to a tribe, people, country, and the like.

eponymy.c: Eponymy E*pon"y*my (?), n. [Gr.? a surname given after some person or thing.] The derivation of the name of a race, tribe, etc., from that of a fabulous hero, progenitor, etc.

epoophoron.c: Epoophoron ‖Ep`o*öph"o*ron (?), n. [NL., from Gr. 'epi` upon +? egg + fe`rein to bear.] (Anat.) See Parovarium.

epopoeia.c: Epopoeia Epopee { Ep"o*pee` (?), ‖Ep`o*pœ"ia (?), } n. [F. épopée, Gr.?; 'e`pos song +? to make. See Epos.] An epic poem; epic poetry.

epopt.c: Epopt Ep"opt (?), n. [Gr.? one initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries.] One instructed in the mysteries of a secret system. Carlyle.

epotation.c: Epotation Ep`o*ta"tion (?), n. [L. epotare, epotatum, to drink; e out + potare to drink.] A drinking up; a quaffing. [Obs.] Feltham.

eprouvette.c: eprouvette ‖É`prou`vette" (?), n. [F.] (Gun.) An apparatus for testing or proving the strength of gunpowder.

epsomite.c: Epsomite Ep"som*ite (?), n. Native sulphate of magnesia or Epsom salt.

epsom.c: Epsom salt Epsom salts { Ep"som salts` or Ep"som salt` (?) }. (Med.) Sulphate of magnesia having cathartic qualities; -- originally prepared by boiling down the mineral waters at Epsom, England, -- whence the name; afterwards prepared from sea water; but now from certain minerals, as from siliceous hydrate of magnesia.

epulary.c: Epulary Ep"u*la*ry (?), a. [L. epularis, fr. epulum a feast: cf. F. épulaire.] Of or pertaining to a feast or banquet. [Obs.] Smart.

epulation.c: Epulation Ep`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. epulatio.] A feasting or feast; banquet. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

epulis.c: Epulis ‖E*pu"lis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a gumboil; Gr. 'epi` upon +? gums.] (Med.) A hard tumor developed from the gums.

epulose.c: Epulose Ep"u*lose` (?), a. [L. epulum a feast.] Feasting to excess. [Obs.]

epulosity.c: Epulosity Ep`u*los"i*ty (?), n. A feasting to excess. [Obs.]

epulotic.c: Epulotic Ep`u*lot"ic (?), a. [Gr.?, fr.? to scar over or heal; 'epi` upon, over +? whole.] Promoting the skinning over or healing of sores; as, an epulotic ointment. -- n. An epulotic agent.

epuration.c: Epuration Ep`u*ra"tion (?), n. [L. e out, quite + purare to purify, purus pure.] Purification.

epure.c: epure ‖É`pure" (?), n. [F.] (Fine Arts) A draught or model from which to build; especially, one of the full size of the work to be done; a detailed drawing.

epworth.c: Epworth League Ep"worth League (?). A religious organization of Methodist young people, founded in 1889 at Cleveland, Ohio, and taking its name from John Wesley's birthplace, Epworth, Lincolnshire, England.

equability.c: Equability E`qua*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. aequabilitas, fr. aequabilis. See Equable.] The quality or condition of being equable; evenness or uniformity; as, equability of temperature; the equability of the mind.

equable.c: Equable E"qua*ble (?; 277), a. [L. aequabilis, fr. aequare to make level or equal, fr. aequus even, equal. See Equal.] 1. Equal and uniform; continuing the same at different times; -- said of motion, and the like; uniform in surface; smooth; as, an equable plain or globe.

equableness.c: Equableness E"qua*ble*ness, n. Quality or state of being equable.

equably.c: Equably E"qua*bly, adv. In an equable manner.

equal.c: Equal E"qual (?), a. [L. aequalis, fr. aequus even, equal; akin to Skr.?ka, and perh. to L. unus for older oinos one, E. one.] 1. Agreeing in quantity, size, quality, degree, value, etc.; having the same magnitude, the same value, the same degree, etc.; -- applied to number, degree, quantity, and intensity, and to any subject which admits of them; neither inferior nor superior, greater nor less, better nor worse; corresponding; alike; as, equal quantities of land, water, etc.; houses of equal size; persons of equal stature or talents; commodities of equal value.

Equal E"qual, n. 1. One not inferior or superior to another; one having the same or a similar age, rank, station, office, talents, strength, or other quality or condition; an equal quantity or number; as, “If equals be taken from equals the remainders are equal.”

Equal E"qual, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Equaled (?) or Equalled; p. pr. & vb. n. Equaling or Equalling.] 1. To be or become equal to; to have the same quantity, the same value, the same degree or rank, or the like, with; to be commen?urate with.

equalitarian.c: Equalitarian E*qual`i*ta"ri*an (?), n. One who believes in equalizing the condition of men; a leveler.

equality.c: Equality E*qual"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Equalities (#). [L. aequalitas, fr. aequalis equal. See Equal.] 1. The condition or quality of being equal; agreement in quantity or degree as compared; likeness in bulk, value, rank, properties, etc.; as, the equality of two bodies in length or thickness; an equality of rights.

equalization.c: Equalization E`qual*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of equalizing, or state of being equalized.

equalize.c: Equalize E"qual*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Equalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Equalizing (?).] [Cf. F. égaliser.] 1. To make equal; to cause to correspond, or be like, in amount or degree as compared; as, to equalize accounts, burdens, or taxes.

equalizer.c: Equalizer E"qual*i`zer (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, equalizes anything.

equally.c: Equally E"qual*ly, adv. In an equal manner or degree in equal shares or proportion; with equal and impartial justice; without difference; alike; evenly; justly; as, equally taxed, furnished, etc.

equangular.c: Equangular E*quan"gu*lar (?), a. [See Equiangular.] Having equal angles; equiangular. [R.] Johnson.

equanimity.c: Equanimity E`qua*nim"i*ty (?), n. [L. aequanimitas, fr. aequanimus: cf. F. équanimité. See Equanimous.] Evenness of mind; that calm temper or firmness of mind which is not easily elated or depressed; patience; calmness; composure; as, to bear misfortunes with equanimity.

equanimous.c: Equanimous E*quan"i*mous (?), a. [L. aequanimus, fr. aequus equal + animus mind.] Of an even, composed frame of mind; of a steady temper; not easily elated or depressed. Bp. Gauden.

equant.c: Equant E"quant (?), n. [L. aequans, -antis, p. pr. of aequare: cf. F. équant. See Equate.] (Ptolemaic Astron.) A circle around whose circumference a planet or the center of ann epicycle was conceived to move uniformly; -- called also eccentric equator.

equate.c: Equate E*quate" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Equated; p. pr. & vb. n. Equating.] [L. aequatus, p. p. of aequare to make level or equal, fr. aequus level, equal. See Equal.] To make equal; to reduce to an average; to make such an allowance or correction in as will reduce to a common standard of comparison; to reduce to mean time or motion; as, to equate payments; to equate lines of railroad for grades or curves; equated distances.

equation.c: Equation E*qua"tion (?), n. [L. aequatio an equalizing: cf. F. équation equation. See Equate.] 1. A making equal; equal division; equality; equilibrium.

equator.c: Equator E*qua"tor (?), n. [L. aequator one who equalizes: cf. F. équateur equator. See Equate.] 1. (Geog.) The imaginary great circle on the earth's surface, everywhere equally distant from the two poles, and dividing the earth's surface into two hemispheres.

equatorial.c: Equatorial E`qua*to"ri*al (?), a. [Cf. F. équatorial.] Of or pertaining to the equator; as, equatorial climates; also, pertaining to an equatorial instrument.

Equatorial E`qua*to"ri*al, n. (Astron.) An instrument consisting of a telescope so mounted as to have two axes of motion at right angles to each other, one of them parallel to the axis of the earth, and each carrying a graduated circle, the one for measuring declination, and the other right ascension, or the hour angle, so that the telescope may be directed, even in the daytime, to any star or other object whose right ascension and declination are known. The motion in right ascension is sometimes communicated by clockwork, so as to keep the object constantly in the field of the telescope. Called also an equatorial telescope.

equatorially.c: Equatorially E`qua*to"ri*al*ly, adv. So as to have motion or direction parallel to the equator.

equerry.c: Equerry Eq"uer*ry (?; 277), n.; pl. Equerries (#). [F. écurie stable, for older escurie, escuirie (confused somewhat with F. écuyer, OF. escuyer, squire), LL. scuria, OHG. skiura, sc?ra, barn, shed, G. scheuer, from a root meaning to cover, protect, and akin to L. scutum shield. See Esquire, and cf. Ecurie, Querry.] 1. A large stable or lodge for horses. Johnson.

equestrian.c: Equestrian E*ques"tri*an (?), a. [L. equester, from eques horseman, fr. equus horse: cf. F. équestre. See Equine.] 1. Of or pertaining to horses or horsemen, or to horsemanship; as, equestrian feats, or games.
Equestrian E*ques"tri*an, n. One who rides on horseback; a horseman; a rider.

equestrianism.c: Equestrianism E*ques"tri*an*ism (?), n. The art of riding on horseback; performance on horseback; horsemanship; as, feats equestrianism.

equestrienne.c: Equestrienne E*ques"tri*enne` (?), n. [Formed after analogy of the French language.] A woman skilled in equestrianism; a horsewoman.

equi.c: Equi- E"qui- (?). [L. aequus equal. See Equal.] A prefix, meaning equally; as, equidistant; equiangular.

equiangular.c: Equiangular E`qui*an"gu*lar (?), a. [Equi- + angular. Cf. Equangular.] Having equal angles; as, an equiangular figure; a square is equiangular.

equibalance.c: Equibalance E`qui*bal"ance (?), n. [Equi- + balance.] Equal weight; equiponderance.
Equibalance E`qui*bal"ance, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Equibalanced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Equibalancing (?).] To make of equal weight; to balance equally; to counterbalance; to equiponderate.

equicrescent.c: Equicrescent E`qui*cres"cent (?), a. [Equi- + crescent.] (Math.) Increasing by equal increments; as, an equicrescent variable.

equicrural.c: Equicrural E`qui*cru"ral (?), a. [L. aequicrurius; aequus equal + crus, cruris, leg.] Having equal legs or sides; isosceles. [R.] “Equicrural triangles.” Sir T. Browne.

equidifferent.c: Equidifferent E`qui*dif"fer*ent (?), a. [Equi- + different: cf. F. équidifférent.] Having equal differences; as, the terms of arithmetical progression are equidifferent.

equidistant.c: Equidistant E`qui*dis"tant (?), a. [L. aequidistans, -antis; aequus equal + distans distant: cf. F. équidistant.] Being at an equal distance from the same point or thing. -- E`qui*dis"tant*ly, adv. Sir T. Browne.

equidiurnal.c: Equidiurnal E`qui*di*ur"nal (?), a. [Equi- + diurnal.] Pertaining to the time of equal day and night; -- applied to the equinoctial line. Whewell.

equiform.c: Equiform E"qui*form (?), a. [L. aequiformis; aequus equal + forma form.] Having the same form; uniform. -- E`qui*for"mi*ty (#), n. Sir T. Browne.

equilateral.c: Equilateral E`qui*lat"er*al (?), a. [L. aequilateralis; aequus equal + latus, lateris, side: cf. F. équilatéral.] Having all the sides equal; as, an equilateral triangle; an equilateral polygon.
Equilateral E`qui*lat"er*al, n. A side exactly corresponding, or equal, to others; also, a figure of equal sides.

equilibrate.c: Equilibrate E`qui*li"brate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Equilibrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Equilibrating (?).] [L. aequilibratus in equilibrium; aequus equal + libra balance. See Equilibrium.] To balance two scales, sides, or ends; to keep even with equal weight on each side; to keep in equipoise. H. Spenser.

equilibration.c: Equilibration E`qui*li*bra"tion (?), n. 1. Act of keeping a balance, or state of being balanced; equipoise.

equilibrious.c: Equilibrious E`qui*lib"ri*ous (?), a. Evenly poised; balanced. Dr. H. More. -- E`qui*lib"ri*ous*ly, adv.

equilibrist.c: Equilibrist E*quil"i*brist (?), n. One who balances himself in unnatural positions and hazardous movements; a balancer.

equilibrity.c: Equilibrity E`qui*lib"ri*ty (?), n. [L. aequilibritas equal distribution. See Equilibrium.] The state of being balanced; equality of weight. [R.] J. Gregory.

equilibrium.c: Equilibrium E`qui*lib"ri*um (?), n.; pl. E. Equilibriums (#), L. Equilibria (#). [L. aequilibrium, fr. aequilibris in equilibrium, level; aequus equal + libra balance. See Equal, and Librate.] 1. Equality of weight or force; an equipoise or a state of rest produced by the mutual counteraction of two or more forces.

equimomental.c: Equimomental E`qui*mo*men"tal (?), a. [Equi- + momental.] (Mech.) Having equal moments of inertia.

equimultiple.c: Equimultiple E`qui*mul"ti*ple (?), a. [Equi- + multiple: cf. F. équimultiple.] Multiplied by the same number or quantity.

Equimultiple E`qui*mul"ti*ple, n. (Math.) One of the products arising from the multiplication of two or more quantities by the same number or quantity. Thus, seven times 2, or 14, and seven times 4, or 28, are equimultiples of 2 and 4.

equinal.c: Equinal E*qui"nal (?), a. See Equine. “An equinal shape.” Heywood.

equine.c: Equine E"quine (?), a. [L. equinus, fr. equus horse; akin to Gr.?, Skr. a?va, OS. ehu, AS. eh, eoh, Icel. j?r, OIr. ech, cf. Skr. a? to reach, overtake, perh. akin to E. acute, edge, eager, a. Cf. Hippopotamus.] Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a horse.

equinoctial.c: Equinoctial E`qui*noc"tial (?), a. [L. aequinoctials, fr. aequinoctium equinox: cf. F. équinoxial. See Equinox.] 1. Pertaining to an equinox, or the equinoxes, or to the time of equal day and night; as, the equinoctial line.

equinox.c: Equinox E"qui*nox (?), n. [OE. equinoxium, equenoxium, L. aequinoctium; aequus equal + nox, noctis, night: cf. F. équinoxe. See Equal, and Night.] 1. The time when the sun enters one of the equinoctial points, that is, about March 21 and September 22. See Autumnal equinox, Vernal equinox, under Autumnal and Vernal.

equinumerant.c: Equinumerant E`qui*nu"mer*ant (?), a. [Equi- + L. numerans, p. pr. of numerare to number.] Equal as to number. [Obs.] Arbuthnot.

equip.c: Equip E*quip" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Equipped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Equipping.] [F. équiper to supply, fit out, orig. said of a ship, OF. esquiper to embark; of German origin; cf. OHG. scif, G. schiff, Icel. skip, AS. scip. See Ship.] 1. To furnish for service, or against a need or exigency; to fit out; to supply with whatever is necessary to efficient action in any way; to provide with arms or an armament, stores, munitions, rigging, etc.; -- said esp. of ships and of troops. Dryden.

equipage.c: Equipage Eq"ui*page (?; 48), n. [F. équipage, fr. équiper. See Equip.] 1. Furniture or outfit, whether useful or ornamental; especially, the furniture and supplies of a vessel, fitting her for a voyage or for warlike purposes, or the furniture and necessaries of an army, a body of troops, or a single soldier, including whatever is necessary for efficient service; equipments; accouterments; habiliments; attire.

equiparable.c: Equiparable E*quip"a*ra*ble (?) a. [L. aequiparabilis.] Comparable. [Obs. or R.]

equiparate.c: Equiparate E*quip"a*rate (?) v. t. [L. aequiparatus, p. p. of aequiparare.] To compare. [R.]

equipedal.c: Equipedal E*quip"e*dal (?), a. [Equi- + L. pes, pedis, foot.] (Zoöl.) Equal-footed; having the pairs of feet equal.

equipendency.c: Equipendency E`qui*pend"en*cy (?), n. [Equi- + pendency.] The act or condition of hanging in equipoise; not inclined or determined either way. South.

equipensate.c: Equipensate E`qui*pen"sate (?), v. t. [Equi- + pensatus, p. p. of pensare to weigh. Cf. Equipoise.] To weigh equally; to esteem alike. [Obs.]

equipment.c: Equipment E*quip"ment (?), n. [Cf. F. équipement. See Equip.] 1. The act of equipping, or the state of being equipped, as for a voyage or expedition. Burke.

equipoise.c: Equipoise E"qui*poise (?), n. [Equi- + poise.] 1. Equality of weight or force; hence, equilibrium; a state in which the two ends or sides of a thing are balanced, and hence equal; state of being equally balanced; -- said of moral, political, or social interests or forces.

equipollency.c: Equipollency Equipollence { E`qui*pol"lence (?), E`qui*pol"len*cy (?) }, n. [Cf. F. équipollence. See Equipollent.] 1. Equality of power, force, signification, or application. Boyle.

equipollent.c: Equipollent E`qui*pol"lent (?), a. [L. aequipollens; aequus equal + pollens, -entis, p. pr. of pollere to be strong, able: cf. F. équipollent.] 1. Having equal power or force; equivalent. Bacon.

equipollently.c: Equipollently E`qui*pol"lent*ly, adv. With equal power. Barrow.

equiponderancy.c: Equiponderancy Equiponderance { E`qui*pon"der*ance (?), E`qui*pon"der*an*cy (?) }, n. [Equi- + ponderance: cf. F. équipondérance.] Equality of weight; equipoise.

equiponderant.c: Equiponderant E`qui*pon"der*ant (?), a. [Cf. F. équipondérant.] Being of the same weight.

equiponderate.c: Equiponderate E`qui*pon"der*ate (?), v. i. [Equi- + L. ponderare to weigh. See Ponderate.] To be equal in weight; to weigh as much as another thing. Bp. Wilkins.
Equiponderate E`qui*pon"der*ate, v. t. To make equal in weight; to counterbalance. “More than equiponderated the declension in that direction.” De Quincey.

equiponderous.c: Equiponderous E`qui*pon"der*ous (?), a. [Equi- + L. pondus, ponderis, weight.] Having equal weight. Bailey.

equipondious.c: Equipondious E`qui*pon"di*ous (?), a. [L. aequipondium an equal weight; aequus equal + pondus weight.] Of equal weight on both sides; balanced. [Obs.] Glanvill.

equipotential.c: Equipotential E`qui*po*ten"tial (?), a. [Equi- + potential.] (Mech. & Physics) Having the same potential.

equiradical.c: Equiradical E`qui*rad"i*cal (?) a. [Equi- + radical.] Equally radical. [R.] Coleridge.

equirotal.c: Equirotal E`qui*ro"tal (?), a. [Equi- + L. rota wheel.] Having wheels of the same size or diameter; having equal rotation. [R.]

equisetaceous.c: Equisetaceous E`qui*se*ta"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Belonging to the Equisetaceæ, or Horsetail family.

equisetiform.c: Equisetiform E`qui*set"i*form (?), a. [Equisetum- + -form.] (Bot.) Having the form of the equisetum.

equisetum.c: Equisetum ‖Eq`ui*se"tum (?), n.; pl. Equiseta (#). [L., the horsetail, fr. equus horse + seta a thick,, stiff hair, bristle.] (Bot.) A genus of vascular, cryptogamic, herbaceous plants; -- also called horsetails.

equisonance.c: Equisonance E*quis"o*nance (?), n. [Equi- + L. sonans, p. pr. of sonare to sound: cf. F. équisonnance. See Sonant.] (Mus.) An equal sounding; the consonance of the unison and its octaves.

equisonant.c: Equisonant E*quis"o*nant (?) a. Of the same or like sound.

equitable.c: Equitable Eq"ui*ta*ble (?), a. [F. équitable, from équité. See Equity.] 1. Possessing or exhibiting equity; according to natural right or natural justice; marked by a due consideration for what is fair, unbiased, or impartial; just; as, an equitable decision; an equitable distribution of an estate; equitable men.

equitableness.c: Equitableness Eq"ui*ta*ble*ness, n. The quality of being equitable, just, or impartial; as, the equitableness of a judge, a decision, or distribution of property.

equitably.c: Equitably Eq"ui*ta*bly, adv. In an equitable manner; justly; as, the laws should be equitably administered.

equitancy.c: Equitancy Eq"ui*tan*cy (?), n. [Cf. LL. equitantia. See Equitant.] Horsemanship.

equitant.c: Equitant Eq"ui*tant (?), a. [L. equitans, -antis, p. pr. of equitare to ride, fr. eques horseman, fr. equus horse.] 1. Mounted on, or sitting upon, a horse; riding on horseback.

equitation.c: Equitation Eq`ui*ta"tion (?), n. [L. equitatio, fr. equitare: cf. F. équitation.] A riding, or the act of riding, on horseback; horsemanship.

equitemporaneous.c: Equitemporaneous E`qui*tem`po*ra"ne*ous (?), a. [L. aequus equal + tempus, temporis, time.] Contemporaneous. [Obs.] Boyle.

equites.c: Equites ‖Eq"ui*tes (?) n. pl [L., pl. of eques a horseman.] (Rom. Antiq.) An order of knights holding a middle place between the senate and the commonalty; members of the Roman equestrian order.

equity.c: Equity Eq"ui*ty (?), n.; pl. Equities (#). [F. équité, L. aequitas, fr. aequus even, equal. See Equal.] 1. Equality of rights; natural justice or right; the giving, or desiring to give, to each man his due, according to reason, and the law of God to man; fairness in determination of conflicting claims; impartiality.

equivalence.c: Equivalence E*quiv"a*lence (e*kwĭv"ȧ*leins), n. [Cf. F. équivalence, LL. aequivalentia.] 1. The condition of being equivalent or equal; equality of worth, value, signification, or force; as, an equivalence of definitions.
Equivalence E*quiv"a*lence, v. t. To be equivalent or equal to; to counterbalance. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

equivalent.c: Equivalent E*quiv"a*lent (e*kwĭv"ȧ*leint), a. [L. aequivalens, -entis, p. pr. of aequivalere to have equal power; aequus equal + valere to be strong, be worth: cf. F. équivalent. See Equal, and Valiant.] 1. Equal in worth or value, force, power, effect, import, and the like; alike in significance and value; of the same import or meaning.
Equivalent E*quiv"a*lent (e*kwĭv"ȧ*leint), n. 1. Something equivalent; that which is equal in value, worth, weight, or force; as, to offer an equivalent for damage done.
Equivalent E*quiv"a*lent, v. t. To make the equivalent to; to equal; equivalence. [R.]

equivalently.c: Equivalently E*quiv"a*lent*ly, adv. In an equal manner.

equivalue.c: Equivalue E`qui*val"ue (?), v. t. To put an equal value upon; to put (something) on a par with another thing. W. Taylor.

equivalved.c: Equivalved Equivalve { E"qui*valve (?), E"qui*valved (?), } a. [Equi- + valve.] (Zoöl.) Having the valves equal in size and from, as in most bivalve shells.

equivalvular.c: Equivalvular E`qui*val"vu*lar (?), a. (Zoöl.) Same as Equivalve or Equivalved.

equivocal.c: Equivocal E*quiv"o*cal (?), a. [L. aequivocus: aequus equal + vox, vocis, word. See Equal, and Voice, and cf. Equivoque.] 1. (Literally, called equally one thing or the other; hence:) Having two significations equally applicable; capable of double interpretation; of doubtful meaning; ambiguous; uncertain; as, equivocal words; an equivocal sentence.
Equivocal E*quiv"o*cal, n. A word or expression capable of different meanings; an ambiguous term; an equivoque.

equivocally.c: Equivocally E*quiv"o*cal*ly, adv. In an equivocal manner.

equivocalness.c: Equivocalness E*quiv"o*cal*ness, n. The state of being equivocal.

equivocate.c: Equivocate E*quiv"o*cate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Equivocated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Equivocating.] [L. aequivocatus, p. p. of aequivocari to be called by the same name, fr. L. aequivocus: cf. F. équivoquer. See Equivocal, a.] To use words of equivocal or doubtful signification; to express one's opinions in terms which admit of different senses, with intent to deceive; to use ambiguous expressions with a view to mislead; as, to equivocate is the work of duplicity.
Equivocate E*quiv"o*cate (?), v. t. To render equivocal or ambiguous.

equivocation.c: Equivocation E*quiv`o*ca"tion (?), n. The use of expressions susceptible of a double signification, with a purpose to mislead.

equivocatory.c: Equivocatory E*quiv"o*ca*to*ry (?), a. Indicating, or characterized by, equivocation.

equivoke.c: Equivoke Equivoque { Eq"ui*voque, Eq"ui*voke } (?), n. [F. équivoque. See Equivocal.] 1. An ambiguous term; a word susceptible of different significations. Coleridge.

equivorous.c: Equivorous E*quiv"o*rous (?), a. [L. equus horse + vorare to eat greedily.] Feeding on horseflesh; as, equivorous Tartars.

equus.c: Equus ‖E"quus (?), n. [L., horse.] (Zoöl.) A genus of mammals, including the horse, ass, etc.

er.c: -er -er (?). 1. [AS. -ere; akin to L. -arius.] The termination of many English words, denoting the agent; -- applied either to men or things; as in hater, farmer, heater, grater. At the end of names of places, -er signifies a man of the place; as, Londoner, i. e., London man.

era.c: Era E"ra (?), n.; pl. Eras (#). [LL. aera an era, in earlier usage, the items of an account, counters, pl. of aes, aeris, brass, money. See Ore.] 1. A fixed point of time, usually an epoch, from which a series of years is reckoned.

eradiate.c: Eradiate E*ra"di*ate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Eradiated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Eradiating (?).] [Pref. e- + radiate.] To shoot forth, as rays of light; to beam; to radiate. Dr. H. More.

eradicable.c: Eradicable E*rad"i*ca*ble (?), a. Capable of being eradicated.

eradicate.c: Eradicate E*rad"i*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Eradicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Eradicating (?).] [L. eradicatus, p. p. of eradicare to eradicate; e out + radix, radicis, root. See Radical.] 1. To pluck up by the roots; to root up; as, an oak tree eradicated.

eradication.c: Eradication E*rad`i*ca"tion (?), n. [L. eradicatio: cf. F. éradication.] 1. The act of plucking up by the roots; a rooting out; extirpation; utter destruction.

eradicative.c: Eradicative E*rad"i*ca*tive (?), a. [Cf. éradicatif.] Tending or serving to eradicate; curing or destroying thoroughly, as a disease or any evil.
Eradicative E*rad"i*ca*tive, n. (Med.) A medicine that effects a radical cure. Whitlock.

erasable.c: Erasable E*ras"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being erased.

erase.c: Erase E*rase" (e*rās"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Erased (e*rāst"); p. pr. & vb. n.. Erasing.] [L. erasus, p. p. of eradere to erase; e out + radere to scrape, scratch, shave. See Rase.] 1. To rub or scrape out, as letters or characters written, engraved, or painted; to efface; to expunge; to cross out; as, to erase a word or a name.

erased.c: Erased E*rased" (rāst"), p. p. & a. 1. Rubbed or scraped out; effaced; obliterated.

erasement.c: Erasement E*rase"ment (rās"meint), n. The act of erasing; a rubbing out; expunction; obliteration. Johnson.

eraser.c: Eraser E*ras"er (?), n. One who, or that which, erases; esp., a sharp instrument or a piece of rubber used to erase writings, drawings, etc.

erasion.c: Erasion E*ra"sion (?), n. The act of erasing; a rubbing out; obliteration.

erastian.c: Erastian E*ras"tian (?; 106), n. (Eccl. Hist.) One of the followers of Thomas Erastus, a German physician and theologian of the 16th century. He held that the punishment of all offenses should be referred to the civil power, and that holy communion was open to all. In the present day, an Erastian is one who would see the church placed entirely under the control of the State. Shipley.

erastianism.c: Erastianism E*ras"tian*ism (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) The principles of the Erastains.

erasure.c: Erasure E*ra"sure (?; 135), n. [From Erase.] 1. The act of erasing; a scratching out; obliteration.

erative.c: Erative Er"a*tive (?), a. Pertaining to the Muse Erato who presided over amatory poetry. Stormonth.

erato.c: Erato Er"a*to (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to love.] (Class. Myth.) The Muse who presided over lyric and amatory poetry.

erbium.c: Erbium Er"bi*um (?), n. [NL. from Ytterby, in Sweden, where gadolinite is found. Cf. Terbium, Yttrium, Ytterbium.] (Chem.) A rare earth element of the lanthanide series associated with several other rare elements in the mineral gadolinite from Ytterby in Sweden. Symbol Er. It has atomic number 68 and an atomic weight of 167.26. The pure element is metallic with a bright, silvery luster. It is relatively stable in air, not oxidizing as quickly as some other rare earths. Its salts are rose-colored and give characteristic spectra, and the pink oxide has been added as a colorant in glass and porcelain enamel glazes. Its sesquioxide Er2O3 is called erbia. HCP61

ercedeken.c: Ercedeken Er`ce*de"ken (?), n. [OE., fr. pref. erce- = archi- + deken a deacon.] An archdeacon. [Obs.]

erd.c: Erd Erd (ẽrd), n. [OE. erd, eard, earth, land, country, AS. eard; akin to OS. ard dwelling place, OHG. art plowing, tillage, Icel. örð crop, and to L. arare to plow, E. ear to plow.] The earth. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.

ere.c: Ere Ere (ār or âr; 277), prep. & adv. [AS. ǣr, prep., adv., & conj.; akin to OS., OFries., & OHG. ēr, G. eher, D. eer, Icel. ār, Goth. air. √204. Cf. Early, Erst, Or, adv.] 1. Before; sooner than. [Archaic or Poetic]
Ere Ere (?), v. t. To plow. [Obs.] See Ear, v. t. Chaucer.

erebus.c: Erebus Er"e*bus (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?.] 1. (Greek Myth.) A place of nether darkness, being the gloomy space through which the souls passed to Hades. See Milton's “Paradise Lost,” Book II., line 883.

erect.c: Erect E*rect" (?), a. [L. erectus, p. p. of erigere to erect; e out + regere to lead straight. See Right, and cf. Alert.] 1. Upright, or having a vertical position; not inverted; not leaning or bent; not prone; as, to stand erect.

Erect E*rect", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Erected; p. pr. & vb. n. Erecting.] 1. To raise and place in an upright or perpendicular position; to set upright; to raise; as, to erect a pole, a flagstaff, a monument, etc.
Erect E*rect", v. i. To rise upright. [Obs.]

erectable.c: Erectable E*rect"a*ble (?) a. Capable of being erected; as, an erectable feather. Col. G. Montagu.

erecter.c: Erecter E*rect"er (?), n. An erector; one who raises or builds.

erectile.c: Erectile E*rect"ile (?), a. [Cf. F. érectile.] 1. Capable of being erected; susceptible of being erected of dilated; as, erectile tissue.

erectility.c: Erectility E`rec*til"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being erectile.

erection.c: Erection E*rec"tion (?), n. [L. erectio: cf. F. érection.] 1. The act of erecting, or raising upright; the act of constructing, as a building or a wall, or of fitting together the parts of, as a machine; the act of founding or establishing, as a commonwealth or an office; also, the act of rousing to excitement or courage.

erective.c: Erective E*rect"ive (?), a. Making erect or upright; raising; tending to erect.

erectly.c: Erectly E*rect"ly, adv. In an erect manner or posture.

erectness.c: Erectness E*rect"ness, n. Uprightness of posture or form.

erectopatent.c: Erecto-patent E*rec"to-pat"ent (?), a. 1. (Bot.) Having a position intermediate between erect and patent, or spreading.

erector.c: Erector E*rec"tor (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, erects.

erelong.c: Erelong Ere`long" (?; 115), adv. Before the?apse of a long time; soon; -- usually separated, ere long.

eremacausis.c: Eremacausis ‖Er`e*ma*cau"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? quietly +? burning, fr.? to burn.] A gradual oxidation from exposure to air and moisture, as in the decay of old trees or of dead animals.

eremitical.c: Eremitical Eremitic { Er`e*mit"ic (?), Er`e*mit"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to an eremite; hermitical; living in solitude. “An eremitical life in the woods.” Fuller. “The eremitic instinct.” Lowell.

eremitism.c: Eremitism Er"e*mit*ism (?), n. The state of a hermit; a living in seclusion from social life.

ereptation.c: Ereptation E`rep*ta"tion (?), n. [L. erepere to creep out; e out + repere to creep.] A creeping forth. [Obs.]

ereption.c: Ereption E*rep"tion (?), n. [L. ereptio, fr. eripere to snatch away; e out + rapere to snatch.] A snatching away. [Obs.] Cockeram.

erethism.c: Erethism Er"e*thism (?), n. [Gr.? irritation, fr.? to stir, rouse, fr.? to stir: cf. F. éréthisme.] (Med.) A morbid degree of excitement or irritation in an organ. Hoblyn.

erethistic.c: Erethistic Er`e*this"tic (?), a. [Gr.? irritating.] Relating to erethism.

erewhiles.c: Erewhiles Erewhile { Ere`while" (?), Ere`whiles" (?), } adv. Some time ago; a little while before; heretofore. [Archaic]

erf.c: Erf ‖Erf (?), n.; pl. Erven (#). [D.] A garden plot, usually about half an acre. [Cape Colony]

erg.c: Erg Erg (?), n. [Gr.? work.] (Physics) The unit of work or energy in the C. G. S. system, being the amount of work done by a dyne working through a distance of one centimeter; the amount of energy expended in moving a body one centimeter against a force of one dyne (981 dynes exert the same force as a one gram mass in the earth's gravitational field). One foot pound is equal to 13,560,000 ergs. The absolute Joule is equivalent to 107 ergs, which are equivalent to 0.2389 gram-calories at 15° C. See also mechanical equivalent of heat under equivalent.

ergal.c: Ergal Er"gal (?), n. [G., fr. Gr.? work.] (Physics) Potential energy; negative value of the force function.

ergat.c: Ergat Er"gat (?), v. t. [L. ergo therefore.] To deduce logically, as conclusions. [Obs.] Hewyt.

ergmeter.c: Ergmeter Erg"me`ter (?), n. [Erg + -meter.] (Physics) An instrument for measuring energy in ergs.

ergo.c: Ergo ‖Er"go (?), conj. or adv. [L.] Therefore; consequently; -- often used in a jocular way. Shak.

ergograph.c: Ergograph Er"go*graph (?), n. [Gr.? work + -graph.] An instrument for measuring and recording the work done by a single muscle or set of muscles, the rate of fatigue, etc. -- Er`go*graph"ic (#), a.

ergometer.c: Ergometer Er*gom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? work + -meter.] (Physics) A device for measuring, or an instrument for indicating, energy expended or work done; a dynamometer. -- Er`go*met"ric (#), a.

ergon.c: Ergon Er"gon (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? work.] (Physics) (a) Work, measured in terms of the quantity of heat to which it is equivalent. (b) same as Erg.

ergot.c: Ergot Er"got (?), n. [F. ergot, argot, lit., a spur.] 1. A diseased condition of rye and other cereals, in which the grains become black, and often spur-shaped. It is caused by a parasitic fungus, Claviceps purpurea.

ergotic.c: Ergotic Er*got"ic (?), a. Pertaining to, or derived from, ergot; as, ergotic acid.

ergotin.c: Ergotin Er"go*tin (?), n. (Med.) An extract made from ergot.

ergotine.c: Ergotine Er"go*tine (?). (Chem.) A powerful astringent alkaloid extracted from ergot as a brown, amorphous, bitter substance. It is used to produce contraction of the uterus.

ergotism.c: Ergotism Er"go*tism (?), n. [F. ergotisme, fr. L. ergo.] A logical deduction. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Ergotism Er"got*ism (?), n. [From Ergot, n.; cf. F. ergotisme.] (Med.) A diseased condition produced by eating rye affected with the ergot fungus.

ergotized.c: Ergotized Er"got*ized (?), a. Affected with the ergot fungus; as, ergotized rye.

eric.c: Eric Eriach { Er"i*ach (?), Er"ic (?), } n. [Ir. eiric.] (Old Irish Law) A recompense formerly given by a murderer to the relatives of the murdered person.

erica.c: Erica E*ri"ca (?), n. [NL., fr. L. erice heath, Gr.?.] (Bot.) A genus of shrubby plants, including the heaths, many of them producing beautiful flowers.

ericaceous.c: Ericaceous Er`i*ca"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Belonging to the Heath family, or resembling plants of that family; consisting of heats.

ericinol.c: Ericinol E*ric"i*nol (e*rĭs"ĭ*nōl), n. [NL. ericaceae the Heath family + L. oleum oil.] (Chem.) A colorless oil (quickly becoming brown), with a pleasant odor, obtained by the decomposition of ericolin.

ericius.c: Ericius E*ri"ci*us (?), n. [L., a hedgehog.] The Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew word qipōd, which in the “Authorized Version” is translated bittern, and in the Revised Version, porcupine.

ericolin.c: Ericolin E*ric"o*lin (?), n. (Chem.) A glucoside found in the bearberry (and others of the Ericaceæ), and extracted as a bitter, yellow, amorphous mass.

eridanus.c: Eridanus E*rid"a*nus (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?, the Greek name of the River Po.] (Anat.) A long, winding constellation extending southward from Taurus and containing the bright star Achernar.

erigible.c: Erigible Er"i*gi*ble (ĕr"ĭ*jĭ*b'l), a. [See Erect.] Capable of being erected. [Obs.]

erin.c: Erin E"rin (ē"rĭn), n. [Ir. Cf. Aryan.] An early, and now a poetic, name of Ireland.

erinaceous.c: Erinaceous Er`i*na"ceous (?), a. [L. erinaceus hedgehog.] (Zoöl.) Of the Hedgehog family; like, or characteristic of, a hedgehog.

eringo.c: Eringo E*rin"go (?), n. The sea holly. See Eryngo.

erinite.c: Erinite Er"i*nite (?), n. (Min.) A hydrous arseniate of copper, of an emerald-green color; -- so called from Erin, or Ireland, where it occurs.

erinys.c: Erinys E*rin"ys (?), n.; pl. Erinyes (#). [L., fr. Gr.?.] (Class. Myth.) An avenging deity; one of the Furies; sometimes, conscience personified. [Written also Erinnys.]

eriometer.c: Eriometer E`ri*om"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? wool + -meter.] (Opt.) An instrument for measuring the diameters of minute particles or fibers, from the size of the colored rings produced by the diffraction of the light in which the objects are viewed.

eristalis.c: Eristalis ‖E*ris"ta*lis (?), n. [NL.] (Zoöl.) A genus of dipterous insects whose young (called rat-tailed larvæ) are remarkable for their long tapering tail, which spiracles at the tip, and for their ability to live in very impure and salt waters; -- also called drone fly.

eristical.c: Eristical Eristic { E*ris"tic (?), E*ris"tic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?, fr.? to strive, wrangle,? strife.] Controversial. [Archaic]

erke.c: Erke Erke (?), a. [Cf. Irk.] Slothful. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

erlking.c: Erlking Erl"king` (?), n. [G. erlkönig, fr. Dan. ellekonge elfking.] A personification, in German and Scandinavian mythology, of a spirit or natural power supposed to work mischief and ruin, esp. to children.

erme.c: Erme Erme (?), v. i. [OE. ermen, AS. yrman. Cf. Yearn.] To grieve; to feel sad. [Obs.] Chaucer.

ermilin.c: Ermilin Ermelin { Er"me*lin (?), Er"mi*lin (?) }, n. (Zoöl.) See Ermine. Shenstone.

ermin.c: Ermin Er"min (?), n. [OF. Ermin, L. Armenius.] An Armenian. [Obs.] Chaucer.

ermine.c: Ermine Er"mine (?), n. [OF. ermine, F. hermine, prob. of German origin; cf. OHG. harmo, G. hermelin, akin to Lith. szarm?, szarmonys, weasel, cf. AS. hearma; but cf. also LL. armelinus, armellina, hermellina, and pellis Armenia, the fur of the Armenian rat, mus Armenius, the animal being found also in Armenia.] 1. (Zoöl.) A valuable fur-bearing animal of the genus Mustela (M. erminea), allied to the weasel; the stoat. It is found in the northern parts of Asia, Europe, and America. In summer it is brown, but in winter it becomes white, except the tip of the tail, which is always black.
Ermine Er"mine, v. t. To clothe with, or as with, ermine.

ermined.c: Ermined Er"mined (?), a. Clothed or adorned with the fur of the ermine. Pope.

erminois.c: Erminois Ermines Er"mines (?), n., Er"min*ois (?), n. (Her.) See Note under Ermine, n., 4.

erne.c: Erne Ern { Ern, Erne } (?), n. [AS. earn eagle; akin to D. arend, OHG. aro, G. aar, Icel., Sw., & Dan. örn, Goth. ara, and to Gr.? bird. √11. Cf. Ornithology.] (Zoöl.) A sea eagle, esp. the European white-tailed sea eagle (Haliæetus albicilla).

ern.c: Ern Ern (?), v. i. [Cf. Erme.] To stir with strong emotion; to grieve; to mourn. [Obs.]

ernestful.c: Ernestful Er"nest*ful (?), a. [See Earnest, a.] Serious. [Obs.] Chaucer.

erode.c: Erode E*rode" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Eroded; p. pr. & vb. n. Eroding.] [L. erodere, erosum; e out + rodere to gnaw. See Rodent.] 1. To eat into or away; to corrode; as, canker erodes the flesh. “The blood... erodes the vessels.” Wiseman.

eroded.c: Eroded E*rod"ed, p. p. & a. 1. Eaten away; gnawed; irregular, as if eaten or worn away.

erodent.c: Erodent E*rod"ent (?), n. [L. erodens, -entis, p. pr. of erodere. See Erode.] (Med.) A medicine which eats away extraneous growths; a caustic.

erogate.c: Erogate Er"o*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Erogated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Erogating (?).] [L. erogatus, p. p. of erogare; e out + rogare to ask.] To lay out, as money; to deal out; to expend. [Obs.]

erogation.c: Erogation Er`o*ga"tion (?), n. [L. erogatio.] The act of giving out or bestowing. [Obs.] Sir T. Elyot.

eros.c: Eros ‖E"ros (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.? love,? (personified) Eros, fr.? to love.] (Greek Myth.) Love; the god of love; -- by earlier writers represented as one of the first and creative gods, by later writers as the son of Aphrodite, equivalent to the Latin god Cupid.

erose.c: Erose E*rose" (?), a. [L. erosus, p. p. See Erode.] 1. Irregular or uneven as if eaten or worn away.

erosion.c: Erosion E*ro"sion (?), n. [L. erosio. See Erode.] 1. The act or operation of eroding or eating away.

erosive.c: Erosive E*ro"sive (?), a. That erodes or gradually eats away; tending to erode; corrosive. Humble.

erostrate.c: Erostrate E*ros"trate (?), a. [Pref. e- out + rostrate.] (Bot.) Without a beak.

eroteme.c: Eroteme Er"o*teme (?), n. [Gr.? question.] A mark indicating a question; a note of interrogation.

erotesis.c: Erotesis ‖Er`o*te"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a questioning, fr.? to ask.] (Rhet.) A figure of speech by which a strong affirmation of the contrary, is implied under the form of an earnest interrogation, as in the following lines; -

erotical.c: Erotical Erotic { E*rot"ic (?), E*rot"ic*al (?), } a. [Gr.?: cf. F. érotique. See Eros.] Of or pertaining to the passion of love; treating of love; amatory.

erotic.c: Erotic E*rot"ic, n. An amorous composition or poem.

err.c: Err Err (ẽr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Erred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Erring (?; 277, 85).] [F. errer, L. errare; akin to G. irren, OHG. irran, v. t., irrōn, v. i., OS. irrien, Sw. irra, Dan. irre, Goth, aírzjan to lead astray, airzise astray.] 1. To wander; to roam; to stray. [Archaic] “Why wilt thou err from me?” Keble.

errable.c: Errable Er"ra*ble (?), a. Liable to error; fallible.

errableness.c: Errableness Er"ra*ble*ness, n. Liability to error. Dr. H. More.

errabund.c: Errabund Er"ra*bund (?), a. [L. errabundus.] Erratic. “Errabund guesses.” Southey.

errancy.c: Errancy Er"ran*cy (?), n. [L. errantia.] A wandering; state of being in error.

errand.c: Errand Er"rand (?), n. [OE. erende, erande, message, business, AS. ærende, ærend; akin to OS. arundi, OHG. arunti, Icel. eyrendi, örendi, erendi, Sw. ärende, Dan. ærende; perh. akin to AS. earu swift, Icel. örr, and to L. oriri to rise, E. orient.] A special business intrusted to a messenger; something to be told or done by one sent somewhere for the purpose; often, a verbal message; a commission; as, the servant was sent on an errand; to do an errand. Also, one's purpose in going anywhere.

errant.c: Errant Er"rant (?), a. [F. errant, p. pr. fr. OF. errer to travel, LL. iterare, fr. L. iter journey; confused somewhat with L. errare to err. See Eyre, and cf. Arrant, Itinerant.] 1. Wandering; deviating from an appointed course, or from a direct path; roving.
Errant Er"rant, n. One who wanders about. [Obs.] Fuller.

errantia.c: Errantia ‖Er*ran"ti*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. errare to wander. See Err.] (Zoöl.) A group of chætopod annelids, including those that are not confined to tubes. See Chætopoda. [Written also Errantes.]

errantry.c: Errantry Er"rant*ry (?), n. 1. A wandering; a roving; esp., a roving in quest of adventures. Addison.

errata.c: Errata ‖Er*ra"ta (?), n. pl. [L.] 1. Plural of erratum. See Erratum.

erratic.c: Erratic Er*rat"ic (?), a. [L. erraticus, fr. errare to wander: cf. F. erratique. See Err.] 1. Having no certain course; roving about without a fixed destination; wandering; moving; -- hence, applied to the planets as distinguished from the fixed stars.
Erratic Er*rat"ic, n. 1. One who deviates from common and accepted opinions; one who is eccentric or preserve in his intellectual character.

erratical.c: Erratical Er*rat"ic*al (?), a. Erratic. -- Er*rat"ic*al*ly, adv. -- Er*rat"ic*al*ness, n.

erration.c: Erration Er*ra"tion (?), n. [L. erratio. See Err.] A wandering; a roving about. [Obs.] Cockeram.

erratum.c: Erratum ‖Er*ra"tum (?), n.; pl. Errata (#). [L., fr. errare, erratum, to wander, err. See Err.] An error or mistake in writing or printing.

errhine.c: Errhine Er"rhine (?), n. [Gr.?;? in +?,?, nose: cf. F. errhin.] (Med.) A medicine designed to be snuffed up the nose, to promote discharges of mucus; a sternutatory. Coxe. -- a. Causing or increasing secretion of nasal mucus.

erroneous.c: Erroneous Er*ro"ne*ous (?), a. [L. erroneus, fr. errare to err. See Err.] 1. Wandering; straying; deviating from the right course; -- hence, irregular; unnatural. [Obs.] “Erroneous circulation.” Arbuthnot.

error.c: Error Er"ror (?), n. [OF. error, errur, F. erreur, L. error, fr. errare to err. See Err.] 1. A wandering; a roving or irregular course. [Obs.]

errorful.c: Errorful Er"ror*ful (?), a. Full of error; wrong. Foxe.

errorist.c: Errorist Er"ror*ist, n. One who encourages and propagates error; one who holds to error.

ers.c: Ers Ers (?), n. [F., fr. L. ervum a kind of pulse, bitter vetch.] (Bot.) The bitter vetch (Ervum Ervilia).

erse.c: Erse Erse (ẽrs), n. [A modification of Irish, OE. Irishe.] A name sometimes given to that dialect of the Celtic which is spoken in the Highlands of Scotland; -- called, by the Highlanders, Gaelic.
Erse Erse, a. Of or pertaining to the Celtic race in the Highlands of Scotland, or to their language.

erst.c: Erst Erst (ẽrst), adv. [Orig. superlative of ere; AS. ǣrest. See Ere.] [Archaic] 1. First. Chaucer.
