eupatorium.c: Eupatorium Eu`pa*to"ri*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Eupator, king of Pontus, said to have used it as a medicine.] (Bot.) A genus of perennial, composite herbs including hemp agrimony, boneset, throughwort, etc.

eupatrid.c: Eupatrid Eu"pa*trid (?), n. [Gr. e'y^ well +? father.] One well born, or of noble birth.

eupepsy.c: Eupepsy Eupepsia { ‖Eu*pep"si*a (?), Eu*pep"sy (?), } n. [NL. eupepsia, Fr. Gr.?, fr.? easy of digestion; e'y^ well +? to cook, digest.] (Med.) Soundness of the nutritive or digestive organs; good concoction or digestion; -- opposed to dyspepsia.

eupeptic.c: Eupeptic Eu*pep"tic (?), a. [Gr.?.] Of or pertaining to good digestion; easy of digestion; having a good digestion; as, eupeptic food; an eupeptic man.

euphemism.c: Euphemism Eu"phe*mism (ū"fe*mĭz'm), n. [Gr.? fr.? to use word of a good omen; e'y^ well +? to speak: cf. F. euphémisme. See Fame.] (Rhet.) A figure in which a harsh or indelicate word or expression is softened; a way of describing an offensive thing by an inoffensive expression; a mild name for something disagreeable.

euphemistical.c: Euphemistical Euphemistic { Eu`phe*mis"tic (?), Eu`phe*mis"tic*al (?), } a. Pertaining to euphemism; containing a euphemism; softened in expression. -- Eu`phe*mis"tic*al*ly, adv.

euphemize.c: Euphemize Eu"phe*mize (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Euphemized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Euphemizing.] [Gr.?.] To express by a euphemism, or in delicate language; to make use of euphemistic expressions.

euphoniad.c: Euphoniad Eu*pho"ni*ad (?), n. [See Euphony.] (Mus.) An instrument in which are combined the characteristic tones of the organ and various other instruments. [R.]

euphonical.c: Euphonical Euphonic { Eu*phon"ic (?), Eu*phon"ic*al (?), } a. Pertaining to, or exhibiting, euphony; agreeable in sound; pleasing to the ear; euphonious; as, a euphonic expression; euphonical orthography.

euphonicon.c: Euphonicon Eu*phon"i*con (u*fŏn"ĭ*kŏn), n. [See Euphony.] (Mus.) A kind of upright piano.

euphonious.c: Euphonious Eu*pho"ni*ous (?), a. Pleasing or sweet in sound; euphonic; smooth-sounding. Hallam. -- Eu*pho"ni*ous*ly, adv.

euphonism.c: Euphonism Eu"pho*nism (?), n. An agreeable combination of sounds; euphony.

euphonium.c: Euphonium Eu*pho"ni*um (?), n. [NL. See Euphony.] (Mus.) A bass instrument of the saxhorn family.

euphonize.c: Euphonize Eu"pho*nize (?), v. t. To make euphonic. [R.]

euphonon.c: Euphonon Eu"pho*non (?), n. [See Euphony.] (Mus.) An instrument resembling the organ in tone and the upright piano in form. It is characterized by great strength and sweetness of tone.

euphony.c: Euphony Eu"pho*ny (?), n.; pl. Euphonies (#). [L. euphonia, Gr.?, fr.? sweet-voiced; e'y^ well +? sound, voice; akin to? to speak: cf. F. euphonie.] A pleasing or sweet sound; an easy, smooth enunciation of sounds; a pronunciation of letters and syllables which is pleasing to the ear.

euphorbia.c: Euphorbia ‖Eu*phor"bi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. L. euphorbea. See Euphorrium.] (Bot.) Spurge, or bastard spurge, a genus of plants of many species, mostly shrubby, herbaceous succulents, affording an acrid, milky juice. Some of them are armed with thorns. Most of them yield powerful emetic and cathartic products.

euphorbial.c: Euphorbial Euphorbiaceous { Eu*phor`bi*a"ceous (?), Eu*phor"bi*al (?), } a. (Bot.) Of, relating to, or resembling, the Euphorbia family.

euphorbine.c: Euphorbine Euphorbin { Eu*phor"bin, Eu*phor"bine } (?), n. (Med.) A principle, or mixture of principles, derived from various species of Euphorbia.

euphorbium.c: Euphorbium Eu*phor"bi*um (?), n. [NL., fr. L. euphorbeum, from Gr.?; -- so called after Euphorbus, a Greek physician.] (Med.) An inodorous exudation, usually in the form of yellow tears, produced chiefly by the African Euphorbia resinifera. It was formerly employed medicinally, but was found so violent in its effects that its use is nearly abandoned.

euphotide.c: Euphotide Eu"pho*tide (?), n. [Gr. e'y^ well +?,?, light. So called because of its pleasing combination of white and green.] (Min.) A rock occurring in the Alps, consisting of saussurite and smaragdite; -- sometimes called gabbro.

euphrasy.c: euphrasy eu"phra*sy (ū"frȧ*sy̆), n. [NL. euphrasia, fr. Gr. e'yfrasi`a delight, fr. e'yfrai`nein to delight; e'y^ well + frh`n heart, mind: cf. LL. eufrasia, F. eufraise.] (Bot.) The plant eyebright (Euphrasia officionalis), formerly regarded as beneficial in disorders of the eyes.

euphroe.c: euphroe eu"phroe (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A block or long slat of wood, perforated for the passage of the crowfoot, or cords by which an awning is held up. [Written also uphroe and uvrou.] Knight.

euphuism.c: euphuism eu"phu*ism (ū"fu*ĭz'm), n. [Gr. e'yfyh`s well grown, graceful; e'y^ well + fyh` growth, fr. fy`ein to grow. This affected style of conversation and writing, fashionable for some time in the court of Elizabeth, had its origin from the fame of Lyly's books, “Euphues, or the Anatomy of Wit,” and “Euphues and his England.”] (Rhet.) An affectation of excessive elegance and refinement of language; high-flown diction.

euphuist.c: Euphuist Eu"phu*ist, n. One who affects excessive refinement and elegance of language; -- applied esp. to a class of writers, in the age of Elizabeth, whose productions are marked by affected conceits and high-flown diction.

euphuistic.c: Euphuistic Eu`phu*is"tic (?), a. Belonging to the euphuists, or euphuism; affectedly refined.

euphuize.c: Euphuize Eu"phu*ize (?), v. t. To affect excessive refinement in language; to be overnice in expression.

eupione.c: Eupione Eu"pi*one (?), n. [Gr.? very fat; e'y^ well +? fat.] (Chem.) A limpid, oily liquid obtained by the destructive distillation of various vegetable and animal substances; -- specifically, an oil consisting largely of the higher hydrocarbons of the paraffin series. [Written also eupion.]

eupittone.c: Eupittone Eu*pit"tone (?), n. [Pref. eu- + pittacal + -one.] (Chem.) A yellow, crystalline substance, resembling aurin, and obtained by the oxidation of pittacal; -- called also eupittonic acid. [Written also eupitton.]

eupittonic.c: Eupittonic Eu`pit*ton"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, eupittone.

euplastic.c: Euplastic Eu*plas"tic (?), a. [Pref. eu- + -plastic.] (Med.) Having the capacity of becoming organizable in a high degree, as the matter forming the false membranes which sometimes result from acute inflammation in a healthy person. Dunglison.
Euplastic Eu*plas"tic, n. (Med.) Organizable substance by which the tissues of an animal body are renewed.

euplectella.c: Euplectella ‖Eu`plec*tel"la (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? well plaited; e'y^ well +? plaited.] (Zoöl.) A genus of elegant, glassy sponges, consisting of interwoven siliceous fibers, and growing in the form of a cornucopia; -- called also Venus's flower-basket.

euplexoptera.c: Euplexoptera ‖Eu`plex*op"te*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. e'y^ well +? to plait +? a wing.] (Zoöl.) An order of insects, including the earwig. The anterior wings are short, in the form of elytra, while the posterior wings fold up beneath them. See Earwig.

eupnaea.c: Eupnaea ‖Eup*næ"a (?), n. [NL., fr. gr.? easy breathing; e'y^ well +? to breathe.] (Physiol.) Normal breathing where arterialization of the blood is normal, in distinction from dyspnæa, in which the blood is insufficiently arterialized. Foster.

eupyrion.c: eupyrion eu*pyr"i*on (?), n. [Gr. e'y^ well +? fire.] A contrivance for obtaining a light instantaneously, such as a lucifer match. [archaic] Brande & C.

eurafrican.c: Eurafrican Eurafric { Eur*af"ric (?), Eur*af"ri*can (?) }, a. [Europe + Afric, African.] 1. (Geog.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, the continents of Europe and Africa combined.

eurasian.c: Eurasian Eu*ra"sian (?), n. [European + Asian.] 1. A child of a European parent on the one side and an Asiatic on the other.
Eurasian Eu*ra"sian (?), a. Of European and Asiatic descent; of or pertaining to both Europe and Asia; as, the great Eurasian plain.

eurasiatio.c: Eurasiatio Eu*ra`si*at"io (?), a. (Geog.) Of or pertaining to the continents of Europe and Asia combined.

eureka.c: Eureka ‖Eu*re"ka (?). [Gr.? I have found, perfect indicative of? to find.] The exclamation attributed to Archimedes, who is said to have cried out “Eureka! eureka!” (I have found it! I have found it!), upon suddenly discovering a method of finding out how much the gold of King Hiero's crown had been alloyed. Hence, an expression of triumph concerning a discovery.

eurhipidurous.c: Eurhipidurous Eu*rhip`i*du"rous (?), a. [Gr. e'y^ well +? a fan +? a tail.] (Zoöl.) Having a fanlike tail; belonging to the Eurhipiduræ, a division of Aves which includes all living birds.

euripize.c: Euripize Eu"ri*pize (?), v. t. [See Euripus.] To whirl hither and thither. [Obs.]

euripus.c: Euripus Eu*ri"pus (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?; e'y^ well +? a rushing motion.] A strait; a narrow tract of water, where the tide, or a current, flows and reflows with violence, as the ancient frith of this name between Eubœa and Bœotia. Hence, a flux and reflux. Burke.

eurite.c: Eurite Eu"rite (ū"rīt), n. [Cf. F. eurite.] (Min.) A compact feldspathic rock; felsite. See Felsite.

euritic.c: Euritic Eu*rit"ic (?), a. Of or relating to eurite.

euroclydon.c: Euroclydon Eu*roc"ly*don (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.?;? the southeast wind +? wave, billow; according to another reading,?, i. e. a north-east wind, as in the Latin Vulgate Euro-aquilo.] A tempestuous northeast wind which blows in the Mediterranean. See Levanter.

europeanize.c: Europeanize Eu`ro*pe"an*ize (?), v. t. To cause to become like the Europeans in manners or character; to habituate or accustom to European usages.

europium.c: Europium Eu*ro"pi*um (?), n. [NL.; Europe + -ium, as in aluminium.] (Chem.) A metallic element of the rare-earth group (Lanthanide series), discovered spectroscopically by Demarcay in 1896. Symbol, Eu; atomic number 63; at. wt., 151.965 (C=12.011); valence = +2 or +3.

euryale.c: Euryale ‖Eu*ry"a*le (?), n. [NL., fr. Euryale, one of the Gorgons.] 1. (Bot.) A genus of water lilies, growing in India and China. The only species (Euryale ferox) is very prickly on the peduncles and calyx. The rootstocks and seeds are used as food.

euryalida.c: Euryalida ‖Eu`ry*al"i*da (?), n. pl. [NL.] (Zoöl.) A tribe of Ophiuroidea, including the genera Euryale, Astrophyton, etc. They generally have the arms branched. See Astrophyton.

eurycerous.c: Eurycerous Eu*ryc"er*ous (?), a. [Gr.? broad + ke`ras horn.] (Zoöl.) Having broad horns.

eurypteroid.c: Eurypteroid Eu*ryp"ter*oid (?), a. [Eurypterus + -oid.] (Paleon.) Like, or pertaining to, the genus Euryperus.

eurypteroidea.c: Eurypteroidea ‖Eu*ryp`te*roi"de*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Eurypteroid.] (Paleont.) An extinct order of Merostomata, of which the genus Eurypterus is the type. They are found only in Paleozoic rocks. [Written also Eurypterida.]

eurypterus.c: Eurypterus ‖Eu*ryp"te*rus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? broad +? a wing.] (Paleon.) A genus of extinct Merostomata, found in Silurian rocks. Some of the species are more than three feet long.

eurythmy.c: Eurythmy Eu"ryth*my (?), n. [L. eurythmia, Gr.?; e'y^ well +? rhythm, measure, proportion, symmetry: cf. F. eurythmie.] 1. (Fine Arts) Just or harmonious proportion or movement, as in the composition of a poem, an edifice, a painting, or a statue.

eusebian.c: Eusebian Eu*se"bi*an (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) A follower of Eusebius, bishop of Cæsarea, who was a friend and protector of Arius.

eustachian.c: Eustachian Eu*sta"chi*an (?), a. [From Eustachi, a learned Italian physician who died in Rome, 1574.] (Anat.) (a) Discovered by Eustachius. (b) Pertaining to the Eustachian tube; as, Eustachian catheter.

eustyle.c: Eustyle Eu"style` (?), n. [Gr.?, neut. of? with pillars at the best distances; e'y^ well +? pillar: cf. F. eustyle.] (Arch.) See Intercolumnlation.

eutaxy.c: Eutaxy Eu"tax*y (?), n. [Gr.?; e'y^ well +? arrangement: cf. F. eutaxie.] Good or established order or arrangement. [R.] E. Waterhouse.

eutectic.c: eutectic eu*tec"tic (ū*tĕk"tĭk), a. [Gr. e'y`thktos easily melted; e'y^ well + th`kein to melt.] (Physics) Of maximum fusibility; -- said of an alloy or mixture which has the lowest melting point which it is possible to obtain by the combination of the given components.

eutexia.c: Eutexia ‖Eu*tex"i*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a being easily melted.] (Physics) The principle or process of forming from given components the eutectic alloy, or alloy of maximum fusibility.

euterpe.c: Euterpe Eu*ter"pe (?). [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? delightful; e'y^ well +? to delight.] 1. (Class. Myth.) The Muse who presided over music.

euterpean.c: Euterpean Eu*ter"pe*an (?) a. Of or pertaining to Euterpe or to music.

euthanasia.c: Euthanasia Eu`tha*na"si*a (?) n. [NL., fr. Gr.?; e'y^ well +? death,?,?, to die: cf. F. euthanasie.] 1. An easy death; a mode of dying to be desired. “An euthanasia of all thought.” Hazlitt.

euthiochroic.c: Euthiochroic Eu`thi*o*chro"ic (?), a. [Gr. e'y^ well +? sulphur +? color.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or denoting, an acid so called.

euthyneura.c: Euthyneura Eu`thy*neu"ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? straight +? a nerve.] (Zoöl.) A large division of gastropod molluske, including the Pulmonifera and Opisthobranchiata.

eutrophy.c: Eutrophy Eu"tro*phy (?), n. [Gr.?, fr.? nourishing, healthy; e'y^ well +? to nourish.] (Med.) Healthy nutrition; soundless as regards the nutritive functions.

eutychian.c: Eutychian Eu*tych"i*an (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) A follower of Eutyches [5th century], who held that the divine and the human in the person of Christ were blended together as to constitute but one nature; a monophysite; -- opposed to Nestorian.

eutychianism.c: Eutychianism Eu*tych"i*an*ism (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) The doctrine of Eutyches and his followers.

euxanthic.c: Euxanthic Eux*an"thic (?) a. (Chem.) Having a yellow color; pertaining to, derived from, or resembling, euxanthin.

euxanthin.c: Euxanthin Eux*an"thin (?), n. [Gr. e'y^ well +? yellow.] (Chem.) A yellow pigment imported from India and China. It has a strong odor, and is said to be obtained from the urine of herbivorous animals when fed on the mango. It consists if a magnesium salt of euxanthic acid. Called also puri, purree, and Indian yellow.

euxenite.c: Euxenite Eux"e*nite (?), n. [Gr.? hospitable. So named because it contains a number of rare elements.] (Min.) A brownish black mineral with a metallic luster, found in Norway. It contains niobium, titanium, yttrium, and uranium, with some other metals.

evacate.c: Evacate E*va"cate (?), v. t. [Pref. e- + vacate.] To empty. [Obs.] Harvey.

evacuant.c: Evacuant E*vac"u*ant (?), a. [L.evacuans, -antis, p. pr. of evacuare: cf. F. évacuant.] Emptying; evacuative; purgative; cathartic. -- n. (Med.) A purgative or cathartic.

evacuate.c: Evacuate E*vac"u*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Evacuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Evacuating.] [l. evacuatus, p. p. of evacuare to empty, nullify; e out + vacuus empty, vacare to be empty. See Vacate.] 1. To make empty; to empty out; to remove the contents of; as, to evacuate a vessel or dish.
Evacuate E*vac"u*ate, v. i. 1. To let blood [Obs.] Burton.

evacuation.c: Evacuation E*vac`u*a"tion (?), n. [L. evacuatio: cf. F. évacuation.] 1. The act of emptying, clearing of the contents, or discharging. Specifically: (a) (Mil.) Withdrawal of troops from a town, fortress, etc. (b) (Med.) Voidance of any matter by the natural passages of the body or by an artificial opening; defecation; also, a diminution of the fluids of an animal body by cathartics, venesection, or other means.

evacuative.c: Evacuative E*vac"u*a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. évacuatif.] Serving of tending to evacuate; cathartic; purgative.

evacuator.c: Evacuator E*vac"u*a`tor (?), n. One who evacuates; a nullifier. “Evacuators of the law.” Hammond.

evade.c: Evade E*vade" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Evaded; p. pr. & vb. n.. Evading.] [L. evadere, evasum, e out + vadere to go, walk: cf. F. s'évader. See Wade.] To get away from by artifice; to avoid by dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to elude; to escape from cleverly; as, to evade a blow, a pursuer, a punishment; to evade the force of an argument.
Evade E*vade", v. t. 1. To escape; to slip away; -- sometimes with from. “Evading from perils.” Bacon.

evadible.c: Evadible E*vad"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being evaded. [R.]

evagation.c: Evagation Ev`a*ga"tion (?), n. [L. evagatio, fr. evagari to wander forth: cf. F. évagation. See Vagary.] A wandering about; excursion; a roving. [R.] Ray.

evaginate.c: Evaginate E*vag"i*nate (?), a. [L. evaginatus, p. p., unsheathed. See Evagination.] Protruded, or grown out, as an evagination{2}; turned inside out; unsheathed; evaginated; as, an evaginate membrane.
Evaginate E*vag"i*nate (?), v. i. & t. [imp. & p. p. Evaginated; p. pr. & vb. n. Evaginating.] To become evaginate; to cause to be evaginate.

evagination.c: Evagination E*vag`i*na"tion (?), n. [L. evaginatio an extending, evaginare to unsheathe; e out + vagina sheath.] 1. The act of unsheathing.

eval.c: Eval E"val (ē"vail), a. [L. aevum lifetime, age, eternity.] Relating to time or duration. [Obs.]

evaluate.c: Evaluate E*val"u*ate (e*văl"u*āt), v. t. [See Evaluation.] To fix the value of; to rate; to appraise.

evaluation.c: Evaluation E*val`u*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. évaluation, LL. evaluatio.] Valuation; appraisement. J. S. Mill.

evanesce.c: Evanesce Ev`a*nesce" (ĕv`ȧ*nĕs"), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Evanesced (ĕv`ȧ*nĕst"); p. pr. & vb. n. Evanescing. (ĕv`ȧ*nĕs"sĭng).] [L. evanescere; e out + vanescere to vanish, fr. vanus empty, vain. See Vain, and cf. Evanish.] To vanish away; to become dissipated and disappear, like vapor.

evanescence.c: Evanescence Ev`a*nes"cence (?), n. The act or state of vanishing away; disappearance; as, the evanescence of vapor, of a dream, of earthly plans or hopes. Rambler.

evanescent.c: Evanescent Ev`a*nes"cent (?), a. [L. evanescens, -entis, p. pr. of evanescere.] 1. Liable to vanish or pass away like vapor; vanishing; fleeting; as, evanescent joys.

evanescently.c: Evanescently Ev`a*nes"cent*ly, adv. In a vanishing manner; imperceptibly. Chalmers.

evangel.c: evangel e*van"gel (e*văn"jĕl), n. [F. évangile, L. evangelium, Gr. e'yagge`lion good news, glad tidings, gospel, fr. e'ya`ggelos bringing good news; e'y^ well + 'a`ggelein to bear a message. See Eu-, and Angel and cf. Evangely.] Good news; announcement of glad tidings; especially, the gospel, or a gospel. Milton.

evangelian.c: Evangelian E`van*ge"li*an (?), a. Rendering thanks for favors.

evangelic.c: Evangelic E`van*gel"ic (?), a. [L. evangelicus, Gr. e'yaggeliko`s: cf. F. évangélique. See Evangel.] Belonging to, or contained in, the gospel; evangelical. “Evangelic truth.” J. Foster.

evangelical.c: Evangelical E`van*gel"ic*al (?), a. 1. Contained in, or relating to, the four Gospels; as, the evangelical history.
Evangelical E`van*gel"ic*al, n. One of evangelical principles.

evangelicalism.c: Evangelicalism E`van*gel"ic*al*ism (?), n. Adherence to evangelical doctrines; evangelism. G. Eliot.

evangelically.c: Evangelically E`van*gel"ic*al*ly, adv. In an evangelical manner.

evangelicalness.c: Evangelicalness E`van*gel"ic*al*ness, n. State of being evangelical.

evangelism.c: evangelism e*van"gel*ism (e*văn"jĕl*ĭz'm), n. The preaching or promulgation of the gospel. Bacon.

evangelist.c: evangelist e*van"gel*ist (e*văn"jĕl*ĭst), n. [F. évangéliste, L. evangelista, fr. Gr. e'yaggelisth`s.] A bringer of the glad tidings of Church and his doctrines. Specifically: (a) A missionary preacher sent forth to prepare the way for a resident pastor; an itinerant missionary preacher. (b) A writer of one of the four Gospels (With the definite article); as, the four evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. (c) A traveling preacher whose efforts are chiefly directed to arouse to immediate repentance.

evangelistary.c: Evangelistary E*van`gel*is"ta*ry (?), n. [LL. evangelistarium.] A selection of passages from the Gospels, as a lesson in divine service. Porson.

evangelistic.c: Evangelistic E*van`gel*is"tic (?), a. Pertaining to the four evangelists; designed or fitted to evangelize; evangelical; as, evangelistic efforts.

evangelization.c: Evangelization E*van`gel*i*za"tion (?) n. The act of evangelizing; the state of being evangelized.

evangelize.c: evangelize e*van"gel*ize (e*văn"jĕl*īz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. evangelized (e*văn"jĕl*īzd); p. pr. & vb. n. evangelizing (e*văn"jĕl*ī*zĭng)]. [F. évangélisre, LL. evangelizare, fr. Gr. e'yaggeli`zesqai.] 1. To instruct in the gospel; to preach the gospel to; to convert to Christianity; as, to evangelize the world.
Evangelize E*van"gel*ize, v. i. To preach the gospel.

evangile.c: Evangile E*van"gile (?), n. [F. évangile. See Evangel.] Good tidings; evangel. [R.]

evanid.c: Evanid E*van"id (?), a. [L. evanidus, fr. evanescere. See Evanesce.] Liable to vanish or disappear; faint; weak; evanescent; as, evanid color. [Obs.]

evanish.c: Evanish E*van"ish (?), v. i. [Pref. e- + vanish: cf. L. evanescere. See Evanesce, vanish.] To vanish.

evanishment.c: Evanishment E*van"ish*ment (?), n. A vanishing; disappearance. [R.] T. Jefferson.

evaporable.c: Evaporable E*vap"o*ra*ble (?), a. Capable of being converted into vapor, or dissipated by evaporation.

evaporate.c: Evaporate E*vap"o*rate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Evaporated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Evaporating (?).] [L. evaporatus, p. p. of evaporare; e out + vapor steam or vapor. See Vapor.] 1. To pass off in vapor, as a fluid; to escape and be dissipated, either in visible vapor, or in particles too minute to be visible.
Evaporate E*vap"o*rate, v. t. 1. To convert from a liquid or solid state into vapor (usually) by the agency of heat; to dissipate in vapor or fumes.
Evaporate E*vap"o*rate (?), a. [L. evaporatus, p. p.] Dispersed in vapors. Thomson.

evaporation.c: Evaporation E*vap`o*ra"tion (?), n. [L. evaporatio: cf. F. évaporation.] 1. The process by which any substance is converted from a liquid state into, and carried off in, vapor; as, the evaporation of water, of ether, of camphor.

evaporative.c: Evaporative E*vap"o*ra*tive (?), a. [L. evaporatius: cf. F. évaporatif.] Pertaining to, or producing, evaporation; as, the evaporative process.

evaporator.c: Evaporator E*vap"o*ra`tor (?), n. 1. An apparatus for condensing vegetable juices, or for drying fruit by heat.

evaporometer.c: Evaporometer E*vap`o*rom"e*ter (?), n. [L. evaporare to evaporate + -meter: cf. F. évapormètre.] (Physics) An instrument for ascertaining the quantity of a fluid evaporated in a given time; an atmometer.

evasible.c: evasible e*va"si*ble (e*vā"sĭ*b'l), a. That may be evaded. [R.]

evasion.c: evasion e*va"sion (e*vā"zhŭn), n. [L. evasio: cf. F. évasion. See Evade.] The act of eluding or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogation; artful means of eluding.

evasive.c: evasive e*va"sive (e*vā"sĭv), a. [Cf. F. évasif. See Evade.] Tending to evade, or marked by evasion; elusive; shuffling; avoiding by artifice.

evectics.c: Evectics E*vec"tics (?), n. [Gr. e'yektiko`s healthy.] The branch of medical science which teaches the method of acquiring a good habit of body. [Obs.]

evection.c: Evection E*vec"tion (?). [L. evectio a going up, fr. evehere to carry out; e out + vehere to carry: cf. F évection.] 1. The act of carrying up or away; exaltation. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

even.c: Even E"ven (ēv"'n) n. [OE. eve, even, efen, æfen. AS. ǣfen; akin to OS. āband, OFries, āvend, D. avond, OHG. āband, Icel. aptan, Sw. afton, Dan. aften; of unknown origin. Cf. Eve, Evening.] Evening. See Eve, n. 1. [Poetic.] Shak.

Even E"ven, a. [AS. efen. efn; akin to OS. eban, D. even, OHG. eban, G. efen, Icel. jafn, Dan. jevn, Sw. jämn, Goth. ibns. Cf. Anent, Ebb.] 1. Level, smooth, or equal in surface; not rough; free from irregularities; hence uniform in rate of motion of action; as, even ground; an even speed; an even course of conduct.
Even E"ven (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Evened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Evening (?)] 1. To make even or level; to level; to lay smooth.
Even E"ven (?), v. i. To be equal. [Obs.] R. Carew.
Even E"ven, adv. [AS. efne. See Even, a., and cf. E'en.] 1. In an equal or precisely similar manner; equally; precisely; just; likewise; as well. “Is it even so?” Shak.

evene.c: Evene E*vene" (?), v. i. [L. evenire. See Event.] To happen. [Obs.] Hewyt.

evener.c: Evener E"ven*er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which makes even.

evenfall.c: Evenfall E"ven*fall` (?), n. Beginning of evening. “At the quiet evenfall.” Tennyson.

evenhanded.c: Evenhanded E"ven*hand`ed, a. Fair or impartial; unbiased. “Evenhanded justice.” Shak. -- E"ven*hand`ed*ly, adv. -- E"ven*hand`ed*ness, n. Froude.

evening.c: Evening E"ven*ing (?), n. [AS. ǣfnung. See even, n., and cf. Eve.] 1. The latter part and close of the day, and the beginning of darkness or night; properly, the decline of the day, or of the sun.

evenly.c: Evenly E"ven*ly (?), adv. With an even, level, or smooth surface; without roughness, elevations, or depression; uniformly; equally; comfortably; impartially; serenely.

evenness.c: Evenness E"ven*ness, n. The state of being ven, level, or disturbed; smoothness; horizontal position; uniformity; impartiality; calmness; equanimity; appropriate place or level; as, evenness of surface, of a fluid at rest, of motion, of dealings, of temper, of condition.

evensong.c: Evensong E"ven*song` (?), n. [AS. ǣfensang.] A song for the evening; the evening service or form of worship (in the Church of England including vespers and compline); also, the time of evensong. Wyclif. Milton.

event.c: Event E*vent" (?), n. [L. eventus, fr. evenire to happen, come out; e out + venire to come. See Come.] 1. That which comes, arrives, or happens; that which falls out; any incident, good or bad. “The events of his early years.” Macaulay.
Event E*vent" (?), v. t. [F. éventer to fan, divulge, LL. eventare to fan, fr., L. e out + ventus wind.] To break forth. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

eventerate.c: Eventerate E*ven"ter*ate (?), v. t. [L. e out + venter the belly: cf. F. éventer.] To rip open; to disembowel. [Obs.] Sir. T. Brown.

eventful.c: Eventful E*vent"ful (?) a. Full of, or rich in, events or incidents; as, an eventful journey; an eventful period of history; an eventful period of life.

eventide.c: Eventide E"ven*tide` (?) n. [AS. ǣfentīd. See Tide.] The time of evening; evening. [Poetic.] Spenser.

eventilate.c: Eventilate E*ven"ti*late (?), v. t. [L. eventilatus, p. p. of eventilare to fan. See Ventilate.] 1. To winnow out; to fan. [Obs.] Cockeram.

eventilation.c: Eventilation E*ven`ti*la"tion (?), n. The act of eventilating; discussion. [Obs.] Bp. Berkely.

eventless.c: Eventless E*vent"less (?), a. Without events; tame; monotonous; marked by nothing unusual; uneventful.

eventognathi.c: Eventognathi ‖Ev`en*tog"na*thi (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Dr. e'y^ well +? within gna`qos the jaw.] (Zoöl.) An order of fishes including a vast number of freshwater species such as the carp, loach, chub, etc.

eventration.c: Eventration E`ven*tra*tion (?), n. [L. e out + venter belly.] (Med.) (a) A tumor containing a large portion of the abdominal viscera, occasioned by relaxation of the walls of the abdomen. (b) A wound, of large extent, in the abdomen, through which the greater part of the intestines protrude. (c) The act of disemboweling.

eventual.c: Eventual E*ven"tu*al (?), a. [Cf. F. éventiel. See Event.] 1. Coming or happening as a consequence or result; consequential. Burke.

eventuality.c: Eventuality E*ven`tu*al"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Eventualities (#). [Cf. F. éventualité.] 1. The coming as a consequence; contingency; also, an event which comes as a consequence.

eventually.c: Eventually E*ven"tu*al*ly (?), adv. In an eventual manner; finally; ultimately.

eventuate.c: Eventuate E*ven"tu*ate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Eventuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Eventuating.] To come out finally or in conclusion; to result; to come to pass.

eventuation.c: Eventuation E*ven`tu*a"tion (?), n. The act of eventuating or happening as a result; the outcome. R. W. Hamilton.

ever.c: Ever Ev"er (?) adv. [OE. ever, æfre, AS. æfre; perh. akin to AS. ā always. Cf. Aye, Age,Evry, Never.] [Sometimes contracted into e'er.] 1. At any time; at any period or point of time.

everglade.c: Everglade Ev`er*glade (?), n. A swamp or low tract of land inundated with water and interspersed with hummocks, or small islands, and patches of high grass; as, the everglades of Florida. [U. S.]

evergreen.c: Evergreen Ev"er*green (?) a. (Bot.) Remaining unwithered through the winter, or retaining unwithered leaves until the leaves of the next year are expanded, as pines cedars, hemlocks, and the like.
Evergreen State Evergreen State. Washington; -- a nickname alluding to the abundance of evergreen trees.

everych.c: Everych Everich { Ev"er*ich (?), Ev"er*ych }, a. [OE. see Every.] each one; every one; each of two. See Every. [Obs.] Chaucer.

everychon.c: Everychon Everichon { Ev`er*ich*on", Ev`er*ych*on" } (?), pron. [OE. everich + oon, on, one. See Every, and One.] Every one. [Obs.] Chaucer.

everlasting.c: Everlasting Ever*last"ing (?) a. 1. Lasting or enduring forever; exsisting or continuing without end; immortal; eternal. “The Everlasting God.” Gen. xx1. 33.
Everlasting Ev`er*last"ing, n. 1. Eternal duration, past or future; eternity.

everlastingly.c: Everlastingly Ev`er*last"ing*ly, adv. In an everlasting manner.

everlastingness.c: Everlastingness Ev`er*last"ing*ness, n. The state of being everlasting; endless duration; indefinite duration.

everliving.c: Everliving Ev`er*liv"ing (?), a. 1. Living always; immoral; eternal; as, the everliving God.

evermore.c: Evermore Ev`er*more" (?), adv. During eternity; always; forever; for an indefinite period; at all times; -- often used substantively with for.

evernic.c: Evernic E*ver"nic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to Evernia, a genus of lichens; as, evernic acid.

everse.c: Everse E*verse" (?), v. t. [L. eversus, p. p. of evertere to turn out, overthrow; e out + vertere to turn. Cf. Evert.] To overthrow or subvert. [Obs.] Glanvill.

eversion.c: Eversion E*ver"sion (?), n. [L. eversio: cf. F. éversion.] 1. The act of eversing; destruction. Jer. Taylor.

eversive.c: Eversive E*ver"sive (?), a. Tending to evert or overthrow; subversive; with of.

evert.c: Evert E*vert" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Everted; p. pr. & vb. n. Everting.] [L. evertere. See Everse.] 1. To overthrow; to subvert. [R.] Ayliffe.

every.c: Every Ev"er*y (?), a. & a. pron. [OE. everich, everilk; AS. ǣfre ever + ælc each. See Ever, each.] 1. All the parts which compose a whole collection or aggregate number, considered in their individuality, all taken separately one by one, out of an indefinite number.

everyday.c: Everyday Ev"er*y*day` (?), a. Used or fit for every day; common; usual; as, an everyday suit of clothes.

everyone.c: Everyone Ev"er*y*one` (?), n. [OE. everychon.] Everybody; -- commonly separated, every one.

everything.c: Everything Ev"er*y*thing` (?), n. Whatever pertains to the subject under consideration; all things.

everywhen.c: Everywhen Ev"er*y*when` (?), adv. At any or all times; every instant. [R.] “Eternal law is silently present everywhere and everywhen.” Carlyle.

everywhere.c: Everywhere Ev"er*y*where` (?), adv. In every place; in all places; hence, in every part; thoroughly; altogether.

evestigate.c: Evestigate E*ves"ti*gate (?), v. t. [L. evestigatus traced out; e out + vestigatus, p. p. of vestigare. See Vestigate.] To investigate. [Obs.] Bailey.

evet.c: Evet Ev"et (?), n. [See Eft, n.] (Zoöl.) The common newt or eft. In America often applied to several species of aquatic salamanders. [Written also evat.]

evibrate.c: Evibrate E*vi"brate (?), v. t. & i. [L. evibrare. See Vibrate.] To vibrate. [Obs.] Cockeram.

evict.c: Evict E*vict" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Evicted; p. pr. & vb. n. Evicting.] [L. evictus, p. p. of evincere to overcome completely, evict. See Evince.] 1. (Law) To dispossess by a judicial process; to dispossess by paramount right or claim of such right; to eject; to oust.

eviction.c: Eviction E*vic"tion (?), n. [L. evictio: cf. F. éviction.] 1. The act or process of evicting; or state of being evicted; the recovery of lands, tenements, etc., from another's possession by due course of law; dispossession by paramount title or claim of such title; ejectment; ouster.

evidence.c: Evidence Ev"i*dence (?), n. [F. évidence, L. Evidentia. See Evident.] 1. That which makes evident or manifest; that which furnishes, or tends to furnish, proof; any mode of proof; the ground of belief or judgement; as, the evidence of our senses; evidence of the truth or falsehood of a statement.
Evidence Ev"i*dence, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Evidenced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Evidencing (?).] To render evident or clear; to prove; to evince; as, to evidence a fact, or the guilt of an offender. Milton.

evidencer.c: Evidencer Ev"i*den*cer (?), n. One who gives evidence.

evident.c: Evident Ev"i*dent (?), a. [F. évinent, l. evidens, -entis; e out + videns, p. pr. of videre to see. See Vision.] Clear to the vision; especially, clear to the understanding, and satisfactory to the judgment; as, the figure or color of a body is evident to the senses; the guilt of an offender can not always be made evident.

evidential.c: Evidential Ev`i*den"tial (?), a. Relating to, or affording, evidence; indicative; especially, relating to the evidences of Christianity. Bp. Fleetwood. “Evidential tracks.” Earle.. -- Ev`i*den"tial*ly, adv.

evidentiary.c: Evidentiary Ev`i*den"ti*a*ry (?), a. Furnishing evidence; asserting; proving; evidential.

evidently.c: Evidently Ev"i*dent*ly (?), adv. In an evident manner; clearly; plainly.

evidentness.c: Evidentness Ev"i*dent*ness, n. State of being evident.

evigilation.c: Evigilation E*vig`i*la"tion (?), n. [L. evigilatio; e out + vigilare to be awake. See Vigilant.] A waking up or awakening. [Obs.]

evil.c: Evil E*vil (ē"v'l) a. [OE. evel, evil, ifel, uvel, AS. yfel; akin to OFries, evel, D. euvel, OS. & OHG. ubil, G. übel, Goth. ubils, and perh. to E. over.] 1. Having qualities tending to injury and mischief; having a nature or properties which tend to badness; mischievous; not good; worthless or deleterious; poor; as, an evil beast; and evil plant; an evil crop.

Evil E"vil (ē"v'l) n. 1. Anything which impairs the happiness of a being or deprives a being of any good; anything which causes suffering of any kind to sentient beings; injury; mischief; harm; -- opposed to good.
Evil E"vil, adv. In an evil manner; not well; ill; badly; unhappily; injuriously; unkindly. Shak.
Evil eye E"vil eye` (?). See Evil eye under Evil, a.

evileyed.c: Evil-eyed E"vil-eyed (?) a. Possessed of the supposed evil eye; also, looking with envy, jealousy, or bad design; malicious. Shak.

evilfavored.c: Evil-favored E"vil-fa`vored (?), a. Having a bad countenance or appearance; ill-favored; blemished; deformed. Bacon.

evilly.c: Evilly E"vil*ly (?), adv. In an evil manner; not well; ill. [Obs.] “Good deeds evilly bestowed.” Shak.

evilminded.c: Evil-minded E"vil-mind`ed (?), a. Having evil dispositions or intentions; disposed to mischief or sin; malicious; malignant; wicked. -- E"vil-mind`ed*ness, n.

evilness.c: Evilness E"vil*ness, n. The condition or quality of being evil; badness; viciousness; malignity; vileness; as, evilness of heart; the evilness of sin.

evince.c: Evince E*vince" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Evinced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Evincing (?).] [L. evincere vanquish completely, prevail, succeed in proving; e out + vincere to vanquish. See Victor, and cf. Evict.] 1. To conquer; to subdue. [Obs.]

evincement.c: Evincement E*vince"ment (?), n. The act of evincing or proving, or the state of being evinced.

evincible.c: Evincible E*vin"ci*ble (?), a. Capable of being proved or clearly brought to light; demonstrable. Sir. M. Hale.

evincive.c: Evincive E*vin"cive (?), a. Tending to prove; having the power to demonstrate; demonstrative; indicative.

evirate.c: Evirate E"vi*rate (?), v. t. [L. eviratus, p. p. of evirare to castrate; e out + vir man.] To emasculate; to dispossess of manhood. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

eviscerate.c: Eviscerate E*vis"cer*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Eviscerated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Eviscerating (?).] [L. evisceratus, p. p. of eviscerare to eviscerate; e out + viscera the bowels. See Viscera.] To take out the entrails of; to disembowel; to gut.

evitable.c: Evitable Ev"i*ta*ble (?), a. [L. evitabilis: cf. F. évitable.] Avoidable. [R.] Hooker.

evitate.c: Evitate Ev"i*tate (?), v. t. [L. evitatus, p. p. of evitare to shun; e out + vitare to shun.] To shun; to avoid. [Obs.] Shak.

evitation.c: Evitation Ev`i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. evitatio.] A shunning; avoidance. [Obs.] Bacon.

evite.c: Evite E*vite" (?), v. t. [Cf. F. éviter. See Evitate.] To shun. [Obs.] Dryton.

eviternal.c: Eviternal Ev`i*ter"nal (?), a. [L. eviternus, aeternus. See Etern.] Eternal; everlasting. [Obs.] -- Ev`i*ter"nal*ly, adv. Bp. Hall.

evocate.c: Evocate Ev"o*cate (?), v. t. [L. evocatus, p. p. of evocare. See Evoke.] To call out or forth; to summon; to evoke. [R.] Stackhouse.

evocation.c: Evocation Ev`o*ca"tion (?), n. [L. evocatio: cf. F. évocation.] The act of calling out or forth. Sir. T. Browne.

evocative.c: Evocative E*vo"ca*tive (?), a. Calling forth; serving to evoke; developing.

evocator.c: Evocator Ev"o*ca`tor (?), n. [L.] One who calls forth. [R.]

evoke.c: Evoke E*voke" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Evoked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Evoking.] [L. evocare; e out + vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, voice: cf. F évoquer. See Voice, and cf. Evocate.] 1. To call out; to summon forth.

evolatical.c: Evolatical Evolatic { Ev`o*lat"ic (?), Ev`o*lat"ic*al (?), } a. [L. evolare to fly away; e out + volare to fly.] Apt to fly away. [Obs. or R.] Blount.

evolation.c: Evolation Ev`o*la"tion (?), n. [L. evolatio.] A flying out or up. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

evolute.c: Evolute Ev"o*lute (?), n. [L. evolutus unrolled, p. p. of evolvere. See Evolve.] (Geom.) A curve from which another curve, called the involute or evolvent, is described by the end of a thread gradually wound upon the former, or unwound from it. See Involute. It is the locus of the centers of all the circles which are osculatory to the given curve or evolvent.

evolutility.c: Evolutility Ev`o*lu*til"i*ty (ĕv`o*lu*tĭl"ĭ*ty̆), n. [See Evolution.] (Biol.) The faculty possessed by all substances capable of self-nourishment of manifesting the nutritive acts by changes of form, of volume, or of structure. Syd. Soc. Lex.

evolution.c: Evolution Ev`o*lu"tion (ĕv`o*lū"shŭn), n. [L. evolutio an unrolling: cf. F. évolution evolution. See Evolve.] 1. The act of unfolding or unrolling; hence, any process of growth or development; as, the evolution of a flower from a bud, or an animal from the egg.

evolutional.c: Evolutional Ev`o*lu"tion*al (?), a. Relating to evolution. “Evolutional changes.” H. Spenser.

evolutionary.c: Evolutionary Ev`o*lu"tion*a*ry (?), a. Relating to evolution; as, evolutionary discussions.

evolutionism.c: Evolutionism Ev`o*lu"tion*ism (?), n. The theory of, or belief in, evolution. See Evolution, 6 and 7.

evolutionist.c: Evolutionist Ev`o*lu"tion*ist (?), n. 1. One skilled in evolutions.

evolve.c: Evolve E*volve" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Evolved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Evolving.] [L. evolvere, evolutum; e out + volvere to roll. See Voluble.] 1. To unfold or unroll; to open and expand; to disentangle and exhibit clearly and satisfactorily; to develop; to derive; to educe.
Evolve E*volve", v. i. To become open, disclosed, or developed; to pass through a process of evolution. Prior.

evolvement.c: Evolvement E*volve"ment (?), n. The act of evolving, or the state of being evolved; evolution.

evolvent.c: Evolvent E*volv"ent (?), n. [L. evolvens, -entis, unrolling, p. pr. of evolvere.] (Geom.) The involute of a curve. See Involute, and Evolute.

evomit.c: Evomit E*vom"it (?), v. t. [L. evomitus, p. p. of evomere to vomit forth; e out + vomere.] To vomit. [Obs.]

evomition.c: Evomition Ev`o*mi"tion (?), n. The act of vomiting. [Obs.] Swift.

evulgate.c: Evulgate E*vul"gate (e*vŭl"gāt) v. t. [L. evulgatus, p. p. of evulgare to publish.] To publish abroad. [Obs.]

evulsion.c: Evulsion E*vul"sion (e*vŭl"shŭn), n. [L. evulsio, fr. evellere, evulsum, to pluck out; e out + vellere to pluck; cf. F. évulsion.] The act of plucking out; a rooting out.

ew.c: Ew Ew (ū), n. [See Yew.] A yew. [Obs.] Chaucer.

ewe.c: Ewe Ewe (ū), n. [AS. eówu; akin to D. ooi, OHG. awi, ouwi, Icel. ær, Goth. awēþi a flock of sheep, awistr a sheepfold, Lith. avis a sheep, L. ovis, Gr. 'o`i:s, Skr. avi. √231.] (Zoöl.) The female of the sheep, and of sheeplike animals.

ewenecked.c: Ewe-necked Ewe"-necked` (ū"nĕkt`), a. Having a neck like a ewe; -- said of horses in which the arch of the neck is deficient, being somewhat hollowed out. Youwatt.

ewer.c: Ewer Ew"er (ū"ẽr), n. [OF. ewer, euwier, prop. a water carrier, F. évier a washing place, sink, aiguière ewer, L. aquarius, adj., water carrying, n., a water carrier, fr. aqua water; akin to Goth. ahwa water, river, OHG. aha, G. au, aue, meadow. √219. Cf. Aquarium, Aquatic, Island.] A kind of wide-mouthed pitcher or jug; esp., one used to hold water for the toilet.

ewry.c: Ewry Ewery { Ew"er*y (ū"ẽr*y̆), Ew"ry (ū"ry̆) } n. [From Ewer.] An office or place of household service where the ewers were formerly kept. [Enq.] Parker.

ex.c: Ex- Ex- (ĕks). A prefix from the latin preposition, ex, akin to Gr. 'ex or 'ek signifying out of, out, proceeding from. Hence, in composition, it signifies out of, as, in exhale, exclude; off, from, or out, as in exscind; beyond, as, in excess, exceed, excel; and sometimes has a privative sense of without, as in exalbuminous, exsanguinous. In some words, it intensifies the meaning; in others, it has little affect on the signification. It becomes ef- before f, as in effuse. The form e- occurs instead of ex- before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, and v, as in ebullient, emanate, enormous, etc. In words from the French it often appears as es-, sometimes as s- or é-; as, escape, scape, élite. Ex-, prefixed to names implying office, station, condition, denotes that the person formerly held the office, or is out of the office or condition now; as, ex-president, ex-governor, ex-mayor, ex-wife, ex-convict. The Greek form 'ex becomes ex in English, as in exarch; 'ek becomes ec, as in eccentric.
Ex libris ‖Ex` li"bris (?). [L. ex from + libris books.] An inscription, label, or the like, in a book indicating its ownership; esp., a bookplate.
Ex officio ‖Ex` of*fi"ci*o (?); pl. Ex officiis (#). [L.] From office; by virtue, or as a consequence, of an office; officially.
Ex parte ‖Ex` par"te (?). [L. See Ex-, and Part.] Upon or from one side only; one-sided; partial; as, an ex parte statement.

Ex postfacto Ex post facto { ‖Ex" post` fac"to, or ‖Ex" post`fac"to (ĕks" pōst" făk"to) }. [L., from what is done afterwards.] (Law) From or by an after act, or thing done afterward; in consequence of a subsequent act; retrospective.

exacerbate.c: Exacerbate Ex*ac"er*bate (ĕgz*ăs"ẽr*bāt; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exacerbated (ĕgz*ăs"ẽr*bā`tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Exacerbating (ĕgz*ăs"ẽr*bā`tĭng).] [L. exacerbatus, p. p. of exacerbare; ex out (intens.) + acerbare. See Acerbate.] To render more violent or bitter; to irritate; to exasperate; to imbitter, as passions or disease. Brougham.

exacerbation.c: Exacerbation Ex*ac`er*ba"tion (ĕgz*ăs`ẽr*bā"shŭn) n. [Cf. F. exacerbation.] 1. The act of rendering more violent or bitter; the state of being exacerbated or intensified in violence or malignity; as, exacerbation of passion.

exacerbescence.c: Exacerbescence Ex*ac`er*bes"cence (ĕgz*ăs`ẽr*bĕs"seins), n. [L. exacerbescens, -entis, p. pr. of exacerbescere, incho. of exacerbare.] Increase of irritation or violence, particularly the increase of a fever or disease.

exacervation.c: Exacervation Ex*ac`er*va"tion (?), n. [L. exacervare to heap up exceedingly. See Ex-, and Acervate.] The act of heaping up. [Obs.] Bailey.

exacinate.c: Exacinate Ex*ac"i*nate (?), v. t. [L. ex out + acinus kernel.] To remove the kernel form.

exacination.c: Exacination Ex*ac`i*na"tion (?), n. Removal of the kernel.

exact.c: Exact Ex*act" (?), a. [L. exactus precise, accurate, p. p. of exigere to drive out, to demand, enforce, finish, determine, measure; ex out + agere to drive; cf. F. exact. See Agent, Act.] 1. Precisely agreeing with a standard, a fact, or the truth; perfectly conforming; neither exceeding nor falling short in any respect; true; correct; precise; as, the clock keeps exact time; he paid the exact debt; an exact copy of a letter; exact accounts.

Exact Ex*act", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exacted; p. pr. & vb. n. Exacting.] [From L. exactus, p. p. of exigere; or fr. LL. exactare: cf. OF. exacter. See Exact, a.] To demand or require authoritatively or peremptorily, as a right; to enforce the payment of, or a yielding of; to compel to yield or to furnish; hence, to wrest, as a fee or reward when none is due; -- followed by from or of before the one subjected to exaction; as, to exact tribute, fees, obedience, etc., from or of some one.
Exact Ex*act", v. i. To practice exaction. [R.]

exacting.c: Exacting Ex*act"ing, a. Oppressive or unreasonably severe in making demands or requiring the exact fulfillment of obligations; harsh; severe. “A temper so exacting.” T. Arnold -- Ex*act"ing*ly, adv. -- Ex*act"ing*ness, n.

exaction.c: Exaction Ex*ac"tion (?), n. [L. exactio: cf. F. exaction.] 1. The act of demanding with authority, and compelling to pay or yield; compulsion to give or furnish; a levying by force; a driving to compliance; as, the exaction to tribute or of obedience; hence, extortion.

exactitude.c: Exactitude Ex*act"i*tude (?), n. [Cf. F. exactitude.] The quality of being exact; exactness.

exactly.c: Exactly Ex*act"ly, adv. In an exact manner; precisely according to a rule, standard, or fact; accurately; strictly; correctly; nicely. “Exactly wrought.” Shak.

exactness.c: Exactness Ex*act"ness, n. 1. The condition of being exact; accuracy; nicety; precision; regularity; as, exactness of judgement or deportment.

exactor.c: Exactor Ex*act"or (?), n. [L.: cf. F. exacteur.] One who exacts or demands by authority or right; hence, an extortioner; also, one unreasonably severe in injunctions or demands. Jer. Taylor.

exactress.c: Exactress Ex*act"ress (?), n. [Cf. L. exactrix.] A woman who is an exactor. [R.] B. Jonson.

exacuate.c: Exacuate Ex*ac"u*ate (?), v. t. [L. exacure; ex out (intens.) + acuere to make sharp.] To whet or sharpen. [Obs.] B. Jonson. -- Ex*ac`u*a"tion (#), n. [Obs.]

exaeresis.c: Exaeresis ‖Ex*ær"e*sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a taking away.] (Surg.) In old writers, the operations concerned in the removal of parts of the body.

exaggerate.c: Exaggerate Ex*ag"ger*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exaggerated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Exaggerating. ] [L. exaggeratus, p. p. of exaggerare to heap up; ex out + aggerare to heap up, fr. agger heap, aggerere to bring to; ad to + gerere to bear. See Jest. ] 1. To heap up; to accumulate. [Obs.] “Earth exaggerated upon them [oaks and firs].” Sir M. Hale.

exaggerated.c: Exaggerated Ex*ag"ger*a`ted (?), a. Enlarged beyond bounds or the truth. -- Ex*ag"ger*a`ted*ly, adv.

exaggerating.c: Exaggerating Ex*ag"ger*a`ting (?) a. That exaggerates; enlarging beyond bounds. -- Ex*ag"ger*a`ting*ly, adv.

exaggeration.c: Exaggeration Ex*ag`ger*a"tion (?), n. [L. exaggeratio: cf. F. exagération.] 1. The act of heaping or piling up. [Obs.] “Exaggeration of sand.” Sir M. Hale.

exaggerative.c: Exaggerative Ex*ag"ger*a*tive (?), a. Tending to exaggerate; involving exaggeration. “Exaggerative language.” Geddes. “Exaggerative pictures.” W. J. Linton.

exaggerator.c: Exaggerator Ex*ag"ger*a`tor (?), n. [L.] One who exaggerates; one addicted to exaggeration. L. Horner.

exaggeratory.c: Exaggeratory Ex*ag"ger*a*to*ry (?), a. Containing, or tending to, exaggeration; exaggerative. Johnson.

exagitate.c: Exagitate Ex*ag"i*tate (?), v. t. [L. exagitatus, p. p. of exagitare. See Ex-, and Agitate.] 1. To stir up; to agitate. [Obs.] Arbuthnot.

exagitation.c: Exagitation Ex*ag`i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. exagitatio: cf. OF. exagitation.] Agitation. [Obs.] Bailey.

exalbuminous.c: Exalbuminous Ex`al*bu"mi*nous (?), a. [Pref. ex- + albumen.] (Bot.) Having no albumen about the embryo; -- said of certain seeds.

exalt.c: Exalt Ex*alt" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exalted; p. pr. & vb. n. Exalting.] [L. exaltare; ex out (intens.) + altare to make high, altus high: cf.F. exalter. See Altitude.] 1. To raise high; to elevate; to lift up.

exaltate.c: Exaltate Ex"al*tate (?), a. [L. exaltatus, p. p. of exaltare to exalt.] (Astrol.) Exercising its highest influence; -- said of a planet. [Obs.] Chaucer.

exaltation.c: Exaltation Ex`al*ta"tion (?), n. [L. exaltatio: cf. F.exaltation.] 1. The act of exalting or raising high; also, the state of being exalted; elevation.

exalted.c: Exalted Ex*alt"ed (?), a. Raised to lofty height; elevated; extolled; refined; dignified; sublime.

exalter.c: Exalter Ex*alt"er (?), n. One who exalts or raises to dignity.

examen.c: Examen Ex*a"men (?), n. [L., the tongue of a balance, examination; for exagmen, fr. exigere to weigh accurately, to treat: cf. F. examen. See Exact, a.] Examination; inquiry. [R.] “A critical examen of the two pieces.” Cowper.

exametron.c: Exametron Ex*am"e*tron (?), n. [NL. See Hexameter.] An hexameter. [Obs.] Chaucer.

examinable.c: Examinable Ex*am"i*na*ble (?), a. Capable of being examined or inquired into. Bacon.

examinant.c: Examinant Ex*am"i*nant (?), n. [L. examinans, -antis, examining.] 1. One who examines; an examiner. Sir W. Scott.

examinate.c: Examinate Ex*am"i*nate (?), n. [L. examinatus, p. p. of examinare. See Examine. ] A person subjected to examination. [Obs.] Bacon.

examination.c: Examination Ex*am`i*na"tion (?), n. [L. examinatio: cf. F. examination.] 1. The act of examining, or state of being examined; a careful search, investigation, or inquiry; scrutiny by study or experiment.

examinator.c: Examinator Ex*am"i*na`tor (#), n. [L.: cf. F. examinateur.] An examiner. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

examine.c: Examine Ex*am"ine (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Examined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Examining.] [L. examinare, examinatum, fr. examen, examinis: cf. F. examiner. See Examen.] 1. To test by any appropriate method; to inspect carefully with a view to discover the real character or state of; to subject to inquiry or inspection of particulars for the purpose of obtaining a fuller insight into the subject of examination, as a material substance, a fact, a reason, a cause, the truth of a statement; to inquire or search into; to explore; as, to examine a mineral; to examine a ship to know whether she is seaworthy; to examine a proposition, theory, or question.

examiner.c: Examiner Ex*am"in*er (?), n. One who examines, tries, or inspects; one who interrogates; an officer or person charged with the duty of making an examination; as, an examiner of students for a degree; an examiner in chancery, in the patent office, etc.

examinership.c: Examinership Ex*am"in*er*ship, n. The office or rank of an examiner.

examining.c: Examining Ex*am"in*ing, a. Having power to examine; appointed to examine; as, an examining committee.

examplary.c: Examplary Ex"am*pla*ry (?), a. [From Example, cf. Exemplary.] Serving for example or pattern; exemplary. [Obs.] Hooker.

example.c: Example Ex*am"ple (?), n. [A later form for ensample, fr. L. exemplum, orig., what is taken out of a larger quantity, as a sample, from eximere to take out. See Exempt, and cf. Ensample, Sample.] 1. One or a portion taken to show the character or quality of the whole; a sample; a specimen.

Example Ex*am"ple, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exampled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Exampling (?).] To set an example for; to give a precedent for; to exemplify; to give an instance of; to instance. [Obs.] “I may example my digression by some mighty precedent.” Shak.

exampleless.c: Exampleless Ex*am"ple*less (?), a. Without or above example. [R.]

exampler.c: Exampler Ex*am"pler (?), n. [See Exemplar, Example, and cf. Sampler.] A pattern; an exemplar. [Obs.]

exampless.c: Exampless Ex*am"pless (?), a. Exampleless. [Wrongly formed.] B. Jonson.

exanguious.c: Exanguious Ex*an"gui*ous (?), a. Bloodless. [Obs.] See Exsanguious. Sir T. Browne.

exangulous.c: Exangulous Ex*an"gu*lous (?), a. [Pref ex- + angulous.] Having no corners; without angles. [R.]

exanimate.c: Exanimate Ex*an"i*mate (?), a. [L. exanimatus, p. p. of exanimare to deprive of life or spirit; ex out + anima air, breath, life, spirit.] 1. Lifeless; dead. [R.] “Carcasses exanimate.” Spenser.
Exanimate Ex*an"i*mate (?), v. t. To deprive of animation or of life. [Obs.]

exanimation.c: Exanimation Ex*an`i*ma"tion (?), n.[L. exanimatio.] Deprivation of life or of spirits. [R.] Bailey.

exanimous.c: Exanimous Ex*an"i*mous (?), a. [L. exanimus, exanimis; ex out, without + anima life.] Lifeless; dead. [Obs.] Johnson.

exannulate.c: Exannulate Ex*an"nu*late (?), a. [Pref. ex- + annulate.] (Bot.) Having the sporangium destitute of a ring; -- said of certain genera of ferns.

exanthema.c: Exanthema ‖Ex`an*the"ma (?), n.; pl. Exanthemata (#). [L., fr. Gr.?, fr.? to burst forth as flowers, break out, as ulcers;?,?, out + 'anqei^n to bloom, 'a`nqos flower: cf. F. exanthème.] (Med.) An efflorescence or discoloration of the skin; an eruption or breaking out, as in measles, smallpox, scarlatina, and the like diseases; -- sometimes limited to eruptions attended with fever. Dunglison.

exanthematous.c: Exanthematous Exanthematic { Ex*an`the*mat"ic (?), Ex`an*them"a*tous (?), } a. Of, relating to, or characterized by, exanthema; efflorescent; as, an exanthematous eruption.

exanthesis.c: Exanthesis ‖Ex`an*the"sis (?), n. [NL., from Gr.?. See Exanthema. ] (Med.) An eruption of the skin; cutaneous efflorescence.

exantlate.c: Exantlate Ex*ant"late (?), v. t. [L. exantlatus, p. p. of exantlare, exanclare, to endure.] To exhaust or wear out. [Obs.] “Seeds... wearied or exantlated.” Boyle.

exantlation.c: Exantlation Ex`ant*la"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. exantlation.] Act of drawing out; exhaustion. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

exarate.c: Exarate Ex"a*rate (?), v. t. [L. exaratus, p. p. of exarare to plow up, to write; ex out + arare to plow.] To plow up; also, to engrave; to write. [Obs.] Blount.

exaration.c: Exaration Ex`a*ra"tion (?), n. [L. exaratio.] Act of plowing; also, act of writing. [Obs.] Bailey.

exarch.c: Exarch Ex"arch (?), n. [L. exarchus, Gr.?? commander;?,?, out +? to lead, rule: cf. F. exarque.] A viceroy; in Ravenna, the title of the viceroys of the Byzantine emperors; in the Eastern Church, the superior over several monasteries; in the modern Greek Church, a deputy of the patriarch, who visits the clergy, investigates ecclesiastical cases, etc.

exarchate.c: Exarchate Ex*ar"chate (?), n. [LL. exarchatus, fr. L. exarchus: cf. F. exarchat.] The office or the province of an exarch. Jer. Taylor.

exarillate.c: Exarillate Ex*ar"il*late (?), a. [Pref. ex- + arillate.] (Bot.) Having no aril; -- said of certain seeds, or of the plants producing them.

exarticulate.c: Exarticulate Ex`ar*tic"u*late (?), a. [Pref. ex- + articulate.] (Zoöl.) Having but one joint; -- said of certain insects.

exarticulation.c: Exarticulation Ex`ar*tic`u*la"tion (?), n. [Pref. ex- + articulation.] Luxation; the dislocation of a joint. Bailey.

exasperate.c: Exasperate Ex*as"per*ate (?), a. [L. exasperatus, p. p. of exsasperare to roughen, exasperate; ex out (intens.) + asperare to make rough, asper rough. See Asperity.] Exasperated; imbittered. [Obs.] Shak.

Exasperate Ex*as"per*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exsasperated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Exasperating (?).] 1. To irritate in a high degree; to provoke; to enrage; to excite or to inflame the anger of; as, to exasperate a person or his feelings.

exasperater.c: Exasperater Ex*as"per*a`ter (?), n. One who exasperates or inflames anger, enmity, or violence.

exasperation.c: Exasperation Ex*as`per*a"tion (?), n. [L. exasperatio: cf. F. exaspération.] 1. The act of exasperating or the state of being exasperated; irritation; keen or bitter anger.

exaspidean.c: Exaspidean Ex`as*pid"e*an (?), a. [Gr.? out +?,?, a shield.] (Zoöl.) Having the anterior scutes extending around the tarsus on the outer side, leaving the inner side naked; -- said of certain birds.

exaugurate.c: Exaugurate Ex*au"gu*rate (?), v. t. [L. exauguratus, p. p. of exaugurare to profane; ex out + augurari to act as an augur, fr. augur. ] To annul the consecration of; to secularize; to unhellow. [Obs.] Holland.

exauguration.c: Exauguration Ex*au`gu*ra"tion (?), n. [L. exauguratio desecration.] The act of exaugurating; desecration. [Obs.]

exauthorate.c: Exauthorate Ex*au"thor*ate (?), v. t. [L. exauctoratus, p. p. of exauctorare to dismiss; ex out + auctorare to bind to something, to hire, fr. auctor. See Author.] To deprive of authority or office; to depose; to discharge. [Obs.]

exauthoration.c: Exauthoration Ex*au`thor*a"tion (?), n. Deprivation of authority or dignity; degration. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

exauthorize.c: Exauthorize Ex*au"thor*ize (?), v. t. [Pref. ex- + authorize.] To deprive of uthority. [Obs.] Selden.
Exauthorize Ex*au"thor*ize (?), v. t. [Pref. ex- + authorize.] To deprive of authority. [Obs.] Selden.

excalceate.c: Excalceate Ex*cal"ce*ate (?), v. t. [L. excalceatus, p. p. of excalceare to unshoe. See Calceated.] To deprive of shoes. [Obs.] Chambers.

excalceation.c: Excalceation Ex*cal`ce*a"tion (?), n. The act of depriving or divesting of shoes. [Obs.] Chambers.

excalfaction.c: Excalfaction Ex`cal*fac"tion (?), n. [L. excalfactio.] A heating or warming; calefaction. [Obs.] Blount.

excalfactive.c: Excalfactive Ex`cal*fac"tive (?), a. [L. excalfacere to warm; ex out (intens.) + calfacere to warm.] Serving to heat; warming. [Obs.] Cotgrave.

excalfactory.c: Excalfactory Ex`cal*fac"to*ry (?), a. [L. excalfactorius.] Heating; warming. [Obs.] Holland.

excalibur.c: Excalibur Ex*cal"i*bur (?), n. The name of King Arthur's mythical sword. [Written also Excalibar, Excalibor, Escalibar, and Caliburn.] Tennyson.

excambie.c: Excambie Excamb { Ex*camb" (?), Ex*cam"bie (?), } v. t. [LL. excambiare, excambire; L. ex out + cambire. See Change, and cf. Exchange.] (Scots Law) To exchange; -- used with reference to transfers of land.

excambium.c: Excambium Excambion { ‖Ex*cam"bi*on (?), ‖Ex*cam"bi*um (?), } n. [LL. excambium. See Excamb.] (Scots Law) Exchange; barter; -- used commonly of lands.

excandescence.c: Excandescence Ex`can*des"cence (?), n. [L. excandescentia.] 1. A growing hot; a white or glowing heat; incandescence. [R.]

excandescent.c: Excandescent Ex`can*des"cent (?), a. [L. excandescens, p. pr. of excandescere to take fire, glow; ex out (intens.) + candescere to begin to glisten or glow, fr. candere. See Candid.] White or glowing with heat. [R.] Ure.

excantation.c: Excantation Ex`can*ta"tion (?), n. [L. excantare to charm out. See Ex?, and Chant.] Disenchantment by a countercharm. [Obs.] Gayton.

excarnate.c: Excarnate Ex*car"nate (?), v. t. [LL. excarnatus, p. p. of excarnare; L. ex out + caro, carnis, flesh.] To deprive or clear of flesh. Grew.

excarnation.c: Excarnation Ex`car*na"tion (?), n. The act of depriving or divesting of flesh; excarnification; -- opposed to incarnation.

excarnificate.c: Excarnificate Ex*car"ni*fi*cate (?), v. t. [L. ex out + LL. carnificatus, p. p. carnificare to carnify; cf. L. excarnificare to tear to pieces, torment. See Carnify.] To clear of flesh; to excarnate. Dr. H. More.

excarnification.c: Excarnification Ex*car`ni*fi*ca"tion (?), n. The act of excarnificating or of depriving of flesh; excarnation. Johnson.

excavate.c: Excavate Ex"ca*vate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excavated(?); p. pr. & vb. n. Excavating(?).] [L. excavatus, p. p. of excavare to excavate; ex out + cavare to make hollow, cavus hollow. See Cave.] 1. To hollow out; to form cavity or hole in; to make hollow by cutting, scooping, or digging; as, to excavate a ball; to excavate the earth.

excavation.c: Excavation Ex`ca*va"tion (?), n. [L. excavatio: cf. F. excavation.] 1. The act of excavating, or of making hollow, by cutting, scooping, or digging out a part of a solid mass.

excavator.c: Excavator Ex"ca*va`tor (?), n. One who, or that which, excavates or hollows out; a machine, as a dredging machine, or a tool, for excavating.

excave.c: Excave Ex*cave" (?), v. t. [L. excavare.] To excavate. [Obs.] Cockeram.

excecate.c: Excecate Ex*ce"cate (?), v. t. [L. excaecatus, p. p. of excaecare to blind; ex (intens.) + caecare to blind, caecus blind.] To blind. [Obs.] Cockeram.

excecation.c: Excecation Ex`ce*ca"tion (?), n. The act of making blind. [Obs.] Bp. Richardson.

excedent.c: Excedent Ex*ced"ent (?), n. [L. excedens, -entis, p. pr. of excedere. See Exceed, v. t.] Excess. [R.]

exceed.c: Exceed Ex*ceed" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exceeded; p. pr. & vb. n. Exceeding.] [L. excedere, excessum, to go away or beyond; ex out + cedere to go, to pass: cf. F. excéder. See Cede.] To go beyond; to proceed beyond the given or supposed limit or measure of; to outgo; to surpass; -- used both in a good and a bad sense; as, one man exceeds another in bulk, stature, weight, power, skill, etc.; one offender exceeds another in villainy; his rank exceeds yours.
Exceed Ex*ceed", v. i. 1. To go too far; to pass the proper bounds or measure. “In our reverence to whom, we can not possibly exceed.” Jer. Taylor.

exceedable.c: Exceedable Ex*ceed"a*ble (?), a. Capable of exceeding or surpassing. [Obs.] Sherwood.

exceeder.c: Exceeder Ex*ceed"er (?), n. One who exceeds. Bp. Montagu.

exceeding.c: Exceeding Ex*ceed"ing, a. More than usual; extraordinary; more than sufficient; measureless. “The exceeding riches of his grace.” Eph. ii. 7. -- Ex*ceed"ing*ness, n. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.
Exceeding Ex*ceed"ing, adv. In a very great degree; extremely; exceedingly. [Archaic. It is not joined to verbs.] “The voice exceeding loud.” Keble.

exceedingly.c: Exceedingly Ex*ceed"ing*ly (?), adv. To a very great degree; beyond what is usual; surpassingly. It signifies more than very.

excel.c: Excel Ex*cel" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excelled(?); p. pr. & vb. n. Excelling.] [L. excellere, excelsum; ex out + a root found in culmen height, top; cf. F. exceller. See Culminate, Column.] 1. To go beyond or surpass in good qualities or laudable deeds; to outdo or outgo, in a good sense.
Excel Ex*cel", v. i. To surpass others in good qualities, laudable actions, or acquirements; to be distinguished by superiority; as, to excel in mathematics, or classics.

excellence.c: Excellence Ex"cel*lence (?), n. [F. excellence, L. excellentia.] 1. The quality of being excellent; state of possessing good qualities in an eminent degree; exalted merit; superiority in virtue.

excellency.c: Excellency Ex"cel*len*cy (?), n.; pl. Excellencies (?). 1. Excellence; virtue; dignity; worth; superiority.

excellent.c: Excellent Ex"cel*lent (?), a. [F. excellent, L. excellens, -entis, p. pr. of excellere. See Excel.] 1. Excelling; surpassing others in some good quality or the sum of qualities; of great worth; eminent, in a good sense; superior; as, an excellent man, artist, citizen, husband, discourse, book, song, etc.; excellent breeding, principles, aims, action.
Excellent Ex"cel*lent, adv. Excellently; eminently; exceedingly. [Obs.] “This comes off well and excellent.” Shak.

excellently.c: Excellently Ex"cel*lent*ly, adv. 1. In an excellent manner; well in a high degree.

excelsior.c: Excelsior ‖Ex*cel"si*or, a. [L., compar. of excelsus elevated, lofty, p. p. of excellere. See Excel, v. t.] More lofty; still higher; ever upward.
Excelsior Ex*cel"si*or, n. A kind of stuffing for upholstered furniture, mattresses, etc., in which curled shreds of wood are substituted for curled hair.

excentral.c: Excentral Ex*cen"tral (?), a. [Pref. ex- + central.] (Bot.) Out of the center.

excentrical.c: Excentrical Excentric { Ex*cen"tric (?), Ex*cen"tric*al (?), } a. 1. Same as Eccentric, Eccentrical.

except.c: Except Ex*cept" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excepted; p. pr. & vb. n. Excepting.] [L. exceptus, p. p. of excipere to take or draw out, to except; ex out + capere to take: cf. F. excepter. See Capable.] 1. To take or leave out (anything) from a number or a whole as not belonging to it; to exclude; to omit.
Except Ex*cept", v. i. To take exception; to object; -- usually followed by to, sometimes by against; as, to except to a witness or his testimony.
Except Ex*cept", prep. [Originally past participle, or verb in the imperative mode.] With exclusion of; leaving or left out; excepting.
Except Ex*cept" (ĕk*sĕpt"), conj. Unless; if it be not so that.

excepting.c: Excepting Ex*cept"ing, prep. & conj., but properly a participle. With rejection or exception of; excluding; except. “Excepting your worship's presence.” Shak.

exception.c: Exception Ex*cep"tion (ĕk*sĕp"shŭn), n. [L. exceptio: cf. F. exception.] 1. The act of excepting or excluding; exclusion; restriction by taking out something which would otherwise be included, as in a class, statement, rule.

exceptionable.c: Exceptionable Ex*cep"tion*a*ble (ĕk*sĕp"shŭn*ȧ*b'l), a. Liable to exception or objection; objectionable. -- Ex*cep"tion*a*ble*ness, n.

exceptional.c: Exceptional Ex*cep"tion*al (?), a. [Cf. F. exceptionnel.] Forming an exception; not ordinary; uncommon; rare; hence, better than the average; superior. Lyell.

exceptioner.c: Exceptioner Ex*cep"tion*er (?), n. One who takes exceptions or makes objections. [Obs.] Milton.

exceptious.c: Exceptious Ex*cep"tious (?), a. Disposed or apt to take exceptions, or to object; captious. [Obs.]

exceptive.c: Exceptive Ex*cept"ive (?), a. That excepts; including an exception; as, an exceptive proposition. I. Watts.

exceptor.c: Exceptor Ex*cept"or (?), n. [L., a scribe.] One who takes exceptions. T. Burnet.

excerebration.c: Excerebration Ex*cer`e*bra"tion (?), n. [L. excerebratus deprived of brains; ex out + cerebrum brain.] The act of removing or beating out the brains.

excern.c: Excern Ex*cern" (?), v. t. [L. excernere. See Excrete.] To excrete; to throw off through the pores; as, fluids are excerned in perspiration. [R.] Bacon.

excernent.c: Excernent Ex*cern"ent (?), a. [See Excern.] (Physiol.) Connected with, or pertaining to, excretion.

excerp.c: Excerp Ex*cerp" (?), v. t. [L. excerpere, excerptum; ex out + carpere to pick, gather. See Harvest, and cf. Scarce, a.] To pick out. [Obs.] Hales.

excerpt.c: Excerpt Ex*cerpt" (ĕk*sẽrpt"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excerpted; p. pr. & vb. n. Excerpting.] [From L. excerptus, p. p. See Excerp.] To select; to extract; to cite; to quote.
Excerpt Ex"cerpt (ĕk"sẽrpt; 277), n. An extract; a passage selected or copied from a book or record.

excerption.c: Excerption ‖Ex*cerp"tion (?), n. [L. excerptio.] 1. The act of excerpting or selecting. [R.]

excerptive.c: Excerptive Ex*cerp"tive (?), a. That excerpts, selects, or chooses. D. L. Mackenzie.

excerptor.c: Excerptor Ex*cerp"tor (?), n. One who makes excerpts; a picker; a culler.

excess.c: Excess Ex*cess" (?), n. [OE. exces, excess, ecstasy, L. excessus a going out, loss of self-possession, fr. excedere, excessum, to go out, go beyond: cf. F. excès. See Exceed.] 1. The state of surpassing or going beyond limits; the being of a measure beyond sufficiency, necessity, or duty; that which exceeds what is usual or proper; immoderateness; superfluity; superabundance; extravagance; as, an excess of provisions or of light.

excessive.c: Excessive Ex*cess"ive (ĕk*sĕs"ĭv), a. [Cf. F. excessif.] Characterized by, or exhibiting, excess; overmuch.

exchange.c: exchange ex*change" (ĕks*chānj"), n. [OE. eschange, eschaunge, OF. eschange, fr. eschangier, F. échanger, to exchange; pref. ex- out + F. changer. See Change, and cf. Excamb.] 1. The act of giving or taking one thing in return for another which is regarded as an equivalent; as, an exchange of cattle for grain.

Exchange Ex*change", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exchanged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Exchanging (?).] [Cf.OF. eschangier, F. échanger. See Exchange, n.] 1. To part with give, or transfer to another in consideration of something received as an equivalent; -- usually followed by for before the thing received.
Exchange Ex*change", v. i. To be changed or received in exchange for; to pass in exchange; as, dollar exchanges for ten dimes.
Exchange editor Ex*change" ed"i*tor. An editor who inspects, and culls from, periodicals, or exchanges, for his own publication.

exchangeability.c: Exchangeability Ex*change`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being exchangeable.

exchangeable.c: Exchangeable Ex*change"a*ble (?), a. [Cf.F. échangeable.] 1. Capable of being exchanged; fit or proper to be exchanged.

exchangeably.c: Exchangeably Ex*change"a*bly, adv. By way of exchange.

exchanger.c: Exchanger Ex*chan"ger (?), n. One who exchanges; one who practices exchange. Matt. xxv. 27.

exchequer.c: Exchequer Ex*cheq"uer (?), n. [OE. escheker, OF. eichekier, fr. LL. scaccarium. See Checker, Chess, Check.] 1. One of the superior courts of law; -- so called from a checkered cloth, which covers, or formerly covered, the table. [Eng.]
Exchequer Ex*cheq"uer (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Exchequered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Exchequering.] To institute a process against (any one) in the Court of Exchequer.

excide.c: Excide Ex*cide" (?), v. t. [L. excidere, excisum; ex out + caedere to cut. See Concise, and cf. Excise to cut off.] To cut off. [R.]

excipient.c: Excipient Ex*cip"i*ent (?), a. [L. excipients, -entis, p. pr. of exipere. See Except, v. t.] Taking an exception.

excipulum.c: Excipulum Exciple { Ex"ci*ple (?), ‖Ex*cip"u*lum (?), } n. [NL. excipulum, fr. L. excipere. See Except.] (Bot.) The outer part of the fructification of most lichens.

excisable.c: Excisable Ex*cis"a*ble (?), a. Liable or subject to excise; as, tobacco in an excisable commodity.

excise.c: Excise Ex*cise" (?), n. [Apparently fr. L. excisum cut off, fr. excidere to cut out or off; ex out, off + caedere to cut; or, as the word was formerly written accise, fr. F. accise, LL. accisia, as if fr. L. accidere, accisum, to cut into; ad + caedere to cut; but prob. transformed fr. OF. assise, LL. assisa, assisia, assize. See Assize, Concise.] 1. In inland duty or impost operating as an indirect tax on the consumer, levied upon certain specified articles, as, tobacco, ale, spirits, etc., grown or manufactured in the country. It is also levied to pursue certain trades and deal in certain commodities. Certain direct taxes (as, in England, those on carriages, servants, plate, armorial bearings, etc.), are included in the excise. Often used adjectively; as, excise duties; excise law; excise system.
Excise Ex*cise", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excised (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Excising.] 1. To lay or impose an excise upon.
Excise Ex*cise", v. t. [See Excide.] To cut out or off; to separate and remove; as, to excise a tumor.

exciseman.c: Exciseman Ex*cise"man (?), n.; pl. Excisemen (?). An officer who inspects and rates articles liable to excise duty. Macaulay.

excision.c: Excision Ex*ci"sion (?), n. [L. excisio: cf. F. excision. See Excide.] 1. The act of excising or cutting out or off; extirpation; destruction.

excitability.c: Excitability Ex*cit"a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. excitabilité.] 1. The quality of being readily excited; proneness to be affected by exciting causes.

excitable.c: Excitable Ex*cit"a*ble (?), a. [L. excitabilis inciting: cf. F. excitable.] Capable of being excited, or roused into action; susceptible of excitement; easily stirred up, or stimulated.

excitant.c: Excitant Ex*cit"ant (?), a. [L. excitans, -antis, p. pr. of excitare: cf. F. excitant.] Tending to excite; exciting.
Excitant Ex*cit"ant, n. (Physiol.) An agent or influence which arouses vital activity, or produces increased action, in a living organism or in any of its tissues or parts; a stimulant.

excitate.c: Excitate Ex*cit"ate (?), v. t. [L. excitatus, p. p. of excitare. See Excite.] To excite. [Obs.] Bacon.

excitation.c: Excitation Ex`ci*ta"tion (?) n. [L. excitatio: cf. F. excitation.] 1. The act of exciting or putting in motion; the act of rousing up or awakening. Bacon.

excitative.c: Excitative Ex*cit"a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. excitatif.] Having power to excite; tending or serving to excite; excitatory. Barrow.

excitator.c: Excitator Ex"ci*ta`tor (?), n. [L., one who rouses.] (Elec.) A kind of discarder.

excitatory.c: Excitatory Ex*cit"a*to*ry (?), a. [Cf. F. excitatoire.] Tending to excite; containing excitement; excitative.

excite.c: Excite Ex*cite" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excited; p. pr. & vb. n. exciting.] [L. excitare; ex out + citare to move rapidly, to rouse: cf. OF. esciter, exciter, F. exciter. See Cite.] 1. To call to activity in any way; to rouse to feeling; to kindle to passionate emotion; to stir up to combined or general activity; as, to excite a person, the spirits, the passions; to excite a mutiny or insurrection; to excite heat by friction.

exciteful.c: Exciteful Ex*cite"ful (?), n. Full of exciting qualities; as, an exciteful story; exciteful players. Chapman.

excitement.c: Excitement Ex*cite"ment (?) n. [Cf. OF. excitement, escitement.] 1. The act of exciting, or the state of being roused into action, or of having increased action; impulsion; agitation; as, an excitement of the people.

exciter.c: Exciter Ex*cit"er (?), n. One who, or that which, excites.

exciting.c: Exciting Ex*cit"ing, a. Calling or rousing into action; producing excitement; as, exciting events; an exciting story. -- Ex*cit"ing*ly, adv.

excitive.c: Excitive Ex*cit"ive (?), a. Serving or tending to excite; excitative. [R.] Bamfield.
Excitive Ex*cit"ive, n. That which excites; an excitant. [R.]

excitomotion.c: Excito-motion Ex*ci`to-mo"tion (?), n. (Physiol.) Motion excited by reflex nerves. See Excito-motory.

excitomotor.c: Excito-motor Ex*ci`to-mo"tor (?), a. (Physiol.) Excito-motory; as, excito-motor power or causes.

excitomotory.c: Excito-motory Ex*ci`to-mo"to*ry (?), a. (Physiol.) Exciting motion; -- said of that portion of the nervous system concerned in reflex actions, by which impressions are transmitted to a nerve center and then reflected back so as to produce muscular contraction without sensation or volition.

excitonutrient.c: Excito-nutrient Ex*ci`to-nu"tri*ent (?), a. (Physiol.) Exciting nutrition; said of the reflex influence by which the nutritional processes are either excited or modified.

excitosecretory.c: Excito-secretory Ex*ci`to-se*cre"to*ry (?), a. (Physiol.) Exciting secretion; -- said of the influence exerted by reflex action on the function of secretion, by which the various glands are excited to action.

exclaim.c: Exclaim Ex*claim" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Exclaimed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Exclaiming.] [L. exclamare, exclamatum; ex + clamare to cry out; cf. OF. exclamer. See Clam.] To cry out from earnestness or passion; to utter with vehemence; to call out or declare loudly; to protest vehemently; to vociferate; to shout; as, to exclaim against oppression with wonder or astonishment; “The field is won!” he exclaimed.

exclamation.c: Exclamation Ex`cla*ma"tion (?), n. [L. exclamatio: cf. F. exclamation.] 1. A loud calling or crying out; outcry; loud or emphatic utterance; vehement vociferation; clamor; that which is cried out, as an expression of feeling; sudden expression of sound or words indicative of emotion, as in surprise, pain, grief, joy, anger, etc.

exclamative.c: Exclamative Ex*clam"a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. exclamatif.] Exclamatory. Earle. -- Ex*clam"a*tive*ly, adv.

exclamatory.c: Exclamatory Ex*clam"a*to*ry (?), a. Containing, expressing, or using exclamation; as, an exclamatory phrase or speaker. South. -- Ex*clam"a*to*ti*ly (#), adv.

exclave.c: Exclave Ex*clave" (?), n. [Formed fr. enclave by substitution of ex- for en-] A portion of a country which is separated from the main part and surrounded by politically alien territory. [Recent.]

exclude.c: Exclude Ex*clude" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excluded; p. pr. & vb. n. Excluding.] [L. excludere, exclusum; ex out + claudere to shut. See Close.] 1. To shut out; to hinder from entrance or admission; to debar from participation or enjoyment; to deprive of; to except; -- the opposite to admit; as, to exclude a crowd from a room or house; to exclude the light; to exclude one nation from the ports of another; to exclude a taxpayer from the privilege of voting.

exclusion.c: Exclusion Ex*clu"sion (?), n. [L. exclusio: cf. F. exclusion. See Exclude.] 1. The act of excluding, or of shutting out, whether by thrusting out or by preventing admission; a debarring; rejection; prohibition; the state of being excluded.

exclusionary.c: Exclusionary Ex*clu"sion*a*ry (?), a. Tending to exclude; causing exclusion; exclusive.

exclusionism.c: Exclusionism Ex*clu"sion*ism (?), n. The character, manner, or principles of an exclusionist.

exclusionist.c: Exclusionist Ex*clu"sion*ist, n. One who would exclude another from some right or privilege; esp., one of the anti-popish politicians of the time of Charles II.

exclusive.c: Exclusive Ex*clu"sive (?) a. [Cf. F. exclusif.] 1. Having the power of preventing entrance; debarring from participation or enjoyment; possessed and enjoyed to the exclusion of others; as, exclusive bars; exclusive privilege; exclusive circles of society.
Exclusive Ex*clu"sive, n. One of a coterie who exclude others; one who from real of affected fastidiousness limits his acquaintance to a select few.

exclusiveness.c: Exclusiveness Ex*clu"sive*ness, n. Quality of being exclusive.

exclusivism.c: Exclusivism Ex*clu"siv*ism (?), n. The act or practice of excluding being exclusive; exclusiveness.

exclusivist.c: Exclusivist Ex*clu"siv*ist, n. One who favor or practices any from of exclusiveness or exclusivism.

exclusory.c: Exclusory Ex*clu"so*ry (?), a. [L. exclusorius.] Able to exclude; excluding; serving to exclude.

excoct.c: Excoct Ex*coct" (?) v. t. [L. excoctus, p. p. of excoquere to excoct. See 3d Cook.] To boil out; to produce by boiling. [Obs.] Bacon.

excoction.c: Excoction Ex*coc"tion (?). [L. excoctio.] The act of excocting or boiling out. [Obs.] Bacon.

excogitate.c: Excogitate Ex*cog"i*tate (?) v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excogitated (#); p. pr. & vb. n.. Excogitating.] [L. excogitatus, p. p. of excogitare to excogitate; ex out + cogitare to think. See Cogitate.] To think out; to find out or discover by thinking; to devise; to contrive. “Excogitate strange arts.” Stirling.
Excogitate Ex*cog"i*tate, v. i. To cogitate. [R.] Bacon.

excogitation.c: Excogitation Ex*cog`i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. excogitatio: cf. F. excogitation.] The act of excogitating; a devising in the thoughts; invention; contrivance.

excommune.c: Excommune Ex`com*mune" (?) v. t. [Cf. F. excommuier. See Excommunicate.] To exclude from participation in; to excommunicate. [Obs.]

excommunicable.c: Excommunicable Ex`com*mu"ni*ca*ble (?), a. [See Excommunicate.] Liable or deserving to be excommunicated; making excommunication possible or proper. “Persons excommunicable.” Bp. Hall.

excommunicant.c: Excommunicant Ex`com*mu"ni*cant (?), n. One who has been excommunicated.

excommunicate.c: Excommunicate Ex"com*mu"ni*cate (?), a. [L. excommunicatus, p. p. of communicare to excommunicate; ex out + communicare. See Communicate.] Excommunicated; interdicted from the rites of the church. -- n. One excommunicated.

Excommunicate Ex`com*mu"ni*cate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Excommunicated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Excommunicating (?).] 1. To put out of communion; especially, to cut off, or shut out, from communion with the church, by an ecclesiastical sentence.

excommunication.c: Excommunication Ex`com*mu`ni*ca"tion (?), n. [L. excommunicatio: cf.
